sources.news_title: Pete Hegseth Is About to Get His Ass Kicked
Pete Hegseth Is About to Get His Ass Kicked
sources.text:
It’s been one week since Election Day, and Pete Hegseth is facing a different kind of war. Trump administration officials tell Inner Loop they knew the defense secretary would face a slew of investigations in the next Congress. Now, they think he is on track to be Democrats’ number one target—and Democrats are already planning to make their case as airtight as possible.
“Hegseth is now a passenger in whatever comes next,” says one source close to President Donald Trump. “And all the outcomes are potentially damaging.”
House Democratic aides tell Inner Loop that Democrats are likely to pursue an impeachment inquiry against Hegseth, and also work to narrow the charges against him to issues that Senate Republicans have also complained about, in an effort to attract their support.
Hegseth, who has championed the deeply unpopular and costly Iran war, has spent much of his controversial tenure upending various internal processes at the Defense Department, including firing generals and blocking promotions using criteria that disproportionately affected women and people of color. He has also become known for his notorious role in Signalgate and for military strikes against purported drug traffickers in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean.
Some of those topics have also previously been the subject of complaints from Republicans. The Senate Armed Services Committee chair Roger Wicker criticized Hegseth for the flag officer cuts and once reportedly threatened to block a Trump nominee unless the Pentagon handed over documents.
Last night, House Republicans managed to table an impeachment effort targeting Hegseth that was brought about by Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky. Massie, among other issues, accused Hegseth of waging the Iran war without approval from Congress and directing “extrajudicial killings.” But even though the effort failed, officials privately believe it is practically inevitable that Hegseth will be impeached again and face a Senate trial next year.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries suggested as much after the impeachment failed to progress, telling reporters he would consult with his top members on next steps.
“We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time, and that’ll be led by Adam Smith, soon to be chair of the Armed Services Committee, and Jamie Raskin, next chair of the judiciary,” Jeffries said.
Trump officials tell Inner Loop they still don’t expect Democrats to get enough GOP support to remove Hegseth—but they can’t shield him from wall-to-wall coverage of a trial.
The impeachment articles brought by Massie were seen by some Republicans as overly broad, which made officials think they could spare Hegseth an impeachment trial by having Senate majority leader John Thune dismiss all the charges in a straight-line vote.
But with Democrats taking over the Senate next year, that option is off the table.
It’s not going to be entirely simple, however. Hegseth’s biggest Republican detractors are all leaving Congress at the end of the year. Maine senator Susan Collins, North Carolina senator Thom Tillis, and Louisiana senator Bill Cassidy all lost reelection this midterm cycle, while Iowa senator Joni Ernst and Kentucky senator Mitch McConnell are stepping down after finishing their terms.
But even with his biggest detractors set to retire, at least five other Republican senators have complained about Hegseth’s performance—getting Democrats closer to the 67 votes needed to convict—like Wicker, South Dakota senator Mike Rounds, Kentucky senator Rand Paul, Alaska senator Lisa Murkowski, and Indiana senator Todd Young.
This is why the focus of the Democratic impeachment inquiry is going to have to be specific, and geared to Republican interests, so as to be unassailable.
Hegseth, for what it’s worth, doesn’t seem to want to go anywhere without a fight. In a televised appearance at the Pentagon earlier this week, Hegseth responded to a question about Vice President JD Vance blaming the Republican midterm losses on Iran, and said Vance was a “critical member of the team” and the war effort.
Hegseth then added, “I agree with what the president said, when he said ‘Hey, if I had to do this all over again, would we do it again? Absolutely.’”
Tech (Heart) Troubles
House Republicans are poised to open an investigation into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's interactions with alleged Chinese spy and one-time tech executive Alice Huang, who is not related to the CEO.
The growing push for Congress to stand up its own investigation is set to put Republicans on a collision course with Trump, who has continued to publicly defend the CEO of the world's most valuable chip company.
During a congressional “Gang of Eight” briefing on Monday, officials including director of national intelligence Jay Clayton and CIA director John Ratcliffe gave only the broad brushstrokes of the classified intelligence surrounding Huang’s interactions, which left lawmakers deeply unsatisfied, sources say.
Meeting attendees did not get clear answers as to why there was no defensive briefing provided to Jensen Huang and whether he was initially left off Trump's trip to China this year as a result of the possible national security risk.
On Tuesday, the chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Brian Mast, told reporters he would be open to issuing a subpoena to compel Jensen Huang to provide a briefing behind closed doors if he ignored a request from last week to appear on Capitol Hill.
Mast, together with Rick Crawford, the chair of the House Intelligence Committee, and John Moolenaar, the chair of the China select subcommittee, had asked Jensen Huang to appear before the three panels later this month.
The congressional inquiry follows revelations from The New York Times that secretary of state Marco Rubio drafted a memo for Trump warning that classified intelligence suggested Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security. China has denied any espionage allegations.
This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

sources.news_title: How Pete Hegseth suddenly went from ‘out the door’ to safe as houses
How Pete Hegseth went from ‘out the door’ to safe as houses
sources.text:
How Pete Hegseth suddenly went from ‘out the door’ to safe as houses
Updated ,first published
Washington: A few weeks ago, the conventional wisdom around the corridors of Washington was that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was headed for the exit.
Indeed, speculation raged for months that President Donald Trump wasn’t happy with Hegseth. In particular, a Washington Post story from August reported that Trump and Hegseth had clashed at Camp David about munitions shortages caused by the war in Iran, and why the president had apparently been misled about the problem.
It was the latest in a series of controversies that seemed to pit the Pentagon against the White House. Earlier, reports indicated Hegseth’s department had unilaterally paused weapons shipments to Ukraine and scaled back the US troop presence in Romania.
Moreover, Hegseth clashed with top military personnel and replaced several of them. There was an air of chaos and churn around the defence secretary, and Trump acknowledged receiving complaints.
There were strong parallels with 2006, when Republican president George W. Bush ousted his defence secretary, Donald Rumsfeld, the day after a devastating midterm election when the GOP lost control of both chambers.
Rumsfeld’s resignation also took place amid the increasingly unpopular war in Iraq, which had become the exact kind of quagmire that Rumsfeld famously said: “I don’t do”.
Even though Hegseth was executing Trump’s orders in Iran, he loomed as a potential fall guy for a war that was never popular and grew less so after initial peace plans collapsed.
But the midterm election results – delivering control of both chambers to the Democrats, with large majorities – changed the equation.
The Trump White House is now under siege and preparing to fight. Trump has said so himself, and appointed hardline loyalist Stephen Miller as his chief of staff, replacing the more establishment Republican Susie Wiles.
This is a White House that is going to war, and its instinct is to defend its people. So when Hegseth faced an impeachment push from a Republican congressman, Thomas Massie, he was no longer a liability but a potential victim – and Trump does not want to lose.
“In any normal political environment, getting impeached would be a bad thing for a cabinet member,” said Josh Rogin, security analyst at the Washington Post’s WP Intelligence unit, on CNN this week.
“But in Trump’s mind and in Hegseth’s mind, this is a badge of honour. And what Thomas Massie has done is inadvertently throw Pete Hegseth a lifeline.
“A week ago, we all thought he was on his way out the door. Now he’s got the full backing of the president, and he’s making content off of it.”
The administration managed to keep every House Republican in line to defend Hegseth from impeachment on Tuesday (US time), except for Massie.
The attempt failed after 11 Democrats failed to show up to vote, including former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who returned to San Francisco for a Veterans Day event. Others said they were stuck in traffic after attending an off-site “new member reception”.
While next year’s changing of the guard will mean Democrats can easily impeach Hegseth in the House, they would not have anywhere near the two-thirds majority needed to convict him in the Senate.
As Rogin observed, it allows Hegseth to play the martyr, while Trump can decry the Democrats’ impeachment attempts as lawfare and weaponisation.
In a performance that won praise from the president, Hegseth used a rare Pentagon news conference to link his plight with Trump’s. “They” had impeached Trump twice before, he said. “Now, they’re trying a third time, this time against a member of his cabinet.
“They will fail again. And if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.”
Hegseth’s survival is now a marker of Trump’s success, while his removal would be a signal of the president’s failure.
The defence secretary could still be forced out if it becomes politically expedient. He is reportedly interested in a Senate vacancy caused by the Republican senator for Tennessee, Marsha Blackburn, being elected governor of that state.
But Hegseth is now the face of two wars: the one against Iran, and the one against the Democrats. And it’s the latter that will keep him in the job.

sources.news_title: House Republicans Block Pete Hegseth Impeachment as Democrats Threaten Renewed Push After Taking Control of Congress - Real News Now
sources.text:
House Republicans Block Pete Hegseth Impeachment as Democrats Threaten Renewed Push After Taking Control of Congress
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth survived an impeachment effort Tuesday after House Republicans voted to block a resolution seeking his removal from office, delivering a significant victory for President Trump and his Pentagon chief. The decision effectively ends the immediate attempt to impeach Hegseth, although Democrats are preparing to revisit the controversy when they assume control of Congress in January.
The House voted 211-204 to refer eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, preventing the resolution from advancing to a direct vote on impeachment. The measure was introduced by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who accused the defense secretary of exceeding his constitutional authority during military operations involving Iran and other countries.
Massie was the only Republican to vote against referring the resolution to committee. Every Democrat who participated in the vote opposed the procedural maneuver, demonstrating the party’s willingness to pursue impeachment proceedings against the Pentagon chief.
The result allows Hegseth to remain in his position without facing an immediate impeachment vote. However, the procedural victory does not prevent lawmakers from introducing new articles when the next Congress convenes.
President Trump celebrated the outcome, declaring that the effort to remove his defense secretary had failed and praising Republican lawmakers for standing behind the administration.
In a social media post following the vote, Trump described Hegseth as a great American patriot and characterized the House’s decision as a vindication of his leadership.
The president also singled out Massie for criticism, continuing a longstanding political feud with the Kentucky congressman over the administration’s foreign policy and legislative priorities.
Trump had previously pledged to stand behind Hegseth even if the House voted to impeach him. The president has repeatedly praised the secretary’s management of military operations and defended his handling of the conflict with Iran.
The Pentagon welcomed Tuesday’s vote, describing the outcome as a decisive defeat for the impeachment effort.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell declared that referring the articles to the Judiciary Committee represented a major victory for Hegseth, the department, and American military personnel.
Parnell said the department expected the allegations to be addressed in committee and maintained that the impeachment effort lacked sufficient grounds.
Hegseth had strongly rejected the accusations earlier Tuesday during a news conference at the Pentagon, where he defended his decisions and criticized the political motivations behind the resolution.
The defense secretary described the proceedings as a political spectacle and argued that disagreements over military policy should not automatically become grounds for impeachment.
Hegseth also accused Massie of pursuing a personal political campaign against him rather than focusing on the responsibilities of Congress.
The secretary maintained that his actions had been consistent with his duties and that he remained committed to carrying out President Trump’s national security priorities.
He defended the administration’s military operations, including the campaign against Iran, and said he would make the same decisions again if confronted with similar circumstances.
The impeachment resolution centered largely on the administration’s military campaign against Iran, which has continued for months and generated disagreements over the president’s authority to conduct prolonged military operations without additional congressional authorization.
Massie argued that Hegseth had participated in military activities that violated constitutional limits on executive power and the requirements of the War Powers Resolution.
Three of the eight articles addressed the Iran conflict, alleging that the Pentagon continued military operations beyond the period permitted without congressional authorization.
Other articles concerned American military operations in Yemen and Venezuela, as well as strikes against suspected drug-trafficking vessels in international waters.
The resolution also raised allegations involving the treatment of Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona following his participation in a video discussing the responsibility of military personnel to refuse unlawful orders.
Massie maintained that the secretary’s actions warranted congressional accountability and argued that lawmakers had a constitutional obligation to examine the allegations.
The Kentucky Republican expressed disappointment after the vote, saying Congress had failed to take action despite having the authority to do so.
Massie acknowledged that his impeachment effort was unlikely to advance further during the current congressional session.
He is scheduled to leave Congress in January after losing his Republican primary to a candidate backed by President Trump.
The congressman’s departure means that any renewed impeachment effort would likely need to be introduced by another lawmaker.
Democrats have already indicated that the controversy surrounding Hegseth will remain a priority when they assume control of the House and Senate.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries has expressed support for examining the secretary’s conduct and has accused him of abusing his authority.
Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker when the new Congress convenes, has indicated that Democrats intend to use their congressional oversight powers to investigate the Pentagon’s handling of military operations.
The incoming Democratic majority would have greater authority to schedule hearings, issue subpoenas, and advance legislation or impeachment resolutions without relying on Republican leadership.
That change could allow Democrats to bring articles of impeachment directly to the House floor, something they were unable to accomplish during Tuesday’s vote.
However, impeachment would still require approval by a majority of the House, and removing Hegseth from office would require a subsequent Senate trial and a two-thirds vote to convict.
Even with Democrats controlling the Senate, securing the necessary votes for removal would present a substantial challenge.
The prospect of renewed impeachment proceedings comes as Republicans prepare to surrender control of Congress following their midterm election losses.
Democrats captured majorities in both chambers during the November 3 elections, creating a new political environment for the final two years of President Trump’s second term.
The results have intensified disagreements among Republicans over the administration’s military strategy, particularly the economic and political consequences of the Iran conflict.
Some Republican lawmakers have acknowledged that rising gasoline prices and concerns about the prolonged war contributed to voter dissatisfaction.
Despite those concerns, most House Republicans declined to support Massie’s impeachment effort.
House Speaker Mike Johnson strongly opposed the resolution, arguing that it was an inappropriate response to policy disagreements involving the Pentagon.
Johnson characterized the impeachment attempt as a political maneuver and defended Hegseth’s continued leadership during ongoing military operations.
The outgoing speaker has also warned that Democratic control of Congress could lead to repeated investigations and political confrontations with the Trump administration.
Tuesday’s vote demonstrated that Republicans remained largely united behind the defense secretary despite the party’s recent election losses.
Vice President JD Vance also defended Hegseth, rejecting the argument that the secretary’s conduct constituted an impeachable offense.
Vance argued that Congress possesses numerous tools for expressing disagreement with administration policies without resorting to impeachment.
His remarks reflected the White House’s position that the resolution represented an attempt to transform foreign policy disputes into proceedings intended to remove a Cabinet official.
The controversy has also raised broader questions about the relationship between Congress and the executive branch during military conflicts.
Under the Constitution, Congress possesses the authority to declare war, while the president serves as commander in chief of the armed forces.
The War Powers Resolution establishes procedures and limitations governing certain military operations conducted without specific congressional authorization.
Disagreements over how those requirements apply have emerged under administrations of both political parties, particularly during extended military campaigns overseas.
Massie’s impeachment articles sought to frame the administration’s actions as violations serious enough to justify removing the defense secretary.
The White House and Pentagon have rejected that interpretation and maintained that Hegseth acted within the scope of his responsibilities.
Tuesday’s House vote did not resolve the underlying constitutional disagreements or determine whether the allegations were legally justified.
Instead, lawmakers approved a procedural motion that effectively prevents the current impeachment resolution from advancing before the end of the congressional session.
That distinction is important because Hegseth was not formally acquitted of impeachment charges. The House declined to proceed with consideration of the articles themselves.
The outcome nevertheless provides immediate political relief for the administration as it continues managing the military and diplomatic consequences of the Iran conflict.
President Trump has recently suggested that the military phase of the conflict is largely complete, while American officials continue negotiating arrangements intended to prevent renewed hostilities.
Hegseth has defended the administration’s military objectives and emphasized the importance of maintaining American military strength throughout the negotiations.
The secretary has also argued that the Pentagon must remain focused on national security rather than becoming consumed by congressional political disputes.
His position could face additional scrutiny when Democrats take control of congressional committees in January.
Lawmakers may seek testimony from senior Pentagon officials, request documents concerning military operations, and examine the legal justifications used by the administration.
Any renewed impeachment resolution would represent a separate legislative effort requiring its own consideration and vote.
For now, Hegseth retains the support of President Trump and the overwhelming majority of House Republicans who participated in Tuesday’s vote.
The administration has treated the result as a significant victory, while Democratic leaders have made clear that the change in congressional control could reopen the controversy.
With Republicans preparing to enter the minority, the balance of power on Capitol Hill will soon shift in ways that could create additional challenges for the Pentagon chief.
Tuesday’s decision prevents an immediate impeachment confrontation, but it does not guarantee that Hegseth will avoid further congressional investigations.
The next Congress will determine whether Democrats pursue another impeachment resolution or concentrate on broader oversight of the administration’s military decisions.
Until then, Hegseth remains in office with the president’s backing, and the effort to remove him has been halted for the remainder of the current congressional session.

sources.news_title: Pete Hegseth impeachment effort blocked by House Republicans
sources.text:
Pete Hegseth impeachment effort blocked by House Republicans
Nov 11, 2026, 9:36 AM
(Photo: Nathan Howard, AP)
The House on Tuesday turned aside a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, halting an effort to remove the Pentagon chief for his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran.
The vote came as Republicans grapple with the fallout from sweeping midterm losses that some in the party have blamed on the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gas prices. But after President Donald Trump signaled strong support for Hegseth, GOP lawmakers largely stood by the secretary Tuesday, blocking the effort in a near party-line vote.
The effort was led by Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats. The vote Tuesday may only delay an impeachment push against Hegseth, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take charge in January, stood firmly behind the push, saying Hegseth has “abused his power” and “undermined America’s national security.”
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer endorsed Hegseth’s impeachment as well.
Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, portraying Massie as a rogue lawmaker and arguing he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal. He framed the effort as an indictment against the nation’s service members and their successes and said it was undermining American forces “in real time.”
“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth said. “This is sabotage.”
Massie’s resolution included eight counts of impeachment. It largely focused on the war in Iran but also included references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican leaving Congress in January after losing his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, says Hegseth has “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders.”
Hegseth holds rare press conference
Tuesday morning, Hegseth gave a defiant and politicized defense of his stewardship of the U.S. military in his first news conference at the Pentagon in six months. He chose to hit back at the rising bipartisan anger over battlefield strategy while offering few details about intermittent operations against Iran or fatal strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America.
Hegseth said the impeachment resolution “tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations.”
Trump praised Hegseth’s performance at the briefing in a social media post, while Vice President JD Vance said in his own post that the impeachment effort is “a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking.”
Trump celebrated the House vote later Tuesday, saying on social media that it was the exoneration of “a Great American Patriot.”
Impeachment effort falls short
Massie filed the resolution in the House on Monday as lawmakers returned to Washington. Tuesday’s vote was a procedural attempt to stop the impeachment push outright by sending the matter back to committee. The motion succeeded 211-204, with a number of Democrats missing the vote.
Massie’s resolution had eight counts of impeachment that focused on U.S. military actions or changes on Hegseth’s watch. They include reported reductions in staff and resources at a Pentagon office focused on mitigating civilian harm, which preceded a U.S. missile striking an Iranian primary school during the war, killing up to 168 people.
“The law requires our military to withdraw from hostilities within 60 days if Congress does not authorize the activity,” Massie wrote on social media Tuesday. The Iran war “has been underway for 256 days. Congress has not authorized it. Hegseth is breaking the law.”
Another article of impeachment focused on Hegseth’s attempt to punish Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired Navy pilot, for participating in a video that called on troops to resist unlawful orders. Massie also called out U.S. military strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America and the failure to rescue survivors, which Massie argued will encourage adversaries to treat American forces the same way.
What constitutes “high crimes and misdemeanors” is not spelled out in the Constitution, leaving it to lawmakers to decide what are impeachable acts.
Hegseth said Massie’s concerns are not impeachable, calling them “policy disagreements, not high crimes, not misdemeanors, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson called it a “political gambit for attention” and predicted Republicans would defeat it “one way or the other.”
Some Republicans were critical of Hegseth in the run-up to the vote, but said they didn’t believe he had committed impeachable offenses. Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon, a Republican who is retiring after this year, said he didn’t agree with the “merit” of the impeachment, although he is “critical of the secretary.”
“I have a lot of other things I thought were failures by the secretary,” Bacon said. “We control the agenda. We should be doing hearings.”
This isn’t the first impeachment attempt in recent years
Hegseth cast Massie’s resolution in historic terms, arguing that no defense secretary has been impeached in the nation’s 250-year history “for carrying out lawful military operations.”
But more recently, a Cabinet official in President Joe Biden’s administration, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, was impeached by House Republicans over his handling of the U.S.-Mexico border. The Senate dismissed all impeachment charges, shutting down his trial before arguments even began.
Mayorkas, who did not appear to testify before the impeachment proceedings, put the border crisis squarely on Congress for failing to update immigration laws during a time of global migration. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer had said then, in April 2024, that House Republicans’ charges failed to meet “the high standard of high crimes and misdemeanors” and could set a dangerous precedent.
Before Mayorkas, no sitting Cabinet secretary had ever been impeached. It was nearly 150 years ago that the House voted to impeach President Ulysses S. Grant’s war secretary, William Belknap, over a kickback scheme in government contracts. He resigned before the vote.
Trump offers support for Hegseth
Trump backed Hegseth in the wake of Massie’s impeachment resolution, pointing to the U.S. military raid to capture then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January as well as operations against Iran that he asserts have “obliterated” its navy and air force.
“Pete Hegseth gets an “A” PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social.
Iran, however, has been able to keep striking U.S. military bases in the Middle East and has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz during the more than 8-month-old conflict, driving up global oil prices.

sources.news_title: House Republicans reject Hegseth impeachment effort and elect new leadership after midterm losses
sources.text:
House Republicans reject Hegseth impeachment effort and elect new leadership after midterm losses
House Republicans have defeated an effort to remove Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and elected new party leadership following major losses in the midterm elections.
(NBC)- House Republicans have defeated an effort to remove Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and elected new party leadership following major losses in the midterm elections.
Outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie led the effort to impeach Hegseth over several actions, including his handling of the Iran war.
The measure failed in a 211-204 House vote, with no Republican lawmakers joining Massie’s effort.
President Donald Trump celebrated the outcome, saying the impeachment push had failed and describing Hegseth as a great American patriot.
Hegseth also defended himself against the accusations.
“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said.
Massie argued that Hegseth had “violated the norms of war.”
Although the impeachment effort failed, Democrats could revisit the issue when they take control of Congress in January.
However, some incoming Democratic lawmakers are urging their party to prioritize the economic concerns that helped drive their election victories.
“The question of whether or not cabinet members are doing their job well is a secondary question to how do we address the crisis in folks’ life,” said Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed.
The election results are also prompting discussions about Democratic leadership, with some progressives calling for a challenge to longtime Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer.
Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders expressed support for a leadership change.
“I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change,” Sanders said.
Meanwhile, Republicans have selected Rep. Jim Jordan as their new House minority leader and Rep. Tom Emmer as minority whip for the 120th Congress.
“We will regain the trust and confidence of the American people,” Emmer said.
Sen. John Thune will remain the Senate Republican leader as the party prepares for its new role in Congress.
“I think we have to take the lesson to heart,” Thune said.
Republican leaders say they intend to learn from their election losses while continuing to focus on issues affecting American families.

sources.news_title: Good Morning, News: Hegseth Impeachment Blocked, Stolen Horses in Portland, and the Background Check ICE Never Did
sources.text:
The Mercury provides news and fun every single day—but your help is essential. If you believe Portland benefits from smart, local journalism and arts coverage, please consider making a small monthly contribution, because without you, there is no us. Thanks for your support!
Good morning, Portland! Today, expect overcast skies with a high of 65 degrees and a low of 49.
It’s Veterans Day, in case you’re wondering why mail delivery is paused and some government buildings are closed today. Thank the vets in your life, if that’s a thing that’s applicable to you. For those who served, go get you some free Applebee’s or a Grand Slam at Denny’s. 🇺🇲
For the rest of us, let’s go get caught up on current affairs.
IN LOCAL NEWS:
• The race for the next chair of the Washington County Board of Commissioners is still too close to call. Current Commissioners Pam Treece and Nafisa Fai both ran for the chair’s position. Initial results showed Treece with a slight lead over Fai (about two percentage points), but as of Tuesday, the two are both sitting at 49 percent, with Fai leading by less than 365 votes. If the election is called for Fai, she’d be the first person of color to lead Washington County’s board. OPB reports Tuesday’s count “does not include thousands of ballots challenged due to signature issues.” It could take weeks for the county elections office to verify and count those ballots.
• A woman visiting Portland last weekend from Idaho says she is devastated after someone broke into her rental car and stole about $10,000 worth of horses…well, miniature model horses, to be exact. Molly Worek was in Portland for a model horse show in Tigard. She’d been collecting custom-made, hand-painted resin model horses since she was a young child. She brought her entire collection to the show, and won, taking best in show. After the show, she placed her miniature resin horses back in their soft pouches and stored them in luggage in her rental car. Her hotel in the Pearl District didn’t have a parking lot, so she parked in a garage across the street. Rather than hauling all her luggage back over to the hotel, she kept it in the car. The next morning, she discovered someone had busted the window and rifled through her all her belongings. All her horses—her life’s collection—gone. Worek says she searched the area and asked around, frantically, and discovered an employee at Powell’s Books had been given one. She’s hoping the person who stole them might be giving them out or selling them for cheap, and that Portlanders will recognize them and help reunite her with some of her collection. She’s filed a police report and her initial post on Facebook has been shared numerous times. Keep an eye out for these tiny ponies!
• Portland has its own reflecting pool problems. A leak in the Washington Park fountain is reportedly leaking an estimated 68,000 gallons of water a day. KPTV reports the reflecting pool is separate from an underground drinking water reservoir at the site, which is not leaking, according to the Portland Water Bureau. The Water Bureau is working with a contractor to narrow down the exact source of the leak, which originated somewhere in the fountain’s liner, and get it repaired. Currently, the water is leaking into the stormwater system and doesn’t pose a threat to drinking water, but man, what a waste!
• Two city councilors are pitching a “Fair Share” tax on companies whose CEOs make 50 to 75 times what their average employee makes. If approved, the tax would generate an estimated $72 million in extra revenue for the city each year, while also cutting taxes for the city’s small businesses. Critics say the tax would push out large corporations. In an opinion piece, Sarah Anderson and Steve Silberstein say that’s unlikely, and such a tax is more likely to encourage them to raise worker wages, or just pay the tax.
IN NATIONAL/WORLD NEWS:
• US Senator Bernie Sanders says he won’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer to serve as the next Senate majority leader. Schumer, the current minority leader, is expected to advance to serve as the Senate’s next majority leader after Democrats’ sweeping wins last week. But Sanders and others say it’s time for change, and Schumer represents the old guard. Sanders and Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin held a joint news conference Tuesday to push for different Senate leadership, indicating neither would vote for poor ol’ Chuck. Instead, some are eying Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen for the role, though Van Hollen may be considering a 2028 presidential run. In the US House of Representatives, there have also been calls for Representative and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries to step aside and let someone else serve as House majority leader next term.
• On Tuesday, the US House blocked Republican Rep. Thomas Massie’s effort to impeach “Whiskey” Pete Hegseth, because unlike an actual house that’s built with structural integrity and provides shelter, the House of Representatives is unreliable and doesn’t actually support you or protect you from harmful elements like Pete fucking Hegseth. The “secretary of war” launched the Iran war without Congressional approval. In a 211-204 vote, “the House voted to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively killing it,” CBS explains. Rep. Massie was the lone Republican who voted with Democrats against referring it.
• A student at the University of Maryland who was valedictorian of her high school class just months ago was detained by ICE agents and transferred out of state. Maria Flores Garcia reportedly accompanied her mother to an immigration check-in appointment in Baltimore last week, when both the teen and her mother were detained and transferred to a detention center in Louisiana, according to Flores Garcia’s boyfriend, who’s been in contact with her. Flores Garcia and her family immigrated to the United States from El Salvador when she was a child.
• Speaking of ICE, the New York Times did a background investigation into the agent that shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero earlier this year in Maine. That’s significant because as it turns out, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, was so busy fast-tracking new recruits that it never actually did a background check of its own on David Brouillette before hiring him in 2025 and sending him out for duty. The Times investigation found numerous “red flags” in Brouillette’s history that would normally be disqualifying for a federal agent. Durán Guerrero, 25, was shot in the face while driving his car. A lawyer for his family said he had legal permission to work in the country. Brouillette, the rookie ICE agent, has been accused by at least one of his ex-wives of domestic abuse. He also harbored strong anti-immigrant biases and struggled with bipolar disorder, according to the NYT reporting, and had previously lied in court about being employed by a law enforcement agency in 2019 (he applied to be a cop but was never hired.)
• Congressional races in Alaska and Mississippi still remain too close to call, more than a week after Election Day. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom was about 2,600 votes ahead of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the race for a Senate seat, and in Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola is leading the incumbent, Republican Dan Sullivan, by about 2,500 votes as of Tuesday afternoon, the AP reports.
And finally, someone captured what that mid-week mania feels like…

sources.news_title: Why the Impeachment Pass on Trump?
sources.text:
NOTE: Coming soon! Jacob Hornberger’s newest book The Straight Line in the JFK Assassination.
*****
Yesterday, Republican members of the U.S. House of Representatives succeeded in derailing Congressman Tom Massie’s effort to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. The vote was 211-204 to refer the impeachment resolution to the House Judiciary Committee. Massie was the only Republican voting against the referral.
Among other things, Massie’s impeachment effort against Hegseth was based on the illegal and unconstitutional U.S. war on Iran as well as the manner in which the war has been waged, the illegal and unconstitutional military raid on Venezuela, along with the capture, kidnapping, and rendition of the country’s ruler, Nicolás Maduro, and the Pentagon’s illegal and unconstitutional drug-war assassinations of people in little boats on the high seas near South America.
In my opinion, Massie’s charges against Hegseth were valid. I believe that both Republicans and Democrats should have voted overwhelmingly to impeach him. In fact, I made many of these points in my September 29, 2026, article entitled “Trump Deserves to Be Impeached.”
But notice a critically important difference between my article and Massie’s impeachment efforts. I call for Trump’s impeachment. Massie calls for Hegseth’s impeachment.
That raises an interesting point: Why did Massie give Trump a pass on impeachment? Why did he limit his impeachment efforts to Hegseth?
After all, Hegseth is Trump’s subordinate. He’s the guy who carried out Trump’s orders. But he’s not the guy who initiated the orders. The person who issued the orders to invade Iran, raid Venezuela, and conduct the drug-war assassinations was Hegseth’s military commander, Donald Trump.
In fact, the Trump administration itself has effectively acknowledged this point. In opposing Massie’s impeachment resolution against Hegseth, the White House emphasized that Hegseth was carrying out military operations directed by his commander-in-chief. Precisely! If the military operations were illegal and unconstitutional, as Massie contends, why should the man who ordered them escape impeachment while the man who carried out the orders faces impeachment? Why settle only for trying to remove the subordinate who was given the orders and give a pass to the person who issued the orders?
Now, I’m not saying that Hegseth should be immune from impeachment. He carried out Trump’s orders. As we all know from the Nuremberg War Crimes Tribunal, the “I was only following orders” defense doesn’t work — or at least shouldn’t work.
But why not call for the impeachment of both Trump and Hegseth? Why give Trump an impeachment pass and settle for targeting his subordinate with impeachment? After all, as the old saying goes, the buck stops with Trump. As the commander-in-chief, it is Trump who is ultimately responsible for the offenses that Massie charges Hegseth with.
Another question arises: Why did Massie wait until September 2026 to introduce impeachment articles against Hegseth, and why did he wait until November, when he was about to leave office, to force the House to act on them?
The drug-war assassinations of people in little boats began in September 2025.
The military raid on Venezuela, which resulted in the deaths of around 75-100 people, occurred on January 3, 2026.
The U.S. war of aggression on Iran was launched on February 28, 2026.
The Republican primary, when Massie got defeated owing to Trump’s intervention, was on May 19, 2026.
Why not call for impeachment proceedings against Hegseth (and Trump) back in February or at least before the Republican primary election? Why wait until now, just before Massie is leaving office, to do it?
There is another great big elephant in the room that hardly anyone is talking about: the role of the Pentagon and, specifically, the military personnel who participated in these events. Why should they be given a pass? The generals, the admirals, and the rest of the military personnel who carried out these orders might by immune from impeachment proceedings, but they are certainly not immune from a congressional investigation. Why hasn’t Massie called for a full congressional investigation in which the generals, admirals, and other military personnel involved in these operations could be subpoenaed and questioned under oath? What legal advice did military commanders receive? Were any officers threatened with dismissal or disciplinary action if they refused to participate?
Such a congressional investigation would be especially revealing with respect to those drug-war assassinations of those people in little boats on the high seas near South America. One person who certainly should be required to testify is Admiral Alvin “Bull” Holsey, the Navy officer who headed the U.S. Southern Command. On December 12, 2025, he relinquished command, which was odd because he was only into the first year of a three-year tenure. He resigned shorty after the drug-war assassinations of the people in those little boats began.
Did Holsey resign out of a crisis of conscience over those assassinations? Did he resign because he didn’t want to participate in criminal offenses? Why didn’t he resign before any assassinations took place? Why shouldn’t we know what happened here?
Holsey’s temporary replacement was his deputy, Air Force Gen. Evan L. Pettus. On February 5, 2026, his permanent replacement became Marine Corps Gen. Francis L. Donovan. It would be interesting to see how these two men justify carrying out the orders they received to take out those people in those little boats. In fact, it would also be interesting to discover what “secret” information supposedly existed to justify the extrajudicial killings of all those people.
Thus, now that his impeachment effort against Hegseth has been derailed, in his waning days as a congressman why doesn’t Massie call for a full congressional investigation into the military personnel who carried out what I believe were illegal and unconstitutional orders? Sure, I understand this would be a difficult effort given the longstanding mindset among many Republicans to treat the Pentagon, the CIA, and the NSA — that is, the national-security establishment — as a triune god, one who should never be questioned or challenged. But given that Massie is willing to target Hegseth with impeachment just before Massie leaves office, why not also call for a congressional investigation into the Pentagon’s role in these illegal and unconstitutional acts?
I say: No passes for anyone who engages in illegal and unconstitutional high crimes and misdemeanors. No impeachment pass for Trump. No impeachment pass for Hegseth. And no investigation pass for the Pentagon.

sources.news_title: House Republicans Block Pete Hegseth Impeachment Push as Trump Stands by Defense Secretary Amid Iran War Backlash
sources.text:
House Republicans Block Pete Hegseth Impeachment Push as Trump Stands by Defense Secretary Amid Iran War Backlash
Nov. 11 2026, Updated 11:45 a.m. ET
House Republicans have effectively shut down an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the Iran war and other U.S. military operations.
The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday, November 10, to refer eight articles of impeachment introduced by Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, preventing an immediate vote on the charges.
The decision gives Hegseth a reprieve as President Donald Trump continues to defend his Pentagon chief, despite growing criticism of the administration's military actions.
Democrats are also preparing to take control of both chambers of Congress in January following their sweeping midterm election victories.
GOP Shield Holds Despite Iran War Backlash
The impeachment resolution was introduced by Massie, a longtime Trump critic who lost his Republican primary in May to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein.
Massie was the only Republican to oppose referring his own resolution to committee. The official House tally showed 210 Republicans supported the procedural motion, while 203 Democrats voted against it. One independent also voted in favor of referral.
Seven Republicans and 11 Democrats did not participate, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. The absences helped Republicans secure enough votes to send the resolution to committee rather than proceed with an impeachment vote.
Trump Stands By His Defense Secretary
Trump had already made clear that he was not prepared to abandon Hegseth over the impeachment threat.
During an appearance at the White House on Monday, November 9, the president dismissed Massie as a loser and said he would continue supporting his defense secretary even if the House voted to impeach him.
Trump reiterated his position after the House decision, praising Hegseth's role in overseeing American military operations in Venezuela and Iran.
Speaking to reporters, Trump credited the defense secretary with winning two wars and defended his performance, arguing that the military had made significant progress under his leadership. He also criticized Massie for pursuing the impeachment effort.
Eight Articles And What They Alleged
Massie's 34-page resolution contained eight articles accusing Hegseth of serious misconduct.
Four focused on the Iran conflict, including allegations that the defense secretary continued military operations without proper congressional authorization and violated the War Powers Resolution of 1973.
The resolution also accused Hegseth of failing to adequately protect civilians during military operations, including a February 28 strike on a girls' school in Minab, Iran, that killed scores of children.
Other allegations concerned U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Yemen, as well as deadly strikes against suspected drug-trafficking vessels in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific.
One article also accused Hegseth of retaliating against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly after the Arizona lawmaker and other members of Congress urged military personnel to refuse unlawful orders.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries supported the impeachment effort, arguing that Hegseth had abused his authority and threatened national security. All eight articles contained allegations that Hegseth has rejected.
Hegseth Calls Effort A Farce
Hegseth dismissed the impeachment proceedings during a Pentagon press conference on Tuesday, November 10, describing the effort as a political stunt.
The defense secretary denied wrongdoing and maintained that his actions had been lawful from the beginning. He also accused Massie of pursuing the resolution because of personal hostility toward Trump.
Hegseth further argued that the impeachment campaign endangered American military personnel by putting a target on their backs.
The referral to the Judiciary Committee effectively shelves the effort for the remainder of the current Congress, which ends January 3, 2027. Republicans will retain control of both chambers until the new Congress takes office, despite Democrats' midterm victories.
Democrats are then expected to take control of the House and Senate, potentially giving them another opportunity to pursue the allegations against Hegseth.
However, the committee referral does not automatically guarantee that the impeachment articles will return for another vote.

sources.text:
US House GOP blocks effort to impeach Hegseth
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth testifies during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on July 21, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has survived an impeachment effort, at least for now, after the U.S. House on Tuesday blocked a vote over charges that the Cabinet official oversaw extrajudicial killings and an illegal war against Iran.
The House voted 211-204, largely along party lines, to refer articles of impeachment against Hegseth to a committee — effectively killing the impeachment effort until the end of the current Congress in January. Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans missed the vote.
The vote came hours after Hegseth defended himself in a fiery news conference at the Pentagon, where he denounced the impeachment effort as an attack on American service members.
He called the bid to remove him a “farce” and flatly rejected the notion that he had committed impeachable offenses as the top civilian leader of the military. He likened himself to President Donald Trump, who was twice impeached during his first term.
“Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations,” Hegseth said.
Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment Monday alleging the Defense secretary waged unlawful war against Iran, ordered extrajudicial killings and ignored laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, among other charges.
Impeachment would have represented an extraordinary rebuke of one of the most divisive members of Trump’s Cabinet.
Hegseth, a 46-year-old former Fox News personality who narrowly won Senate confirmation last year, has sought to project a swashbuckling, masculine image as the military’s top civilian leader. He has rebranded the Department of Defense as the “Department of War,” purged numerous high-ranking officers and tried to kick critical media outlets out of the Pentagon.
On Tuesday, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is attempting a “political spectacle” driven by ego and resentment. Massie, who has often clashed with Trump, lost his primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger.
“It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth’s opponents could try again to impeach him during the new Congress, which begins in January. Democrats will hold a large majority in the House at that time.
Earlier in the day, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who will likely become majority leader when his party takes over the chamber, said Hegseth should stand trial in the Senate if impeached.
“Hegseth is already trying to hide behind our troops, falsely claiming that Congress disapproves of our courageous servicemembers even though we have fought to bring them home for months,” Schumer said.
President Donald Trump has so far stood by Hegseth. He praised the Defense secretary in multiple public remarks over the past two weeks, saying he’s “done a fantastic job” in reducing the number of “woke” four-star generals, and for conducting the “war with Venezuela,” which he said “was over in 48 minutes.”
“Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!” Trump wrote in a social media post on Monday.

sources.news_title: House Shelves Hegseth Impeachment, Exposing Washington’s Uniparty
sources.text:
House Shelves Hegseth Impeachment, Exposing Washington’s Uniparty
Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky tried to hold Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accountable for alleged illegal warfare and constitutional violations. Instead, Congress demonstrated just how little appetite either party has for confronting executive overreach.
On Tuesday, 210 Republicans voted to bury his impeachment resolution in committee, while the absence of 11 Democrats helped seal its fate. The House voted 211 to 204 to avoid deciding the charges.
Hegseth dismissed his Republican accuser as “disgruntled” and “resentful.” President Donald Trump stood firmly behind his defense secretary, awarding him an “A PLUS, PLUS, PLUS” for taking on “LOSER” Massie.
A Vote on How Not to Vote
The showdown centered on House Resolution 1655, containing eight articles of impeachment. Massie introduced it Monday as a privileged measure, forcing House action within two legislative days.
Representative Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) offered an escape route: refer the resolution to the House Judiciary Committee. The House adopted his motion Tuesday evening.
The official roll call was revealing. A total of 210 Republicans supported referral, with Massie alone opposing. All 203 Democrats who voted rejected the maneuver. Independent Representative Kevin Kiley of California sided with Republicans. Seven Republicans and 11 Democrats did not vote.
In other words, lawmakers never voted on whether Hegseth committed impeachable offenses. Instead, they sent the allegations to committee, effectively shelving the resolution for the remainder of the congressional session.
That spared Republicans a choice between loyalty to Trump and their constitutional responsibility to authorize war and oversee the executive branch. It also allowed Hegseth to claim victory without Congress resolving a single accusation.
According to The Associated Press, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) dismissed the impeachment effort as a “political gambit for attention.” Representative Don Bacon (R-Neb.), who has criticized Hegseth, said he disagreed with the “merits” of the charges and favored hearings instead.
The White House left little doubt about its position. In a formal policy statement, it urged lawmakers to support referral, portrayed Massie’s charges as an attack on the military, and defended Trump’s authority to direct the disputed operations.
The Democrats Who Did Not Show Up
The Democratic absences proved just as consequential.
Had eight of the 11 missing Democrats voted against referral, the motion would have failed, assuming every other vote remained unchanged. Their absence supplied the margin needed to shelve Massie’s resolution.
The missing Democrats were former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (Calif.), Julia Brownley (Calif.), Lou Correa (Calif.), Laura Gillen (N.Y.), Steven Horsford (Nev.), Jonathan Jackson (Ill.), Brittany Pettersen (Colo.), Melanie Stansbury (N.M.), Haley Stevens (Mich.), Marilyn Strickland (Wash.), and Frederica Wilson (Fla.).
They offered varying explanations. Gillen, Jackson, Stansbury, and Strickland blamed traffic delays in Washington. Pelosi attended a veterans’ event in California. Correa was preparing for a medical procedure, and Horsford’s office cited a personal emergency.
Several insisted they would have opposed referral. Their explanations do not establish deliberate support for Hegseth, but whatever their intentions, the outcome was the same.
California Democrat Sydney Kamlager-Dove was less forgiving:
We knew that this vote was coming, so people should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), who is poised to become the next House speaker, had publicly declared himself a “hard yes” on Hegseth’s impeachment. Yet he failed to muster enough members of his own caucus to keep the resolution alive.
The Accusations Against Hegseth
Massie’s eight impeachment articles allege violations extending far beyond disagreements over military strategy.
The first three concern the War Powers Resolution. They accuse Hegseth of conducting unauthorized hostilities against Iran, disregarding congressional demands for withdrawal, and exceeding statutory limits on military operations.
The 1973 law generally requires the withdrawal of American forces after 60 days without congressional authorization, subject to limited exceptions and extensions. By Tuesday, the war against Iran had continued for 256 days.
Another article accuses Hegseth of dismantling safeguards designed to protect civilians. The resolution cites a deadly strike on an Iranian school in Minab, where as many as 168 people died, almost all of them children. Massie alleges that Hegseth weakened Pentagon protections intended to prevent such tragedies.
The remaining charges concern lethal attacks on suspected drug-running boats, including alleged strikes on survivors; retaliation against Senator Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) for warning against unlawful military orders; the seizure of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro; and unauthorized military operations in Yemen.
An A+ From Trump
At a Pentagon news conference Tuesday, Hegseth lashed out at Massie, dismissing his impeachment effort as “a political spectacle” fueled by personal resentment.
He insisted that the disputed military operations were lawful, ordered by Trump, and reported to Congress. The charges, he argued, reflected mere “policy disagreements.”
Hegseth then cast the attempt to hold him accountable as an attack on American troops:
If they want to come for the warriors, they’re going to have to come through me.
He condemned the impeachment effort as “not patriotism” but “sabotage.”
Addressing service members directly, he urged them, “Don’t blink, ignore the noise, never hesitate.” He dismissed the controversy as “all politics.”
He reserved particularly lavish praise for Trump:
We’ve never had a better commander in chief, full stop.
Trump promptly returned the compliment:
Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!
On Monday, the president had already promised to “stand by” Hegseth even if impeached, offering his own assessment of the secretary’s record:
He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won.
After the vote, Trump celebrated what he called the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.”
He also portrayed the impeachment effort as a Democratic attack, conveniently overlooking two facts: A Republican introduced the resolution, and the absence of 11 Democrats helped defeat it.
The Constitution Comes Last
Massie, who lost his Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger heavily supported by pro-Israel political groups, leaves Congress in January.
The pro-Israel lobby also surfaced in discussions of the Democratic absences. Social media observers quickly noticed a common thread. According to campaign finance records, 10 of the 11 absent Democrats had received generous contributions through AIPAC. The overlap attracted scrutiny.
Massie, meanwhile, compared Republican leaders to passengers determined to remain aboard a sinking ship. Yet he also urged Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats take control of Congress, warning that they will pursue hearings and trials.
Coming from a lawmaker who just accused Hegseth of grave constitutional violations, that suggestion is astonishing. Since when does replacing an official absolve him of alleged crimes?
Democrats won both chambers in the November 3 midterms. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries promised to revisit impeachment in January. Yet he could not even muster enough members of his own caucus to prevent Tuesday’s defeat. Even if Democrats eventually impeach Hegseth, removing him will require a two-thirds Senate majority.
The episode offers a revealing reminder of how readily constitutional principles yield to partisan loyalties and political calculations.
Republicans rallied behind Trump rather than allow a direct vote on serious allegations of executive overreach. Democrats loudly demanded accountability but failed to show up in sufficient numbers to keep the resolution alive.
Congress neither proved nor disproved Massie’s charges. It simply avoided voting on them.
And so the familiar Washington spectacle continues. Both parties invoke the Constitution when politically convenient. But when upholding it requires confronting their own leaders, even the most solemn constitutional principles suddenly become negotiable.

sources.news_title: Impeachment against Pete Hegseth fails completely – The Horn News
sources.text:
The House on Tuesday easily rejected a resolution to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, halting an effort to remove the Pentagon chief for his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran.
The vote came as Republicans grapple with the fallout from sweeping midterm losses that some in the party have blamed on the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gas prices. But after President Donald Trump signaled strong support for Hegseth, GOP lawmakers largely stood by the secretary Tuesday, blocking the effort in a near party-line vote.
The effort was led by outgoing Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats. The vote Tuesday may only delay an impeachment push against Hegseth, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take charge in January, stood firmly behind the push, saying Hegseth has “abused his power” and “undermined America’s national security.”
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer endorsed Hegseth’s impeachment as well.
Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, portraying Massie as a rogue lawmaker and arguing he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal. He framed the effort as an indictment against the nation’s service members and their successes and said it was undermining American forces “in real time.”
“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth said. “This is sabotage.”
Massie’s resolution included eight counts of impeachment. It largely focused on the war in Iran but also included references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican leaving Congress in January after losing his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, says Hegseth has “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders.”
At a news conference, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says his potential impeachment in Congress is the result of a rogue lawmaker targeting him over “policy disagreements”
Hegseth holds rare press conference
Tuesday morning, Hegseth gave a defiant defense of his stewardship of the U.S. military in his first news conference at the Pentagon in six months. He chose to hit back at the rising Democratic anger over battlefield strategy while offering few details about intermittent operations against Iran or fatal strikes on drug-smuggling boats in Latin America.
Hegseth said the impeachment resolution “tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations.”
Trump praised Hegseth’s performance at the briefing in a social media post, while Vice President JD Vance said in his own post that the impeachment effort is “a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking.”
Trump celebrated the House vote later Tuesday, saying on social media that it was the exoneration of “a Great American Patriot.”
Impeachment effort falls short
Massie filed the resolution in the House on Monday as lawmakers returned to Washington. Tuesday’s vote was a procedural attempt to stop the impeachment push outright by sending the matter back to committee. The motion succeeded 211-204, with a number of Democrats missing the vote.
Massie’s resolution had eight counts of impeachment that focused on U.S. military actions or changes on Hegseth’s watch. They include reported reductions in staff and resources at a Pentagon office focused on mitigating civilian harm, which preceded a U.S. missile striking an Iranian primary school during the war, killing up to 168 people.
“The law requires our military to withdraw from hostilities within 60 days if Congress does not authorize the activity,” Massie wrote on social media Tuesday. The Iran war “has been underway for 256 days. Congress has not authorized it. Hegseth is breaking the law.”
Another article of impeachment focused on Hegseth’s attempt to punish Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired Navy pilot, for participating in a video that called on troops to resist unlawful orders. Massie also called out U.S. military strikes on drug-smuggling boats in Latin America and the failure to rescue survivors, which Massie argued will encourage adversaries to treat American forces the same way.
What constitutes “high crimes and misdemeanors” is not spelled out in the Constitution, leaving it to lawmakers to decide what are impeachable acts.
Hegseth said Massie’s concerns are not impeachable, calling them “policy disagreements, not high crimes, not misdemeanors, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson called it a “political gambit for attention” and predicted Republicans would defeat it “one way or the other.”
Some Republicans were critical of Hegseth in the run-up to the vote, but said they didn’t believe he had committed impeachable offenses. Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon, a Republican who is retiring after this year, said he didn’t agree with the “merit” of the impeachment although he is “critical of the secretary.”
“I have a lot of other things I thought were failures by the secretary,” Bacon said. “We control the agenda. We should be doing hearings.”
This isn’t the first impeachment attempt in recent years
Hegseth cast Massie’s resolution in historic terms, arguing that no defense secretary has been impeached in the nation’s 250-year history “for carrying out lawful military operations.”
During President Joe Biden’s administration, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, was impeached by House Republicans over his mishandling of the U.S.-Mexico border crisis. The Senate dismissed all impeachment charges, shutting down his trial before arguments even began.
Mayorkas, who did not appear to testify before the impeachment proceedings, put the border crisis squarely on Congress for failing to update immigration laws during a time of global migration. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer had said then, in April 2024, that House Republicans’ charges failed to meet “the high standard of high crimes and misdemeanors” and could set a dangerous precedent.
Before Mayorkas, no sitting Cabinet secretary had ever been impeached. It was nearly 150 years ago that the House voted to impeach President Ulysses S. Grant’s war secretary, William Belknap, over a kickback scheme in government contracts. He resigned before the vote.
Trump offers support for Hegseth
Trump backed Hegseth in the wake of Massie’s impeachment resolution, pointing to the U.S. military raid to capture then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January as well as operations against Iran that he asserts have “obliterated” its navy and air force.
“Pete Hegseth gets an “A” PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social.
The Associated Press contributed to this article

sources.news_title: US House GOP blocks effort to impeach Hegseth • West Virginia Watch
sources.text:
US House GOP blocks effort to impeach Hegseth
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth testifies during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on July 21, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has survived an impeachment effort, at least for now, after the U.S. House on Tuesday blocked a vote over charges that the Cabinet official oversaw extrajudicial killings and an illegal war against Iran.
The House voted 211-204, largely along party lines, to refer articles of impeachment against Hegseth to a committee — effectively killing the impeachment effort until the end of the current Congress in January. Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans missed the vote.
The vote came hours after Hegseth defended himself in a fiery news conference at the Pentagon, where he denounced the impeachment effort as an attack on American service members.
He called the bid to remove him a “farce” and flatly rejected the notion that he had committed impeachable offenses as the top civilian leader of the military. He likened himself to President Donald Trump, who was twice impeached during his first term.
“Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations,” Hegseth said.
Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment Monday alleging the Defense secretary waged unlawful war against Iran, ordered extrajudicial killings and ignored laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, among other charges.
Impeachment would have represented an extraordinary rebuke of one of the most divisive members of Trump’s Cabinet.
Hegseth, a 46-year-old former Fox News personality who narrowly won Senate confirmation last year, has sought to project a swashbuckling, masculine image as the military’s top civilian leader. He has rebranded the Department of Defense as the “Department of War,” purged numerous high-ranking officers and tried to kick critical media outlets out of the Pentagon.
On Tuesday, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is attempting a “political spectacle” driven by ego and resentment. Massie, who has often clashed with Trump, lost his primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger.
“It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth’s opponents could try again to impeach him during the new Congress, which begins in January. Democrats will hold a large majority in the House at that time.
Earlier in the day, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who will likely become majority leader when his party takes over the chamber, said Hegseth should stand trial in the Senate if impeached.
“Hegseth is already trying to hide behind our troops, falsely claiming that Congress disapproves of our courageous servicemembers even though we have fought to bring them home for months,” Schumer said.
President Donald Trump has so far stood by Hegseth. He praised the Defense secretary in multiple public remarks over the past two weeks, saying he’s “done a fantastic job” in reducing the number of “woke” four-star generals, and for conducting the “war with Venezuela,” which he said “was over in 48 minutes.”
“Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!” Trump wrote in a social media post on Monday.

sources.news_title: House blocks Thomas Massie’s bid to impeach Hegseth
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The House on Tuesday blocked an effort by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, voting 211-204 to refer the eight articles of impeachment to the Judiciary Committee, effectively ending the push for the remainder of the current Congress.
Massie was the only Republican to vote against the procedural motion. All other Republicans present supported referring the resolution to committee, while Democrats present opposed the move. One independent lawmaker also voted in favor of referral. Several members, including about a dozen Democrats, were absent.
The privileged resolution, which Massie reintroduced Monday after a similar effort in September was sidestepped when Speaker Mike Johnson adjourned the House early, forced a vote within two legislative days. Referring the articles to the Republican-led Judiciary Committee, where they are not expected to advance before the session ends, prevented a direct floor vote on impeachment.
The articles targeted Hegseth over the Iran war and related operations, including alleged violations of the War Powers Resolution, strikes in Yemen, Caribbean and Pacific boat strikes against suspected drug traffickers that Massie described as extrajudicial killings, the capture of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro, and alleged retaliation against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly over his public comments to military service members. Massie has argued the actions constituted high crimes and misdemeanors.
Massie lost his Republican primary in May and is leaving Congress in January after the new Democratic majority takes control.
At a Pentagon news conference earlier Tuesday, his first in months, Hegseth dismissed the effort as “a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” calling it “a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment” by “one disgruntled and defeated congressman.” He said the charges amounted to “policy disagreements” rather than impeachable offenses and that “no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations.”
President Donald Trump celebrated the outcome on Truth Social, writing that “The Democrats’ attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!” and that “Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete.” Trump has previously urged Congress to “stand up for Pete” and praised military recruitment and operations under Hegseth’s leadership.
Johnson had earlier described Massie as a “disgruntled congressman” and the push as “a political gambit for attention.”
The referral leaves any future impeachment effort to the next Congress, when Democrats are expected to hold the House. Hegseth remains in office.
