sources.news_title: GOP rebel blasts Republican ‘suicide pact’ after Hegseth impeachment vote fails
House Republicans Stop Hegseth Impeachment Push by Seven Votes as GOP Senator Signals He Would Convict
sources.text:
The Briefing:
- The House voted 211-204 to table the impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, sending the articles to the Judiciary Committee and effectively ending the effort for the duration of this Congress.
- Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) — a lame-duck congressman who lost his primary to a Trump-backed challenger — filed eight articles of impeachment and was the only Republican to vote against tabling, aligning with every Democrat who showed up.
- Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC), who cast the deciding vote to confirm Hegseth in January 2025, publicly declared he would likely vote to convict if the Senate held an impeachment trial — a break from Republican leadership that the White House cannot ignore.
The House of Representatives voted Tuesday night to shut down an impeachment push against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, but a seven-vote margin and an unprecedented act of Republican self-opposition left the White House with a victory that felt more like a warning.
A Procedural Win With a Narrow Foundation
The 211-204 tabling vote dispatched the impeachment resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, where Republican leadership can keep it from ever reaching the floor again. Axios confirmed the procedural maneuver "effectively kills any effort to impeach Hegseth this Congress." Under the parliamentary move, the articles were referred to the Republican-controlled committee, closing off any direct floor debate on whether Hegseth committed impeachable offenses — at least while Republicans still hold the majority.
It Was a Republican Who Pulled the Trigger
What distinguished this episode from a standard Democratic opposition play was its origin inside the GOP itself. Massie filed the resolution Monday, invoking a privileged designation that forced House leadership to bring it to a floor vote within two legislative days — giving Speaker Mike Johnson little room to quietly bury it. His central charge: that Hegseth defied Congress and unlawfully sustained U.S. military operations in Iran without proper legislative authorization.
The eight articles covered Hegseth's conduct across multiple theaters — the Iran conflict, military campaigns in Yemen, the capture of Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, and naval strikes on drug-trafficking vessels in the Caribbean. The articles targeted Hegseth specifically, not President Trump, who ordered the operations. Johnson moved to neutralize the effort quickly, announcing midday Tuesday that the House would "dispense with the impeachment gambit." It did — but only by seven votes.
Eleven Democrats Who Changed the Math
The most telling number from Tuesday may not be 211 — it's 11. That is how many House Democrats did not appear for a vote that their own leadership publicly backed. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Rep. Pete Aguilar each announced they would vote in favor of advancing the impeachment, yet Democratic leadership made no formal effort to whip members into the chamber. Those 11 absences proved decisive.
Had all present Democrats and Massie been joined by even a small number of additional Republicans, the resolution would have survived the tabling motion and advanced directly to a floor debate on the substance of the articles themselves.
Hegseth Swings Back — and So Does Trump
Hegseth held a rare news conference at the Pentagon before the vote — his first public appearance of that kind in more than 180 days — dismissing the impeachment drive as a "farce" and a "stunt." He mounted an aggressive defense of the Iran war and other operations, framing them as lawful decisions carried out at the president's direction. Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson backed his position, stating Hegseth had "carried out direct, lawful orders from the President to secure the nation."
As soon as the vote closed, Trump posted on social media: "The Democrats' attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!" He had signaled the day before that he would stand by his defense secretary regardless of what the House decided. Vice President JD Vance added his voice on X: "Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not."
Tillis Is the Number That Will Not Go Away
Whatever comfort the administration drew from Tuesday's outcome ran into a complication it cannot vote away. Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina told reporters he is "likely to vote against Hegseth" and would vote to convict if a Senate trial were ever held. The statement carried unusual weight because Tillis was the pivotal figure who confirmed Hegseth in the first place: the nomination deadlocked 50-50 in January 2025 before Vice President Vance broke the tie.
Tillis has since described that confirmation as his biggest regret, citing what he called an "amateurish" stewardship of the Pentagon and poor strategic judgment on the Iran conflict. While a Senate conviction remains out of reach — the two-thirds threshold would require 67 votes in a chamber where Republicans hold 53 seats — his public posture confirms that opposition to Hegseth has taken root beyond the House and beyond one departing Kentucky Republican.
The Incoming Congress Starts From a Different Place
The tabling vote landed just one week after midterm elections that returned Democrats to power in a result shaped heavily by public opposition to the Iran war — roughly six in ten voters, according to AP VoteCast, said the United States made the wrong decision by going to war. The incoming Democratic majority, seated in January, will not inherit the procedural tools Republicans used Tuesday to shut the debate down before it began. With no guarantee that a future impeachment push would face the same fragmented opposition, the 211-204 outcome may read less like a final answer than an expiring stay of execution.

sources.news_title: US house rejects impeachment bid against defense secretary
sources.text:
The United States House of Representatives has rejected an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over allegations that he authorised military operations against Iran without congressional approval.
As reported by the BBC on Wednesday, a majority of lawmakers on Tuesday voted to refer the impeachment resolution, introduced by Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, to the House Judiciary Committee, effectively blocking the move.
The vote was 211 to 204, with all Republicans except Massie supporting the referral of the resolution to the Republican-led committee.
The impeachment effort accused Hegseth of waging war against Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, alongside other alleged misconduct, including overseeing extrajudicial killings during US military operations against suspected drug-carrying vessels in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
Massie had introduced eight articles of impeachment, arguing that Hegseth had violated the law and should be held accountable.
However, the attempt was widely considered unlikely to succeed, given the Republicans’ control of the House and their continued support for President Donald Trump.
Reacting to the outcome, Trump celebrated the defeat of the impeachment effort in a post on his Truth Social platform, describing it as a failed attempt against the defence secretary.
He also praised Hegseth, referring to him as a patriot and highlighting what he described as achievements of the administration’s military policies.
Hegseth had earlier dismissed the impeachment effort as a political stunt, describing it as a “farce” and “sabotage”.
Speaking at a news conference on Tuesday, he accused his critics of using the process to undermine the administration.
Massie, however, expressed disappointment over the outcome, although he said he was not surprised by the vote.
According to CBS, he criticised lawmakers who opposed the resolution, arguing that Congress had failed to exercise its responsibility.
The congressman had previously acknowledged that his impeachment effort might not succeed immediately but said it could pressure Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats assumed control of Congress.
Meanwhile, the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, indicated that the opposition party would continue pursuing accountability over the allegations.
“This is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning,” Jeffries said after the vote.
The impeachment resolution could be revisited when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress in January, following their victories in the November 2026 midterm elections.
However, the referral of the measure to the Judiciary Committee effectively ends the current effort, given the limited time remaining in the present congressional session.
House Speaker Mike Johnson had earlier predicted that the impeachment attempt would fail, reflecting the Republican leadership’s opposition to the move.
The development comes amid growing political disagreements over the Trump administration’s military operations against Iran and the extent of congressional authority over the use of military force.

sources.news_title: Massie’s effort to impeach Hegseth fails miserably, but Democrats vow to try again next year
sources.text:
Massie’s effort to impeach Hegseth fails miserably, but Democrats vow to try again next year
The impeachment effort failed on Tuesday, thanks to 11 absentee Democrats.
War Secretary Pete Hegseth avoided the formal initiation of an ugly impeachment fight on Tuesday. His battle to keep his job is, however, far from over.
The effort was initiated on Monday by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who introduced eight articles of impeachment that accused Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors.
'People should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote.'
In addition to accusing the war secretary of waging war in contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, the articles of impeachment accused him ordering extrajudicial killings, suppressing free speech, "ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties," kidnapping Venezuelan ex-President Nicolas Maduro, and conducting an "unlawful war in Yemen."
Democrats appeared more than happy to help Massie oust Hegseth.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.J.), for instance, said that he was a "hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," claiming that the war secretary has "abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe."
RELATED: With Trump's backing, Hegseth vows to fight impeachment
Pete Kiehart/Bloomberg/Getty Images
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) similarly advocated for removing Hegseth and welcomed Massie's resolution.
On Tuesday morning, Hegseth held a press conference where he called the impeachment effort a "farce" and a "political spectacle" driven by Massie's "ego and resentment." He also argued that the allegations from Massie are not high crimes and misdemeanors but rather "policy disagreements."
Several hours later, the House considered whether to hold a floor vote on the articles of impeachment.
The House ultimately voted 211-204 on Tuesday to refer the articles to the GOP-controlled House Judiciary Committee, effectively killing the impeachment effort for the remainder of the current Congress.
Massie, who is leaving Congress in January, was the lone Republican who voted with Democrats to advance the articles of impeachment toward a floor vote. Seven Republicans didn't bother to vote.
Eleven Democrats did not show up to work and therefore did not vote on the procedural motion either. Given their votes would have tipped the scales, many of the no-shows have issued excuses.
RELATED: Iran conflict was 'crucial' factor in Republican rout: Exit polls
Alex Wong/Getty Images
A spokesperson for Rep. Melanie Stansbury claimed, for instance, that the New Mexico Democrat was allegedly "blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due a traffic incident."
Democrat Reps. Jonathan Jackson (Illinois), Marilyn Strickland (Wash.), and Laura Gillen (N.Y) also blamed traffic for their failures to appear.
Virginia Rep. Eugene Vindman said he was at an event; Nevada Rep. Steven Horsford claimed he had a personal emergency; and California Rep. Nancy Pelosi was attending a Veterans Day celebration, reported the Washington Sun.
New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was among the Democrats who were prickled by the absences, telling Forbes, "We're here to do a job, and the same way I had to clock in when I worked at a restaurant, we got to clock in and do our work here."
California Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove appeared especially peeved, telling a reporter, "We knew that this vote was coming, so people should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote. There is no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues."
The Pentagon's rapid response account on X posted an AI-generated image of Massie crying with the caption, "The disgruntled, ousted congressman’s attempt to impeach Secretary Hegseth has FAILED!"
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in statement to Blaze News, "Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists."
"The Department of War has followed the law and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America," added Parnell.
Trump mocked Massie and his Democratic House colleagues over the failed impeachment effort, writing, "The Democrats’ attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED! Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete."
After defending his "victories" in Venezuela and Iran and characterizing the vote as an "EXONERATION" of Hegseth, Trump added that the Democrats' effort "to weaponize and abuse the United States of America" must be stopped.
While Hegseth's job appears to be safe for now, Democrats have signaled they will wield their majorities in both chambers of Congress to remove him next year.
Following the vote, Rep. Jeffries noted that Democrats have secured a "historic" majority in Congress and said of the Hegseth impeach effort, "This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning."
Jeffries is reportedly in the planning stage for a new impeachment effort in the next Congress.
Colorado Rep. Brittany Pettersen, one of the Democrats who missed the vote on Tuesday, tweeted, "Next year House Democrats will impeach Hegseth and neither Johnson nor Trump will be able to stop us."

Trump Gloats as Republicans Kill Bid to Impeach Pete Hegseth
sources.text:
Trump Gloats as Republicans Kill Bid to Impeach Pete Hegseth
Pete Hegseth has dodged impeachment — for now.
Republicans in the House of Representatives successfully blocked an effort to impeach the secretary of defense on Tuesday night amid a controversial, chaotic run as one of Donald Trump’s most loyal Cabinet members, highlighted by a disastrous, still-ongoing war of choice against Iran.
The House voted 211-204 to move the impeachment resolution to committee, where Republicans, who for the rest of the year control the chamber’s committees, can leave it to languish. Eleven Democrats missed the vote, potentially depriving the party of a huge win coming off the midterm elections. The absent Democrats were: Reps. Julia Brownley (D-Calif.), Lou Correa (D-Calif.), Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), Laura Gillen (D-N.Y.), Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.), Brittany Pettersen (D-Colo.), Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.), Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), Marilyn Strickland (D-Wash.), and Frederica Wilson (D-Fla.).
Seven Republicans also missed the vote.
Axios reported that several Democrats who missed the vote were unable to make it because they were attending an Elect Democratic Women event and got stuck in bumper-to-bumper traffic on their way to the Capitol.
Hegseth would have been the second secretary of defense (or war) and third Cabinet member in history to be impeached, after Secretary of War William Belknap in 1876 and Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024.
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has been a thorn in the Trump administration’s side throughout his second term in office, brought articles of impeachment to Congress almost immediately after the midterm elections. Massie’s resolution included eight articles of impeachment, detailing crimes including violations of the War Powers Agreement of 1973, failing to minimize civilian casualties, and conducting extrajudicial killings.
“I hope Hegseth addresses the eight articles of impeachment,” Massie said on Monday afternoon, adding that he hopes Hegseth “doesn’t get up and misquote the Bible in Quentin Tarantino fashion and do some pullups and call everybody fat and gay,” referencing a widely mocked speech Hegseth gave at the Pentagon earlier this year and Hegseth’s obsession with masculinity.
On Tuesday morning, Hegseth called a press conference to respond to Massie’s impeachment inquiry. “This is not about me,” Hegseth said, claiming impeachment proponents were really targeting America’s “warriors.”
Hegseth and Trump celebrated Republicans blocking the vote. “The Democrats’ attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED! Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete,” the president wrote in a post shared by Hegseth. “Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot. The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!”
The Department of Defense, meanwhile, posted an AI-generated image of Massie in tears.
Under Trump, Hegseth, a former Fox News host and Minnesota National Guard infantry officer, redubbed the Department of Defense the “Department of War,” spearheading a comprehensive overhaul of the leviathan U.S. military apparatus in order to make it more masculine, less woke, and more “lethal.” This endeavor included sweeping staff changes, policy adjustments, and the creation of several new taxpayer-funded programs. Hegseth proclaimed that his Department of War would be an “AI-first military,” and instituted new rules for physical fitness and grooming among his troops.
“We are no longer the woke department or the weak department,” Hegseth said at a “State of the Force” speech last month. “No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors. Just tough, ready, committed troops.”
In February, Hegseth became the standard-bearer for Trump’s war on Iran, which has largely caused the economic crisis that eroded Trump’s hold over the party and washed out Republicans in the 2026 midterms. Throughout the war, however, Hegseth has been steadfast in his commitment. He also presided over Trump’s lightning-fast invasion of Venezuela, which resulted in the capture and imprisonment of President Nicolás Maduro. Massie’s articles of impeachment also specifically referenced Hegseth’s actions in combating so-called cartels in Latin America, including the policy of airstrikes on civilian boats in international waters, which have killed dozens, if not hundreds, of people since Trump took office.
A further charge alleged that Hegseth suppressed Sen. Mark Kelly’s First Amendment rights when he “sought to intimidate” Kelly after the senator urged U.S. service members to disobey unlawful orders. Hegseth threatened to recall Kelly from active duty and issued a letter of censure over Kelly’s comments, which Massie argues were protected both by Kelly’s role as a senator and by the First Amendment.
The rift between Massie and Trump began over the botched, partial release of the Epstein files, which Massie correctly recognized as a growing political risk. Massie was unsparing in his critiques of Trump over his associations with notorious pedophile Jeffrey Epstein, which eventually led Trump to endorse his rival in the 2026 primary for his congressional seat in Kentucky.

Democrat Scott Colom won election to the U.S. Senate representing Mississippi, defeating Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday. Colom will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era.
Gearing up for the loss of GOP control in Congress next year, the White House warned Democrats that planned investigations of Trump could cross into criminal conduct. House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office, though Trump and his administration have long denied any wrongdoing.
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, observed Veterans Day at Arlington National Cemetery. His appearance there came a day after nine Kennedy family members asked a judge to block Trump’s plan to build a towering memorial arch, saying the 250-foot structure would cast a shadow over their relatives’ grave sites at the cemetery.
Here’s the Latest:
Descendants of enslaved people among those celebrating Colom’s victory
“I am here to celebrate being on the right side of history,” said Vera Finley, as she awaited Colom’s remarks at his victory celebration in Jackson.
“I am here to celebrate my parents and my grandparents. I am not one generation out of the cotton fields,” Finley continued. “Both of my parents picked cotton. And my great grandmother was sold here as a slave from Virginia to here. So I am so excited to be on this side of history.”
Finley said Colom’s backers “voted for change” and are “so excited about actually seeing that our votes matter.”
She said she hopes his election yields more unity.
“I hope that justice comes out of it,” she said. “I hope that love comes out of it.”
China’s Xi set to attend G20 summit in Florida, State Department says
Chinese leader Xi Jinping is expected to attend the Group of 20 summit in Florida next month, the State Department said, offering the first confirmation of the visit.
Trump travels to China next week to attend an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, where the two leaders also are expected to meet.
In a phone call Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi discussed Trump’s “upcoming travel to the APEC summit in China” and Xi’s “upcoming visit to Florida to attend the G20 summit,” the State Department said.
The Chinese foreign ministry’s readout only said the leaders would support each other in hosting the summits.
The State Department said Rubio and Wang also agreed on the importance of the presidents discussing peace and denuclearization, “including at any potential trilateral leaders meeting with Russia.”
Hyde-Smith shares a concession video on social media after calling Colom
The 67-year-old Republican spoke for two minutes, seated next to an American flag.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
Hyde-Smith, a former state agriculture commissioner, was first appointed to the Senate in 2018. She won a special election and then a full term in 2020.
She said in the video she’s most proud of helping farmers and veterans, opposing abortion rights and securing federal money for Mississippi.
“While my time in the United States Senate may be coming to an end,” she said, “my love for Mississippi and my determination to stand up for what is right never will.”
Why AP called the Mississippi Senate race for Scott Colom
The AP on Wednesday declared Colom the winner in the race for U.S. Senate in Mississippi after several counties reported updated results — including those of last-to-count provisional ballots.
Colom led Hyde-Smith, the Republican incumbent, by 43 votes following the final election night update in Mississippi, which arrived at 3:03 a.m. from Pike County.
Not only has Colom’s lead grown larger as counties in Mississippi have completed their vote count and reported on the outcome of their review of provisional ballots in the days since, but he’s won the vast majority of these final updates — in every region of the state and in all but the most Republican counties — by a large margin.
The AP called the race for the Colom after officials in Jackson County updated their vote count with an additional 2,173 votes.
The update put Colom up by 4,669 votes out of 962,237 counted, or 0.5 percentage points. To come back and take the lead, Hyde-Smith needed to win these final vote updates in GOP-leaning counties such as Jackson. Instead, Colom won the update in Jackson by just over 1 percentage point.
Hyde-Smith has called Colom to concede Mississippi Senate race
A spokesman for the Mississippi Republican confirmed that she has called her Democratic challenger to concede and congratulate him.
Hyde-Smith has been quiet through more than a week of local officials counting absentee and provisional ballots.
She and her advisers previously had not ruled out legal action if the Colom was declared the winner.
Mississippi elects Colom as state’s first Black US senator since Reconstruction
Colom’s victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states.
The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom’s favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old prosecutor, capitalized on the state’s large Black population, discontent with the economy and incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.
Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.

Colom will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era.
Colom’s victory also offers Democrats an unexpected boost in their effort to win control of the Senate.
A local prosecutor, he waged an aggressive campaign to take advantage of a tough national environment for Republicans and the fact that Mississippi has a larger share of Black voters than any other state.
Hyde-Smith, a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, was trying to win her second full term. She was first appointed to fill a vacancy and then won a 2018 special election.
The Associated Press declared Colom the winner at 5:58 p.m. EST.
Trump administration wants to sell public lands and shrink ‘federal estate’
The Trump administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate,” according to a new plan presented by the Interior Department.
Agency officials said the sale of federal property would allow the government to focus resources on “nationally significant” lands, which were not defined.
They offered no details on what parcels could be sold, nor the scope or location of potential sales.
The proposal drew quick pushback from some lawmakers, including Trump’s former Interior secretary, Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke, showing it faces strong headwinds in Congress even before Democrats assume the majority in January.
Trump administration plans to make it harder to get grocery assistance
The Trump administration is planning to make it harder to get food aid through the federal government’s grocery assistance program that serves about 1 in 10 Americans.
The administration says the proposed rule would close a loophole by no longer allowing some people who receive benefits under the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program to automatically qualify for the separate Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
About 6.3 million people could lose eligibility for SNAP by the 2029 fiscal year if the proposed change takes effect, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which administers the program. That is on top of 5.5 million people who already have lost SNAP benefits over the past year.
Conservation group says Trump’s words on arch don’t follow actions
Trump said on Veterans Day that the towering arch he wants to build would be dedicated to the U.S. military and those who served, saying “They’ve been waiting for it for 200 years.”
But arch discussions didn’t include veterans until late in the process, said Jimi Shaughnessy, the veterans program manager with the National Parks Conservation Association.
“It’s a strange position to take when the administration did not consult veteran groups or military organizations at the start,” said Shaughnessy, a veteran. “They brought these groups in at the tail end when there was opposition.”
The arch is embroiled in multiple lawsuits from groups challenging its construction.
The plaintiffs now include three Vietnam veterans, an architectural historian, the District of Columbia and Virginia, and members of the Kennedy family.
Hegseth and his group face reprimand at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery.
Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh can be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that “all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”
“The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored — and will always honor — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe,” chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement. “While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.”
Lawmaker indicates subpoena could be ahead for Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
Rep. John Moolenaar, chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, told Fox Business on Wednesday that there “will likely be subpoenas” for Huang to appear on Capitol Hill if the co-founder of the computer chip company doesn’t respond by day’s end to a request to meet with lawmakers.
Moolenaar, House Foreign Affairs Committee chair Brian Mast and House Intelligence Committee chair Rick Crawford sent a letter last week to Huang, requesting a closed-door briefing on Nvidia’s security protocols and Huang’s interactions with a businesswoman accused of spying for China.
Moolenaar told Fox Business that the Republican lawmakers wanted to know if Beijing was able to access “privileged information” and if it was able to influence U.S. national security policy.
“I think transparency is very important for him at this point,” Moolenaar said.
Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to an AP request for comment.
Colom keeps razor-thin lead in Mississippi Senate race
More than a week after Election Day, Colom leads Hyde-Smith by about 3,800 votes, though Republican-leaning counties like Lee and Jackson have not yet released their final results.
Further updates are expected on Thursday, Nov. 12.
If Colom wins, Democrats will hold 55 seats in the Senate, and will have made the party’s largest midterm gain since 1986, during Ronald Reagan’s second term.
Top Oversight committee lawmakers react to White House warning
Rep. Robert Garcia, who will likely chair the House Oversight Committee when Democrats take over next year, said Trump “is clearly hiding something” after the White House issued a warning about their planned probes.
“He needs to understand that Congress is a coequal branch of government,” Garcia told reporters outside the Capitol.
GOP Rep. James Comer, the committee’s current chair, said the committee is “very independent” when asked about the White House’s attempt to limit its authority.
“Regardless of who is in the White House, there’s always going to be a strong desire for the Oversight Committee to be a check and balance on the executive branch, regardless of the political scenario,” Comer said.
Trump is speaking at Arlington National Cemetery
Trump has told veterans gathered in the amphitheater that service members “are indeed our protection in battle.”
He says military families “are amazing” and are “among the very best of our nation.”
Trump is also recognizing individual veterans and asking them to stand, including a 103-year-old who served in World War II.
Immigration arrests go on unabated despite Trump’s misgivings over GOP’s wipeout
It’s business as usual for Trump’s deportation offensive despite the repudiation of voters in a Republican elections wipeout.
In Los Angeles, armored and masked immigration officers blocked a hospital emergency room driveway in a heavily Latino neighborhood. In Alabama, twin 19-year-olds from Venezuela were arrested while driving back to college. And an 8-year-old Haitian boy was taken away from his uncle in San Diego.
After Democrats trounced the GOP, Trump told CBS’ “60 Minutes” on Friday that his crackdown may have been “too tough” and said “I’d love to do something on immigration” with the rival party. But then he announced Stephen Miller, the architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, as his new chief of staff.
“Deportations will continue,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin posted the day after the election. “This includes on Thanksgiving, Christmas, and Election Day.”
Bessent moves to a military base over safety concerns, an AP source says
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was forced to relocate to a military base over concerns for his safety after spending months executing a massive economic campaign against Iran aimed at severing all of Tehran’s remaining financial ties around the world.
A person familiar with the matter, who spoke to The Associated Press on Wednesday on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details, said the relocation was partly due to media reports that helped identify Bessent’s home address. The relocation was earlier reported by The New York Times.
Other top Trump administration officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, live on military bases.
Trump observes Veterans Day at Arlington National Cemetery
The president laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown soldier to honor the nation’s veterans. He’ll also deliver remarks at the amphitheater.
Trump’s motorcade took a different route to the revered burial ground instead of traveling over Memorial Bridge and around a traffic circle where he wants to build a triumphal arch.
Trump’s appearance at the cemetery comes a day after nine Kennedy family members joined several lawsuits seeking to block construction, saying the towering 250-foot (76-meter) arch would cast a shadow over their relatives’ grave sites there.
Rubio speaks with Chinese counterpart before Trump-Xi meeting
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi had a positive and constructive phone talk with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday, Chinese state media reported.
Trump is set to travel to Asia next week and meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Wang told Rubio that China is willing to strengthen communications and cooperation with the U.S. and properly handle differences and sensitive issues.
The State Department didn’t immediately release a readout of the call.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent extolled the U.S.-China bond as “one of this century’s most consequential relationships” at a Tuesday night gala in New York with Chinese ambassador to the U.S. Xie Feng.
Mississippi’s Senate seat remains too early to call
Democrat Scott Colom was about 3,000 votes ahead of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday with 98% of the votes counted.
Tuesday was the deadline for receiving mail-in absentee ballots. Counties are required to submit their certified election results — including tallies of provisional ballots — to the state by Friday. It is unclear exactly how many ballots are left to count.
Unlike in some other states, there is no central vote reporting system for Mississippi, and few counties release election results online. Instead, Associated Press journalists and analysts communicate with each of the state’s 82 counties directly for the latest available information on vote counts.
The state will certify its results on Dec. 3.
The AP may declare a winner if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
Kennedy family members ask judge to block Trump’s arch
A legal filing by nine members of the Kennedy political dynasty argues that Trump’s plan to build a towering, 250-foot (76-meter) high memorial arch would cast a permanent shadow over their relatives’ grave sites at Arlington National Cemetery, fundamentally altering the experience for visitors.
Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump’s health and human services secretary, did not join his relatives’ motion before U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, who temporarily prohibited the Trump administration last week from breaking ground.
Senators Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy were buried close to the eternal flame marking the grave site of their slain brother, President John F. Kennedy. The trio of memorials draw millions of visitors each year.
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said it’s unfortunate that “some members of the Kennedy family” are seeking “to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation.”
Zelenskyy urges US to pressure Russia to end the war
Kyiv’s delegation was expected to meet later Wednesday with representatives of Europe and NATO who were closed out of the talks. Moscow doesn’t want European countries, which are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations.
Kushner said a goal of his Moscow meeting Thursday is to get Europeans added to the talks. Both Ukraine and Russia need clarity on postwar security arrangements, and European countries, the EU and NATO have to be involved to build consensus, Kushner said.
“Ukraine’s priority is to end the war as soon as possible with a dignified peace,” Zelenskyy said on X. “We believe that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy. It is essential that the United States have a strong position and exert influence on the source of this war — that is Russia.”

A legal filing by nine members of the Kennedy political dynasty argues that Trump’s plan to build a towering, 250-foot (76-meter) high memorial arch would cast a permanent shadow over their relatives’ grave sites at Arlington National Cemetery, fundamentally altering the experience for visitors.
Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump’s health and human services secretary, did not join his relatives’ motion before U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, who temporarily prohibited the Trump administration last week from breaking ground.
Senators Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy were buried close to the eternal flame marking the grave site of their slain brother, President John F. Kennedy. The trio of memorials draw millions of visitors each year.
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said it’s unfortunate that “some members of the Kennedy family” are seeking “to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation.”
Zelenskyy urges US to pressure Russia to end the war
Kyiv’s delegation was expected to meet later Wednesday with representatives of Europe and NATO who were closed out of the talks. Moscow doesn’t want European countries, which are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations.
Kushner said a goal of his Moscow meeting Thursday is to get Europeans added to the talks. Both Ukraine and Russia need clarity on postwar security arrangements, and European countries, the EU and NATO have to be involved to build consensus, Kushner said.
“Ukraine’s priority is to end the war as soon as possible with a dignified peace,” Zelenskyy said on X. “We believe that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy. It is essential that the United States have a strong position and exert influence on the source of this war — that is Russia.”

sources.news_title: House Republicans narrowly block Hegseth impeachment
sources.text: House Republicans narrowly block Hegseth impeachment November 11, 2026 US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (Shutterstock) (Shutterstock) House Republicans narrowly block Hegseth impeachment Tweet Join Group Join WhatsApp Group Email https://worldisraelnews.com/house-republicans-narrowly-block-hegseth-impeachment/ Email Print House Republicans block bid to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Iran war as Trump declares victory. By World Israel News Staff Republicans in the US House of Representatives blocked an attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday, voting 211-204 to derail an effort by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky to remove the Pentagon chief over his handling of the war against Iran and other military operations. The House voted to refer Massie’s eight articles of impeachment to the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee, effectively preventing them from reaching a full House vote before the current Congress ends in January. The procedural motion received support from 210 Republicans and one independent, while all 203 Democrats who participated in the vote opposed it. Massie was the only Republican to vote against referring the resolution to committee. President Donald Trump celebrated the result, declaring in a Truth Social post that the effort to remove Hegseth had “miserably FAILED!” Trump praised the defense secretary’s performance and attacked Massie, who has repeatedly criticized the administration’s military campaign against Iran. The president said US military victories in Iran and Venezuela, along with improvements in military recruitment, had led to the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.” Massie introduced the eight articles of impeachment Monday, accusing Hegseth of violating federal law and the Constitution during military operations in Iran, Yemen, Venezuela, the Caribbean Sea and the Eastern Pacific. Read Trump denies he considered firing Hegseth after Republican defeat Three of the articles focused on the war against Iran, which began in February. Massie argued that the Trump administration launched the campaign without obtaining congressional authorization and subsequently disregarded legislation directing the withdrawal of American forces from the conflict. “By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable,” Massie said in a statement announcing the impeachment effort. The Kentucky congressman also accused Hegseth of continuing military operations beyond the deadlines established under the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which generally requires presidents to end unauthorized military engagements within 60 days, with a possible additional 30-day withdrawal period. Another impeachment article accused Hegseth of weakening Pentagon procedures intended to minimize civilian casualties during military operations, including those conducted against Iran. The remaining articles concerned American strikes against suspected drug-smuggling vessels in waters near South America, the January operation that captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, military operations in Yemen and alleged retaliation against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona. Massie accused the defense secretary of targeting Kelly for participating in a video reminding American service members that they are obligated to refuse unlawful military orders. Hegseth strongly rejected the allegations during a Pentagon press conference Tuesday morning, describing the impeachment effort as politically motivated retaliation by a departing Republican lawmaker. Read Trump warns Iran would use nukes within 24 hours, predicts war will end soon “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said. The defense secretary argued that presidents from both political parties had conducted military operations without specific congressional authorization and that no previous defense secretary had been impeached for carrying out such missions. He maintained that the operations under scrutiny were lawful and had been conducted under Trump’s authority as commander in chief. Hegseth also accused Massie of attempting to undermine American service members and the administration’s military achievements. “This is not patriotism. This is sabotage,” he declared. The White House separately issued a statement opposing the impeachment resolution, arguing that it would consume congressional time and undermine the administration’s national security agenda. Vice President JD Vance also defended Hegseth, dismissing the impeachment effort as unjustified. “Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not,” Vance wrote on X. Massie, who lost his Republican primary earlier this year to Trump-backed former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein, has remained one of the administration’s most vocal Republican critics over the Iran war. Before the vote, Massie argued that his resolution offered Republicans an opportunity to address Hegseth’s conduct before Democrats take control of Congress in January. “My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what’s coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year,” Massie warned. sources.news_title: US Republicans derail bid to impeach Pentagon chief
sources.text:
US Republicans derail bid to impeach Pentagon chief
Republicans still hold a narrow House majority until January, when Democrats take control
Republicans in the US House of Representatives on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war, handing President Donald Trump a victory days after his party's crushing midterm election defeat.
The House voted 211 to 204 to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively derailing a planned vote Wednesday on whether to bring formal charges against the embattled Pentagon chief.
The resolution was introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, a Trump critic who was the only member of his party to oppose the procedural maneuver, according to US media.
The impeachment drive had threatened to deepen Trump's troubles after Democrats swept last week's midterms, with anger at the sputtering Iran war and soaring fuel prices helping drive voters to a historic rejection of Republicans.
Republicans still hold a narrow House majority until January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. And 11 Democrats missed the vote.
Trump hailed the procedural defeat as an "EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," in a post on Truth Social, while Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, in a post on X, called the vote as a "TOTAL VICTORY!"
"We look forward to ending this sham impeachment in the committee room, where facts will continue to prevail and this distraction can be put to rest," Parnell added.
Hegseth earlier Tuesday dismissed the impeachment effort as a "farce" and defended his record leading the Iran war and other military operations under Trump.
"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," he said at a Pentagon press conference, branding the accusations "slander" and "sabotage."
Moments after Hegseth's televised appearance, Trump signaled his support.
"Pete Hegseth gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS," the 80-year-old president wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Vice President JD Vance also backed the defense secretary, saying he had "obviously not" committed impeachable offenses.
'Would do it again'
Massie's eight articles of impeachment accused Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorization and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.
Several related to the eight-month Iran war, accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution, which places limits on US military interventions without congressional authorization.
Other allegations involved the 2025 conflict with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which Massie branded "extrajudicial killings."
He also accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech by trying to punish Democratic Senator Mark Kelly over a video urging military and intelligence personnel to refuse illegal orders.
Hegseth defended the operations in Yemen, Iran, Venezuela and against alleged drug smugglers, while seeking to equate the impeachment effort with an attack on US troops.
"I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow," he said.
The decision to send the resolution to committee halts the immediate impeachment drive but does not prevent Democrats from reviving the effort after taking control of Congress in January.
Massie, who lost his Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger, will leave Congress at the end of his term.

sources.news_title: House Republicans SAVE Pete Hegseth from Impeachment... Will the Dems Go After Him in January?
sources.text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has survived an impeachment attempt after House Republicans blocked a resolution accusing him of misconduct involving U.S. military operations overseas.
The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to send the measure to committee, effectively ending the effort for now.
Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, introduced the resolution over Hegseth’s handling of the war in Iran and military actions in Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean.
Massie was the only Republican to vote alongside Democrats against shelving the measure.
“Hegseth has violated the norms of war, and it’s to the disadvantage and the dishonor of our country, and to the danger of our soldiers in future conflicts,” Massie argued.
Hegseth fired back during a Pentagon news conference earlier Tuesday, dismissing the impeachment effort as politically motivated.
“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” he declared.
The defense secretary maintained that the military operations in question were lawful and defended his loyalty to Trump.
“If standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week,” Hegseth said, referencing Trump’s previous impeachments.
Trump quickly backed his Cabinet member, awarding him an “A PLUS, PLUS, PLUS” on Truth Social.
Although Hegseth remains in office, Democrats could revisit his conduct when they assume control of the House in January. Hakeem Jeffries, who will most likely be named House of Representatives Speaker that month, has already said that he’s a “hard yes” on impeacing Hegseth.

sources.news_title: House GOP blocks Thomas Massie's attempt to impeach Pete Hegseth
sources.text:
(Daily Caller News Foundation) — House Republicans blocked an immediate vote on Republican Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie’s resolution Tuesday to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth in a procedural vote.
Massie introduced the articles of impeachment Monday, which included eight charges accusing Hegseth of “operating in contravention of three specific provisions of the War Powers Resolution of 1973.” House leadership’s procedural vote referred Massie’s resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, where Republicans are currently in the majority.
Unless the Judiciary Committee passes the resolution, Massie’s impeachment effort would remain stalled throughout the remainder of the 119th Congress. House Democrats could revive impeachment efforts when they are in the majority in January.
Massie said he would request a separate vote on each article if leadership blocked the vote.
“I’ve heard from several members they agree with some of the Articles of Impeachment but not all of them,” Massie said on X. “If the motion to kill my resolution by referring it to committee fails, and we proceed to the Articles themselves, I’ll request a vote on each of the Articles separately.”
House and Senate Democrats supported the impeachment effort, meaning they could successfully move forward with impeaching Hegseth when they reclaim the majority in the next Congress. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he was a “hard yes” on impeaching Hegseth.
Massie accused Hegseth of extrajudicial killings, stating he oversaw the killings of at least 221 individuals in international waters, and of suppressing free speech by allegedly intimidating Democratic Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly for calling on service members to “refuse illegal orders.” He alleged Hegseth waged an unlawful war in Yemen.
The resolution alleged that Hegseth “executed unlawful orders” through the U.S. involvement in the Iran war. Massie argued that Hegseth “directed and caused” U.S. Armed Forces to be involved in hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran without Congress’ approval or declaration of war against the regime.
Massie alleged Hegseth continued to direct the U.S. Armed Forces to engage in hostilities against Iran after the House and Senate passed a concurrent war powers resolution, which directed the president to remove the Armed Forces from “unauthorized hostilities.” The resolution was concurrent, meaning President Donald Trump’s administration had no legal obligation to comply with the directive since concurrent resolutions have no force of law.
The resolution alleged Hegseth would “remain a threat to the Constitution” if he remained in office.
Hegseth dismissed the impeachment articles, calling the effort a “political spectacle” during a Tuesday press conference.
“What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” Hegseth said.
Massie initially introduced the articles on Sept. 15, although the House left early for the October recess before a floor vote could be held.
At least six Republican senators appeared open to a trial, including Republican Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy, who lost his primary to a Trump-endorsed challenger. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina said he would vote to oust Hegseth from his position if given the chance.
Republican Sens. John Curtis of Utah, John Boozman of Arkansas and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia said Tuesday they would examine the evidence of wrongdoing.
Massie lost his primary to Republican Kentucky Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, who received Trump’s endorsement. Trump wanted Massie ousted from Congress due to his criticisms of his actions in Iran and his push to release the files surrounding Jeffrey Epstein.
This article was originally published by the Daily Caller News Foundation.

sources.news_title: Democrats blame everyone but themselves for botched impeachment vote
sources.text:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth survived impeachment in Congress because 11 Democrats were caught in traffic, CBS News reported after the vote Tuesday evening. With those 11 votes, Hegseth would have been impeached.
Axios reporter Andrew Solender reported on X, "Per several members: Some of the House Democrats who missed the Hegseth impeachment vote were on their way back from an Elect Democratic Women event at a venue about 1.5 miles down Pennsylvania Ave. but got caught in a bumper-to-bumper traffic jam on Independence Ave. (The road on the House side of the Capitol complex). Some members found other ways to get back to the Capitol because their cars were effectively stopped on the road."
As Solender explained, one Democrat got out of the car and walked to make it. Another went around the traffic and did a drop-off on the U.S. Senate side and got to the Capitol from there. The event was only 1.5 miles away.
Rep. Eugene Vindman (D-Va.) told Politico's Mark Satter the Democrats were “at an event and didn’t make it back in time."
He added that it “should have never happened, but that's the way it played out."
Two members posted that they added their vote after the fact.
Progressives online are furious.
"BS excuse. They went to the event knowing full well they had a duty to be back on time for the impeachment vote, and they failed to show up on time. That is unprofessional. Stop the bulls—— excuses for these grown-up folks," complained Adua Sam.
Another noted that if Republicans can roll in "half-dead [Mitch] McConnell," these members can walk a mile to the building to cast their vote.
Andrew Noh, Rep. Marilyn Strickland’s (D-Wash.) chief of staff, said, “The congresswoman was stuck behind a motorcade and missed the vote by one minute. She would have voted against the motion to refer.” She was among those members who entered her vote for the record but it was late.
"For two days everyone knew the vote was at 5:30pm and that Republicans would use every tool they had in their toolbox to table the impeachment with a committee referral vote. Shame on you," one woman told Strickland. "The stakes are too big. You should have been in the chamber an hour early to vote, not an hour late due to 'traffic.' Did you go to the Merrick Garland School of Driving?"
Some Democrats are now complaining that the Republicans should have kept the vote open longer.
"Try that one with your boss," said the Jack Hopkins Show host. "Or your customers. Winners leave early. Losers explain late. You knew the vote was coming. Show up or step aside."
Some critics questioned if the hold up was the result of dirty tricks.
There is a historic example of politicians using traffic jams to their advantage, most notably Gov. Chris Christie's (R-N.J.) "Bridgegate" scandal.
In 2004, Wisconsin Democratic campaign workers slashed tires on vehicles Republicans had rented to transport voters and poll monitors. The Chicago Tribune reported that 25 cars and vans were disabled, delaying the transportation operation. The four staffers pleaded no contest.
In Brazil on Election Day 2022, federal highway police stopped vehicles and buses carrying voters, particularly in the northeast, where Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had strong support against incumbent Jair Bolsonaro. The electoral court ordered the operations to stop.
There was even an episode of "The West Wing" in which President Jeb Bartlett's staff sent the presidential motorcade through New York City traffic, causing additional jams. It left his Republican opponent embarrassingly late for a major event benefiting Catholic Charities.

sources.news_title: Pete Hegseth impeachment resolution sent to Judiciary Committee after House vote
sources.text:
The FINANCIAL — The Pete Hegseth impeachment resolution was sent to the House Judiciary Committee on Tuesday after the House voted 211–204 to refer it, halting an immediate vote on whether to impeach the defense secretary while leaving the measure before a committee.
The official roll call, No. 317 of the 119th Congress, recorded the vote at 6:02 p.m. The question before members was a motion to refer H. Res. 1655, titled “Impeaching Peter Brian Hegseth, Secretary of Defense, for high crimes and misdemeanors.”
The House Clerk’s record shows 210 Republicans and one independent voting to send the resolution to committee. All 203 Democrats who voted opposed the motion, as did Representative Thomas Massie, the Kentucky Republican who introduced the resolution. Eighteen members did not vote.
The procedural result meant the House did not vote on the articles of impeachment themselves. Instead, the resolution was referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it can be considered under the committee’s procedures. The House floor record shows that Representative Darrell Issa, Republican of California, moved to refer the measure after an hour of debate.
The vote was carried prominently by CBS News, Fox News and the BBC. Those reports agreed on the vote total and on the immediate procedural result: the resolution would not proceed to a full House impeachment vote at this stage.
Massie had announced on Monday that he would force a vote on the measure. In a statement from his office, he said the resolution contained articles concerning Hegseth’s conduct as defense secretary, including an allegation that the Iran war had continued in contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973.
The resolution’s text, posted by Massie’s office, identifies eight articles. The filing is an accusation by its sponsor, not a finding of fact by the House. The referral vote did not decide whether the allegations were true, whether they constituted impeachable conduct or whether Hegseth should be removed.
Hegseth rejected the effort during a Pentagon news conference Tuesday, according to CBS News. The outlet reported that he called the initiative a “farce” and a “political spectacle” and argued that the allegations amounted to policy disagreements rather than high crimes or misdemeanors.
The White House issued a formal statement before the vote urging House members to support the motion to refer. Its statement of administration policy called the proposal politically motivated and said the president has authority to direct military operations to protect national security interests.
The Constitution gives the House the sole power to impeach, but a formal impeachment requires the House to approve articles by a majority vote. If the House impeaches an official, the Senate holds the trial. A referral to committee is not an impeachment and does not initiate a Senate trial.
The House historian’s account of impeachment says committees may investigate allegations, determine whether to pursue articles and report their recommendations to the full House. A committee can take no further action, conduct oversight, hold hearings or report articles to the chamber. None of those later steps occurred in Tuesday’s vote.
The impeachment mechanism has rarely been used against Cabinet officials.
House history records two Cabinet secretaries who have been impeached: Secretary of War William W. Belknap in 1876 and Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. The House historian notes that the Senate acquitted Belknap, while the Senate dismissed the articles against Mayorkas without holding a trial.
Belknap was impeached after House investigators examined allegations that he had accepted payments linked to appointments of post traders at military forts. His case reached the Senate even after he resigned. Mayorkas was impeached by the House over his handling of the southern border, and the Senate later dismissed the articles.
Those precedents do not determine the outcome of H. Res. 1655. They illustrate the limited number of Cabinet impeachments in American history and the separate roles assigned to the two chambers.
Tuesday’s vote reflected a sharply divided House, but the division followed party lines in an unusual direction for the underlying resolution. Republicans overwhelmingly backed the referral. Democrats overwhelmingly opposed it, voting to keep the resolution on a path toward a possible House decision. Massie was the only Republican to vote against referral, according to the official tally.
CBS News reported that the measure accused Hegseth of a series of actions involving military operations and the administration’s conduct of the Iran war. Fox News reported that the resolution contained eight articles and that Republican leaders had sought to avoid a direct floor vote on impeachment.
The partisan vote does not reveal how members would have voted on each article had the resolution reached that stage. The recorded question was limited to whether the House should refer the measure to the Judiciary Committee.
The House’s daily record identifies the measure as a privileged matter. Such resolutions can receive expedited consideration under House rules, which is why Massie was able to bring the proposal to the floor. The House then chose the referral route through a recorded vote.
Massie’s office said before the vote that he was using the resolution to seek accountability for what it described as unlawful conduct. The White House said the administration opposed the resolution because it viewed it as an attempt to contest national-security decisions through impeachment. Those are competing positions from the sponsor and the executive branch.
The roll call also sets clear numerical boundaries around the vote. It was not a vote to convict or acquit, and it did not produce findings on any factual allegation. It was a decision to refer the resolution. The official vote record identifies the motion, the total and each member’s position, providing the formal account on which the subsequent political statements rest.
Hegseth remains in office, and no impeachment trial is pending in the Senate. The House’s recorded action was a committee referral, not a judgment on the merits of the allegations.
The immediate next public step will depend on the Judiciary Committee. The committee has not announced a hearing, a vote or a timetable for H. Res. 1655. The House Clerk’s record lists the referral action, but no committee disposition was shown in the official material available early Wednesday.
The vote came during a period of close attention to congressional oversight of the administration’s military policy. Yet the formal result was narrower than the public debate around it: 211 members voted to refer the resolution, 204 voted against referral, and the House did not decide whether to impeach the secretary.
For now, the measure remains a House resolution before the Judiciary Committee. Any move from referral to a full impeachment vote would require further action by the committee or the House, and any impeachment approved by the House would require a separate Senate trial.

Trump Impeachment Bombshell Unfolds in House
The House voted 211-204 to refer articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, effectively ending the effort for the remainder of the current Congress. Massie had reintroduced eight articles on Monday, accusing Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors related to the Iran war, strikes on alleged drug boats, the capture of Nicolás Maduro, and actions involving Sen. Mark Kelly. The privileged resolution would have forced consideration within two legislative days. The referral vote prevented that from occurring.
Hegseth called the effort a “farce” and a “stunt” during a Pentagon news conference earlier that day. “I stand behind every one of these operations,” he said. “I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow.” Trump said he would stand by Hegseth, noting “He won two wars.”
This was Massie’s second attempt. An earlier version prompted an early recess before the midterms, causing it to expire. Democrats have said they will pursue vigorous investigations of the Pentagon once they take the majority in January. Jeffries has said of Hegseth, “He’s got to go.”
The 211-204 vote was largely along party lines. Several members of both parties were absent. The referral means the articles will not receive a full House vote before the current session ends. Democrats control the next Congress and have indicated the matter remains open.
Massie said after the vote that he was disappointed but not surprised. He has indicated he does not plan to reintroduce the resolution again in the current Congress. The procedural outcome preserves Hegseth’s position through the end of the session.
The articles focused on authorization questions surrounding the Iran operations and related actions. Hegseth defended those operations as lawful and ordered by the president. The referral vote avoided a direct up-or-down decision on the merits of the articles.
Trump posted that the effort had failed. The White House and Pentagon treated the referral as a victory. Democrats framed it as a temporary delay rather than a final resolution.
The privileged-resolution tool forced the House to act. Leadership used the referral motion to dispose of the measure without a vote on the articles themselves. That is a standard procedural option when a privileged resolution reaches the floor.
Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans missed the vote, according to the clerk’s tally. Massie was the sole Republican opposing the referral. The margin was seven votes.
The outcome ends the current impeachment push. Democrats have stated they will examine Hegseth’s record once they organize the House in January. Whether that leads to new articles remains undecided.

sources.news_title: 11 Democrats miss the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote, it fails to pass by 7 votes: 'A major Hakeem Jeffries fail'
sources.text:
Anger is rising among Democrats after the House voted to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The motion, introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, was voted down 211-204, meaning it failed by just seven votes. Eleven Democrats missed the vote and are now facing fury from their constituents as they try to explain what happened.
The eleven Democrats in question are: Julia Brownley, Lou Correa and Nancy Pelosi of California; Laura Gillen of New York; Steven Horsford of Nevada; Jonathan Jackson of Illinois; Brittany Pettersen of Colorado; Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico; Haley Stevens of Michigan; Marilyn Strickland of Washington; and Frederica Wilson of Florida.
Each of them is facing scrutiny as to why they weren’t there to cast their votes, though Hakeem Jeffries, leader of the House Democratic Caucus and House minority leader, is also facing heavy criticism. Krystal Ball of Breaking Points, described this as a “major Hakeem Jeffries fail” and MeidasTouch’s Pablo Manríquez said, “If the caucus actually showed up to vote tonight, Hegseth would be impeached. This is a serious leadership problem.”
What are their excuses?
Several of the Democrats who missed the vote have taken to social media to explain what happened. For example, Rep. Melanie Stansbury explained she was “blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due to a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus.” Reps. Laura Gillen and Jonathan L. Jackson were apparently caught in the same traffic, with Gillen saying “I would have voted no” if she’d been there and Jackson saying he was stuck behind a bus.
Meanwhile, Pelosi’s office has explained that she missed the vote because she returned to San Francisco to accept a lifetime achievement award. Rep. Brittany Pettersen was a little more cagey, saying she “was denied the ability to vote on this motion” without explaining why she was “denied.” Lou Correa gave a medical excuse, saying that he’s been told to “avoid travel until I’m medically cleared.”
It’s worth noting that Massie’s effort was already a long shot for Hegseth’s actual removal, as impeachment requires a House majority and conviction and removal requires a two-thirds Senate vote (per Senate.gov). But these 11 votes would have forced further votes and potentially a Senate trial process before Democrats take control of Congress in Jan. 2027 (per Daily Beast).

sources.text:
House Republicans have foiled an attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth by referring the articles of impeachment to a committee.
Dissident Republican Rep. Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorization.
The resolution included eight charges against Hegseth, largely related to the U.S. war with Iran and other military actions ordered by President Donald Trump.
The House introduced a procedural motion to put the resolution to vote, referring it to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee on Tuesday.
The House Republicans voted en bloc, except Massie, to kill the resolution in a 211-204 vote.
The measure failed for the time being as the Republican party currently holds a majority in the House, but Democrats will take control in January as they won 256 seats in the mid-term election against the Republicans' 168 seats.
After Massie's effort to impeach Hegseth failed on the floor, Trump attacked the Kentucky Republican by calling him "a major loser."
"The Democrats' attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED! Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
"Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," Trump added, apparently referring to the show of unity by the GOP lawmakers in thwarting a humiliating vote for him.

During a press briefing at the Pentagon, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".
Hegseth said the impeachment resolution presented to the House of Representatives is over policy disagreements, not the sort of offenses identified in the impeachment clause. He also said the threat of impeachment sends a troubling signal to the nation's adversaries.

"We destroyed terror regimes' capabilities, we sank the boats carrying poison into our communities, we put a narco-dictator in handcuffs," he said. "These are not high crimes. This is the job, and it's a job well done."

sources.news_title: GOP blocks attempt to impeach Hegseth after blue wave of midterm elections
sources.text:
The House of Representatives referred a measure to impeach U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to a committee on Tuesday, effectively blocking the effort to remove the Trump cabinet official.
The motion carried on a mostly party-line vote, 211-204.
The House Judiciary Committee acts as the primary legal and constitutional oversight body of the House. It has the authority to handle articles of impeachment. Historically, it settled impeachment resolutions for presidents Andrew Johnson, Richard Nixon, Bill Clinton and Donald Trump.
Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez voiced her frustration over the close margin vote, after not all state representatives attended the occasion.
“I don’t know why people weren’t here. Someone may have a health issue. I don’t know. But obviously, having a vote like that on attendance is hard. That hurts,” CNN quoted her as telling reporters.
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who introduced the articles of impeachment against Hegseth, was the only Republican to vote against it. Democrats uniformly voted against the motion.
The vote was an early test of whether Republicans might seek to break with President Trump over the Iran war after the crushing midterm defeat that the GOP suffered in the midterm elections last week.
The eight articles of impeachment that Massie laid against Hegseth accused the secretary of defense of waging an illegal war against Iran, among other “high crimes and misdemeanors.”
Trump wrote on Truth Social that the Democrats’ attempt to impeach Hegseth “miserably failed.”
“Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete,” the president said. “Again, victories in Venezuela and Iran, the best recruitment numbers in the history of the military (long waiting lists to get in!), and spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot."
New data released by the U.S. Defense Department on Nov. 2 showed strong recruiting growth for the third consecutive year, with enlistment for branches such as the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Space Force meeting or exceeding recruitment goals for 2026.
Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell dubbed the outcome of the vote “total victory” in a post on X.
“The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House Judiciary Committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter,” he wrote, referring to the Defense Department by its secondary title.
He described the impeachment effort a political exercise devoid of “evidence or seriousness …, We will not indulge the political theater driven by a disgruntled soon-to-be former congressman and others who have chosen grandstanding over governing.”
Parnell continued, “We look forward to ending this sham impeachment in the committee room, where facts will continue to prevail and this distraction can be put to rest.”
TOTAL VICTORY!
The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House Judiciary Committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter. From the beginning, this effort has been a political exercise devoid of merit,… pic.twitter.com/ySqBEmfhns
— Sean Parnell (@SeanParnellASW) November 10, 2026
Hegseth was defiant about his potential impeachment during his first news conference in months earlier on Tuesday.
“It’s not oversight and it’s not accountability,” he said. “It’s a political spectacle. A personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”
He apparently referred to Massie when he said that the measure was driven by “one man’s final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president, this country and, most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it."
