sources.news_title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Republicans in the US House of Representatives blocked an effort on Tuesday to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, winning a reprieve for the polarizing Pentagon chief before Democrats take control of Congress next year and possibly try again. 
The vote on a procedural motion came just hours after Hegseth blasted efforts to impeach him as a farce and delivered a defiant defense of his record at the helm of the US military, winning praise from President Donald Trump.
The chamber voted 211 to 204 in favor of a motion to refer eight articles of impeachment to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, a move that the sponsor of the impeachment push, US Representative Thomas Massie, warned would kill it.
Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, had hoped to draw votes from Republicans upset with Hegseth’s policies and wary of the unpopularity of the eight-month-old Iran war but no other Republicans joined him. The US-Israeli led conflict has never been approved by Congress, which is the only branch of government constitutionally permitted to declare war.
Democrats had voiced strong support for the impeachment articles, which accuse Hegseth of the “high crimes and misdemeanors” of illegally ordering the military to wage war in Iran and Yemen, attack boats in the Caribbean Sea and capture Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. But 11 Democrats, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, did not vote.
If eight of them had, the procedural measure would have been defeated, paving the way for a full House impeachment vote.
Ian Krager, a spokesperson for Pelosi, said she had missed the vote because she had returned to San Francisco for an annual event to honor veterans, but would have voted against the procedural measure.
Trump cheered the results in a social media post, saying the effort to impeach Hegseth “has miserably FAILED!” He wrote that Hegseth’s performance on Iran, Venezuela and other issues “led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.”
Hegseth would have been the first US defense secretary to be impeached. The last time any civilian leader of the US military was impeached was in 1876, when William Belknap held the title “secretary of war.”
Hegseth calls himself secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and “woke” when he took office last year. Trump cannot change the name of the Defense Department without approval from Congress.
IRAN WAR ANGER
Voter anger over the Iran war, which has settled into an effective stalemate focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday found a majority of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress, which takes office in January, to act to end the war with Iran once and for all.
Although Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned the war and blamed it for the Republicans’ midterm rout, he voiced support for Hegseth on Tuesday.
“This isn’t about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon,” Vance wrote on social media.
Before the vote, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday: “Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America’s national security, and he’s the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran.”
Hegseth has repeatedly defended the conflict, calling Trump courageous and saying Iran’s military has been left in ruins. He also said his orders to US forces were lawful, despite Massie’s accusations of “high crimes and misdemeanors”.
“History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now,” Hegseth said on Tuesday at his first Pentagon briefing in six months.
Jeffries said he would talk to members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next Congress. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.
A Democratic-led push to impeach Hegseth could be far more intense, with lawmakers calling in top brass to testify, including generals and admirals fired by Hegseth who have remained silent so far. Hegseth, who has railed against diversity efforts at the Pentagon, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who is Black, and the Navy’s top admiral, a woman, among others.
In such an effort, Democrats could also raise other issues of concern to voters including Pentagon policy toward Ukraine and the US military’s strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Caribbean and Pacific waters.
Some Republicans say Hegseth’s strained relations with Congress are becoming a political liability as the Trump administration seeks a huge increase in the military’s budget to $1.5 trillion from $950 billion.
Massie said he was disappointed by the vote, comparing Republicans to passengers content to go down with the Titanic.
“They know it’s a sinking ship but committed to stay on board,” he said.

It had not been clear whether GOP lawmakers, including several who were unexpectedly defeated or won reelection far more narrowly than they anticipated, would rally to support him.
The vote came hours after Hegseth defended himself defiantly at a Pentagon news briefing, equating the criticisms of him to critiques of U.S. troops.
“I stand behind every one of these operations,” Hegseth said of the military actions cited in the articles as unlawful misconduct. “I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow.”
He castigated Massie, the Kentucky Republican who lost his primary this year to a Trump-backed challenger and spearheaded the impeachment effort, for pursuing what called a “political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” and dismissed his accusations.

sources.news_title: House Republicans block move to impeach Hegseth, handing embattled defense secretary a win
sources.text:
House Republicans on Tuesday successfully blocked an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the Iran war and other alleged “high crimes” against the nation, handing President Donald Trump and his embattled defense secretary a win.
“The Democrats’ attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!” Trump posted to social media shortly after.
Largely along party lines, and with some members absent, the House voted 211-204 to send the resolution to impeach Hegseth brought by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., on Monday to a committee, effectively killing it.
Massie was the only Republican to join Democrats. Eleven Democrats were absent.
Hegseth, who reposted Trump’s remarks to his own social media, had earlier derided the effort as a “political spectacle” brought by a rogue Republican lawmaker over mere “policy disagreements,” and promised to “never back down.”
“In the 250 years of our American republic, no secretary of war or secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations,” Hegseth told reporters Tuesday morning, during his first news briefing at the Pentagon in six months.
Trump had backed Hegseth, writing, “Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!”
Massie’s resolution largely focuses on the war in Iran, arguing that Hegseth launched it without necessary congressional authorization, among other things. It also accuses Hegseth of violating the law in military actions against Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, in the U.S. capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in that country in January, and in missile strikes on alleged drug boats in international waters around the U.S.
In his post after the vote, Trump noted that Massie was the lone Republican to vote against Hegseth — and praised Hegseth’s leadership record in Iran and elsewhere.
“Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot,” Trump wrote. “The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!”
In his last months in office after losing his primary to a Trump-backed challenger in May, Massie has long been a thorn in the administration’s side, including as a sponsor of legislation that forced the Justice Department to release millions of pages of records related to the late disgraced financier and convicted sexual abuser Jeffrey Epstein.
Massie spearheaded that effort, and another war powers resolution aimed at reining in the Iran conflict, alongside Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Fremont — who this week joined other Democrats in rallying behind the Hegseth impeachment, in part by citing Democrats’ sweeping wins in last week’s midterm elections.
“Now the voters have spoken. They want us to end this war. That begins with impeaching Pete Hegseth and convicting him in the Senate,” Khanna said in a video posted Monday.
Massie said earlier Tuesday that he had “heard from several members they agree with some of the Articles of Impeachment but not all of them,” and that if the motion to kill his resolution by referring it back to committee failed, and the House proceeded with a vote on the articles themselves, he would “request a vote on each of the Articles separately.”
That was not to be. The vote sending the resolution to committee all but kills it — at least until the many Democrats elected last week take office next year.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and many other Democrats — including from California — had come out in favor of the impeachment measure in advance of Tuesday’s vote.
Rep. Dave Min, D-Irvine, who co-sponsored a previous attempt to impeach the Defense secretary, said Hegseth should not only be impeached but also “should be facing criminal investigations, potentially for murder.”
Min said that throughout the Democratic caucus and among some Republicans, there is “not just frustration but an outrage that Hegseth is so cavalierly breaking the law, so cavalierly putting troops in harm’s way, and so cavalierly ignoring or throwing contempt on our attempts to exert oversight over” the Department of Defense.
Rep. Mike Levin, D-San Juan Capistrano, said Hegseth deserves to be impeached for sending the nation into a war that was never approved by Congress and that the House repeatedly voted to end, for breaking the law by ordering the killing of two men who survived a U.S. strike on an alleged drug boat in the Caribbean, and for refusing to provide answers about a U.S. missile strike on a girls’ elementary school in Iran.
The impeachment effort would have faced even steeper odds in the Senate, where a two-thirds majority would have needed to vote to convict Hegseth for him to be removed. Two Cabinet members have been impeached in U.S. history; none has been convicted.
California’s Democratic senators — Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff — have long called for Hegseth’s removal. Schiff said Tuesday he supports Hegseth’s removal from office for various reasons, including his handling of the Iran war, his authorizing deadly strikes on alleged drug boats, and his having “abused the power of his office to punish those who have been critical of his leadership, including one of my colleagues.”
Schiff was referring to Hegseth launching an investigation into Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., after Kelly joined other lawmakers in telling members of the military not to comply with illegal orders. Massie’s articles of impeachment include a charge related to that episode, accusing Hegseth of violating the 1st Amendment in an attempt to intimidate Kelly.
The impeachment effort was an early — and perhaps too early — attempt at a reckoning over the unpopular Iran war after blistering midterms in which voters moved sharply toward Democrats — delivering the party control of both the House and Senate next year. Much of that swing has been attributed to the Iran war and the related surge in gas prices and other costs.
Vice President JD Vance blamed the midterm losses entirely on the Iran war, and Hegseth has repeatedly been questioned about those remarks as he has tried to defend the war as necessary and his leadership of the military as responsible.
On Tuesday, Vance put his own weight behind Hegseth too, calling the question of whether the latter has committed impeachable crimes “absurd,” and saying the answer is “obviously not.”
“Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements. Rather than use them, they’re going to try to impeach Pete Hegseth. They did the same to Donald Trump,” Vance said in a social media post — a reference to Trump being impeached twice during his first term in office.
Hegseth — who calls himself the “secretary of war” despite no move by Congress to change the name of the Defense Department he oversees — has driven a radical reshaping of top brass within the Pentagon and of Pentagon policy — inspired largely by his fierce opposition to diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, transgender troops and others he deems insufficiently masculine, aggressive or ideologically loyal to the president.
“We are no longer the Woke Department or the Weak Department,” he said in a September speech. “Simple translation of that: No fatties. No trannies. No beardos. No weirdos. No wimps. No radicals. Just warriors.”
Such language — including the slur for transgender people — and Hegseth’s related reshaping of leadership have been denounced by Democrats and former military leaders as beneath the leader of the U.S. military and unfair to women, LGBTQ+ people and people of color.
Pentagon officials have attempted to show a unified front against impeachment and in support of Hegseth, with many posting an image of Hegseth emblazoned with the words, “Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also defended Hegseth, asserting that all of the actions he has been challenged on were at Trump’s direction. “Not only did Pete execute on a direct order from the commander in chief, who, in our Constitution, is empowered and trusted with the job of keeping Americans safe, but they did it quite effectively on all those fronts,” Rubio said.
After Tuesday’s vote, Jeffries said Democrats would discuss whether to pursue Hegseth’s impeachment anew once they’ve taken power next year.

Jeffries said he would talk to members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next Congress. "We'll have that conversation at the appropriate time," he said.
A Democratic-led push to impeach Hegseth could be far more intense, with lawmakers calling in senior military leaders to testify, including generals and admirals fired by Hegseth who have remained silent so far.
Hegseth, who has railed against diversity efforts at the Pentagon, fired the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who is Black, and the Navy's top admiral, a woman, among others.
In such an effort, Democrats could also raise other issues of concern to voters, including Pentagon policy toward Ukraine and the U.S. military's strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Caribbean and Pacific waters.
Some Republicans say Hegseth's strained relations with Congress are becoming a political liability as the Trump administration seeks a huge increase in the military's budget to $1.5 trillion from $950 billion.
Massie said he was disappointed by the vote, comparing Republicans to passengers content to go down with the Titanic.
"They know it's a sinking ship but are committed to staying on board," he said.

sources.text:
House Republicans block effort to hold Hegseth impeachment vote
WASHINGTON — The Republican-controlled US House of Representatives on Tuesday effectively killed a push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a surprising show of unity from a party battered after last week’s midterm drubbing.
In a Truth Social post, President Donald Trump celebrated the failed efforts and called GOP Rep. Thomas Massie, who led the impeachment drive, a “major loser.”
Democrats — who voted unanimously against shelving the impeachment charges — will have a large House majority next year after winning at least 255 seats in last week's midterm elections. They have already vowed to try to remove Hegseth from office when they take control of Congress.
"In the majority, one of the first things we're gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker, said at a rally last month.
Eleven Democrats missed Tuesday's vote, which succeeded in blocking the charges by a 211 to 204 margin.
Rep. Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, reintroduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, alleging that the embattled Pentagon chief had committed "high crimes and misdemeanors" and abused the power of his office by violating the War Powers Resolution, conducting military operations without congressional authorization and ordering unlawful military actions in several countries.
On Tuesday, Massie was the only Republican who broke with his party and voted to keep the articles of impeachment alive.
Before Tuesday's vote, Hegseth struck a defiant tone in a Pentagon news briefing. He described the impeachment efforts as "a farce" and insisted that "none of these are high crimes or misdemeanors — they are partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military."
He added, "That's what it is. Policy disagreements. Not high crimes. Not misdemeanors. Not treason. Not bribery. Not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause."
While Hegseth did not mention Massie by name, he criticized the actions of a "disgruntled congressman" and said the "proper remedy" for a policy disagreement was legislation.
"It's a political spectacle," Hegseth said. "A personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. Time for one man's final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president."
He added, "This is not patriotism. This is sabotage."
Hegseth also said the resolution suggested the US would punish its own military for carrying out its job.
"Let's be clear about what this resolution actually does," he said. "It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership."
President Trump celebrated Tuesday night's House vote on Truth Social, where he said that Democrats' attempt to impeach Hegseth "miserably FAILED!"
Earlier in the day, Trump posted on Truth Social that Hegseth had earned an "'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS" for his defense against Massie, and described the defense secretary as "perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country," adding, "Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached."
The expected impeachment filing came as Congress returned to Washington, D.C., to begin a lame-duck session following the historic rout that the GOP suffered in last week's midterm elections.
Hegseth has been facing intense political backlash over the United States' costly and unpopular war with Iran, which some top Republicans — including Trump — blame in part for the drubbing that cost them control of Congress.
"Despite the absence of a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by an attack upon the United States," Massie said in a speech on the House floor, "Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation."
Massie said Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law."
His actions thus "warrant impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States," the Kentucky Republican said.
Earlier, Trump told CNN at a White House press conference he would "stand by him," saying that he believes Massie "has a lot of hatred in his heart."
Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the GOP primary — first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote.
It's unclear whether Massie's impeachment effort would have succeeded on the House floor under Republican control. Massie had previously told ABC News he was "confident" there would have been "enough GOP defectors for it to pass."
Trump has repeatedly insisted that he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief, at least not yet.
"No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump told reporters last week.
The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the US Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state's next governor.
"I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn's seat.
CBS News, however, reported last week that Trump "has been asking advisers" whether he should stay or go.
Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the US and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices.
He has also been among the advisers urging Trump to restart the war. He and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of US Central Command, have supported a return to major combat operations against Iran during recent briefings on military options, the Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 6, while Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff have pushed for diplomacy to end the conflict.
Trump acknowledged on Nov. 4 that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vance was unequivocal.
"The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X. "The reason we lost is the war."
The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did.
Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces "a reckoning."
"He is one of the reasons why we don't have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need," Tillis said on election night. "I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress."
Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him.
Rep. James Comer of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said on Nov. 6 that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth."
"We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran," Comer told NewsNation. "No one's happy about Iran."
When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth's handling of the military is high on their list.
Hegseth, for his part, has remained defiant.
In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to X on Nov. 5, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he's implemented as Pentagon chief and praised Trump's leadership while dismissing Massie's impeachment pursuit.
"A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly," Hegseth said. "It didn't work with President Trump and it won't work with me."

sources.news_title: House Successfully Blocks Impeachment Effort Against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
sources.text:
The House of Representatives officially blocked an impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday. Lawmakers voted 211-204 to refer the measure to the House Judiciary Committee. This tight procedural vote essentially kills the impeachment effort for the remainder of the current Congress.
Republican Representative Thomas Massie initially spearheaded the controversial resolution. He brought forward eight distinct articles of impeachment against Hegseth earlier this week. The accusations primarily centered on Hegseth’s aggressive handling of international military operations. Massie criticized the secretary for initiating hostilities against Iran without securing proper congressional authorization. He also strongly condemned the department for a series of lethal boat strikes. The resolution claimed those strikes killed over 200 people in the Caribbean Sea. Massie additionally accused Hegseth of retaliating against a sitting member of Congress for their speech. Furthermore, Massie highlighted the controversial arrest of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro as an extrajudicial action.
Hegseth fiercely defended his military record during a rare press briefing at the Pentagon. He described the Republican-led impeachment push as a dangerous political stunt driven by personal resentment. Hegseth argued that policy disagreements simply do not constitute high crimes or misdemeanors. He insisted the founders never intended for the impeachment clause to settle standard legislative debates.
“We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities,” Hegseth proudly stated. He proudly added that the operations were completely lawful and represented a job well done. He warned that the impeachment threat sent a very troubling signal to international adversaries.
Following the vote, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell publicly declared total victory for the department. President Donald Trump also mocked the impeachment effort, stating that the push had miserably failed. Trump praised the defense secretary and offered Hegseth an A+++ grade for his overall performance.
This aligns with the CBS News report, House Blocks Massie’s Effort To Impeach Hegseth, Voting To Kill. However, Democratic leaders quickly signaled that the underlying political issue might not be entirely resolved. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries warned the press that this vote was just the beginning. Democrats will retake control of both chambers of Congress in early January following the midterms. The impending change in power could easily revive scrutiny over the defense secretary’s policy decisions.
For now, Hegseth remains firmly in office, avoiding the historic stigma of a full trial. Only two Cabinet secretaries have ever been impeached in the entire history of the United States. The successful vote to shelve the resolution allows the Pentagon to avoid a lengthy Senate distraction. Hegseth promised to continue his agenda and urged American troops to ignore the political noise.

sources.news_title: Massie’s Hegseth Impeachment Push Crashes With Zero GOP Backup
sources.text:
The House on Tuesday voted 211-204 to refer Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-KY) impeachment resolution against War Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, sidelining the effort. Massie was the lone Republican to oppose the procedural motion, joining all present Democrats in the losing vote.
The vote marked a final and decisive defeat for the outgoing Kentucky congressman, who introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth over the administration’s military operations in Iran, Yemen, Venezuela, and the Caribbean. Massie had attempted to launch impeachment proceedings before the midterm elections in September, but the House was adjourned before representatives could come to a vote.
Massie lost his Republican primary earlier this year to Trump-backed Ed Gallrein and will leave Congress in January.
Republicans outside of Massie voted unanimously to shut down the effort, even as some have criticized Hegseth’s leadership of the Pentagon. Several GOP lawmakers said before the vote that they disagreed with the secretary’s decisions but did not believe they amounted to the “high crimes and misdemeanors” required for impeachment.
Massie defended his resolution on the House floor, arguing that Hegseth “has violated the norms of war, and it’s to the disadvantage and the dishonor of our country, and to the danger of our soldiers in future conflicts,” Massie said on Tuesday, according to NBC. “Somebody’s got to put their foot down and say, are we going to follow the laws that are on the books? Are we going to follow the Constitution?”
The resolution included eight articles accusing Hegseth of unlawful conduct. Three focused on the war in Iran, alleging that he waged military operations without congressional authorization, defied congressional directives, and continued hostilities in violation of the War Powers Resolution. Another accused him of failing to take sufficient steps to minimize civilian casualties, citing a strike on an Iranian school.
The remaining articles targeted U.S. strikes against suspected drug-smuggling vessels in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, the operation that captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, the military campaign in Yemen, and Hegseth’s treatment of Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) after the senator participated in a video urging service members to refuse unlawful orders.
Hegseth dismissed the impeachment effort during a Tuesday morning news conference at the Pentagon, calling it a “farce” and a “stunt.” He maintained that the military operations cited by Massie were lawful and argued that the resolution undermined American troops.
“We destroyed terror regimes’ capabilities. We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities. We put a narco dictator in handcuffs,” Hegseth said. “These are not high crimes. This is the job, and it’s the job well done.”
President Donald Trump also stood firmly behind his defense secretary, praising Hegseth’s performance and attacking Massie on Truth Social as a “disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman” and a “TOTAL LOSER.”
Even some of Hegseth’s Republican critics rejected Massie’s approach. Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE), who is retiring, said he had serious disagreements with the secretary, particularly over the removal of senior military officers, but did not support impeachment.
“I don’t think he’s been a good secretary, but do you impeach a guy for that? It has to be a high crime or misdemeanor,” Bacon said Monday.
Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA), also leaving Congress, suggested Massie was pursuing the effort in part because of his primary defeat. Issa argued that even if the resolution passed the House, the Senate would not have the votes necessary to convict Hegseth.
Democratic leaders, meanwhile, have promised to continue pursuing Hegseth after taking control of Congress in January. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), who is expected to become speaker, previously called himself a “hard yes” on impeachment and said Democrats would “run Pete Hegseth out of town.”
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer also endorsed the effort.
Tuesday’s procedural vote prevents Massie’s resolution from advancing to a full impeachment vote under the current Republican-led House. With Democrats preparing to assume control of both chambers next year, however, Hegseth could face renewed pressure from congressional investigators and Democratic lawmakers.

sources.news_title: Rep. Horsford misses Hegseth vote; 10 other Democrats also absent
sources.text:
Rep. Horsford misses Hegseth vote; 10 other Democrats also absent
A personal emergency prevented Rep. Steven Horsford, D-Nev., from voting in the possible impeachment of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, according to his office.
Democrats fell short of stopping a Republican-led resolution to table the impeachment attempt introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky.
Eleven Democrats, including Horsford, missed Tuesday’s 211-204 vote that kicked Massie’s proposal to a committee, essentially tabling it indefinitely.
Speaking from the House floor Wednesday, Horsford said he would’ve voted against the delay, and that he was taking responsibility for his absence.
“Our constituents put their faith in us to show up,” he said. “Yesterday, a personal emergency delayed my arrival to the House floor, and I missed an important vote.”
Horsford didn’t expound on the emergency.
“The accountability I demand of others applies to me, too,” he said.
The night before, Horsford’s office said that that he supports the effort to oust Hegseth and that he would say as much on the congressional record.
Horsford’s Democratic Nevada colleagues, Rep. Dina Titus and Susie Lee, voted no on the Republican resolution. Rep. Mark Amodei, R-Nev., voted with his party.
No Democrat voted yes and only Massie defected from Republicans.
Other Democrats who missed the vote include Rep. Nancy Pelosi and two of her California colleagues, and Rep. Haley Stevens from Michigan.
Seven Republicans also were absent, leveling the playing field for Democrats who hold the House minority.
Massie’s resolution included eight counts of impeachment. It largely focused on the war in Iran but also included references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
Had the Republican resolution failed, the House still needed to vote on Massie’s impeachment proposal for it to proceed to the Senate for trial.
Removal there requires a two-thirds majority.
Contact Ricardo Torres-Cortez at rtorres@reviewjournal.com. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: House Republicans derail Massie's impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
Hegseth dodges bullet but wants troops to believe they did, too
sources.text:
Observers are reporting that absent Democrats likely torpedoed Thomas Massie's attempt to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth in the House last night. The vote to refer his eight articles of impeachment to the judiciary committee for a sure death, passed 211-204.
Hegseth and his compadres in the Pentagon are no doubt feeling vindicated since he spent Tuesday morning boasting of his handling of the war policies in Yemen, the Caribbean, Venezuela, and in particular, Iran. In order to do this he had to engage in some serious fabrications about the state of the war: that it was "won," that Iran's military is "in ruin," the "ironclad blockade (is) unbroken," that "we control the Strait of Hormuz." It is worth watching in full.
"For the first time in American history, a cabinet secretary overseeing America's military is being attacked not for losing conflicts with our enemies, but for winning them," Hegseth declared. That reporters were threatened ahead of time in the briefing room ahead of the morning spectacle meant that he received no questions asking him to explain or issue evidence for his more audacious flights from reality.
Worse than all of that is that Hegseth used active duty service members and veterans as props for his own play for survival and suggested they would be next if Massie's "personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment" wasn't stopped. He did this while invoking Veterans Day.
To quote from his briefing:
"As it happens, tomorrow is Veterans Day. This year, the operators of Absolute Resolve and the warriors of Epic Fury will mark it for the first time. They stand shoulder to shoulder with the pilots of Midnight Hammer, and the sailors of Rough Rider who went before them. They answered the call, they executed, they won. And on the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime. Their service was not a crime. These are heroes, and no politician in Washington will tell them otherwise while I hold this office."
"This (Massie) resolution is the next step," he continued. "Put the secretary on trial today, and the men and women who carried out those orders tomorrow. If they want to come for the warriors, they're going to have to come through me."
But no one was "coming for" the military soldiers, sailors, Marines, or airmen executing the current war policies. Massie was coming for Hegseth. As the Kentucky Republican exhaustively explained in the eight articles of impeachment, the secretary stands accused of acting "in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law" in the context of the U.S.Constitution — which Hegseth promised to serve when he raised his right hand on January 25, 2025.
"Massie's impeachment resolution has nothing to do with the troops, it's not only peak hyperbole but also peak politicization of the force to insinuate that the troops would be under any kind of legal threat," Jim Webb, who served with the U.S. Marines in the Iraq War, told RS.
Hegseth is of course engaging in the tried and more often failed method of hiding behind members of the U.S. military in order to avoid accountability — in this case, for a war policy that is so unpopular with the American people that they are sending the biggest new freshman class since 1933 to Washington with the mandate of shutting it down. That he is using Veterans Day to deflect should be an insult to all veterans across the country, whether they support him or not. The holiday is not for politicians to argue the rightness of their policies; it is to acknowledge the sacrifices of men and women who carried out their duties regardless of the rightness — or wrongness — of those policies.
Webb points out that if anyone has put troops at risk, it's Hegseth, and Congress has the power to investigate it.
Massie wants "Hegseth to account for committing those in his charge to a war that not only was not in the American interest, but also one which his troops were not prepared for. That's the complete opposite of how leaders are supposed to act," charged Webb. "It has been clear from before we attacked Iran that it was a bad idea, so a true leader would speak truth to power in that regard, and would have stood between his people and that decision."
As for reading the room, Hegseth has spent so much time in the bubble, firing anyone who disagrees, and talking at the military about testosterone and God, kicking teeth and lethality, that he might have missed some big clues about "his warriors" along the way. In one recent poll of active-duty service members, veterans, and military families nationwide, 49% said they did not approve of the Iran war. As for push-up Pete, some 50% said they disapproved of how he was handling his job, and that number went up to 54% among active duty members in the poll, according to the cross tabs provided to RS.
Moreover, 57% of all respondents said they disapproved of military strikes against so-called drug boats in the Caribbean. Overall, 64% said veterans and military families "are being left behind by politicians and society," and 51% (including 55% of active duty) disagreed that morale in the ranks is better under the Trump Administration, i.e., under Secretary Hegseth.
Now the sampling was small and this is one poll, but it is just a reminder that the military community is not a monolith. According to exit polling from last week's midterms, 10% of those who voted were veterans. Of them, 41% voted Democrat, while 57% voted Republican.
Hegseth should know better. The conservative veterans organization that he led a over a decade ago, Concerned Veterans for America, came right out with this statement after it was obvious the war in Iran had fueled the blue wave last week: "Americans clearly showed that sound foreign policy is a pressing priority and that voters’ desire to end the reckless war in Iran is particularly linked to ongoing economic consequences felt at home."
This does not sound like veterans who want to to be used as props. Hegseth served in Afghanistan. He has no doubt heard the voices of those veterans who now question if their service was "worth it"; he knows many of them counted on Donald Trump to prevent Washington from sending men and women into another war they cannot explain. "(Operation) Epic Fury has never been that, and it never will be," Hegseth insisted on Tuesday.
Joe Kent, another veteran of the 9/11 wars (11 tours of combat duty in Army Special Forces), has a completely different take. He resigned his position in the Trump administration because he could not support "that" war again. Unlike Hegseth, who wants us to believe veterans are afraid of being targeted by Massie's impeachment articles, Kent was and is motivated by a completely different fear.
"I was like, I am not going to be the GWOT veteran that gets the next generation in the exact same war that I fought in, that I knew was based on a lie," he said to a public audience in Austin last month. "When I saw that happening, I was like, I have to leave. I just can't. I can't be here."
That doesn't sound like the kind of veteran who thinks any criticism of the Trump war policies is "taking issue with the troops."
If anything Hegseth is likely to double down on what he now sees as a winning communications strategy, particularly if Democrats try to resurrect an impeachment under the new congress. His Pentagon spokesman and friend Sean Parnell didn't waste time in reinforcing it.
"The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House Judiciary Committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter," Parnell posted. "From the beginning, this effort has been a political exercise devoid of merit, evidence, or seriousness. It collapses under the weight of Secretary Hegseth’s record of restoring the warrior ethos, delivering results, and putting the mission first. The American people see through it."
We could say the same about politicians who use veterans and the rank and file for grandstanding, or worse, for cover. But that is for another day. This day is supposed to be for them.

sources.news_title: US House blocks Hegseth impeachment as battle shifts to January
sources.text:
US House blocks Hegseth impeachment as battle shifts to January
The impeachment push against United States Secretary of War Pete Hegseth was blocked Tuesday evening as Republicans in the House of Representatives rallied around the Cabinet member.
The resolution vote was 211-204, sending it to the Committee on the Judiciary, which first received the impeachment articles authored by Rep. Thomas Massie, the outgoing Kentucky representative.
Republicans argued that Hegseth's actions did not amount to "high crimes and misdemeanors" as stated in Massie's articles denouncing the execution of "unlawful orders" in Iran, the Caribbean, Venezuela, and Yemen.
President Donald Trump has reiterated support for Hegseth, who called the impeachment effort a "political spectacle ... a farce and a stunt" during a news conference at the Pentagon.
"We will not apologize for putting Americans' lives first... stopping the flow of drugs that kill our citizens... destroying the capability of a regime that chants death to America. We remain locked and loaded," he declared.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell described the referral of the "baseless impeachment articles" to the House Judiciary Committee as a "total victory" for Hegseth, the Department of War, and service members.
The official said the action was "a political exercise devoid of merit, evidence, or seriousness," and collapsed under the weight of the secretary's record of restoring the warrior ethos, delivering results, and putting the mission first.
Parnell slammed the "disgruntled soon-to-be former congressman and others who have chosen grandstanding over governing," saying the department looks forward to ending the impeachment at the committee level.
Rep. Maxine Dexter, D-OR, stated that Republicans may have buried the vote, but a new Congress will answer to the American people in January. "And Pete Hegseth will answer to it as well," she added.
"This is not the end of it; this is the beginning," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-NY, who is poised to be elected speaker when the Democrats take over Congress in about eight weeks.

sources.news_title: Why Did Republicans Block the Impeachment of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth?
sources.text:
Republicans in the US House of Representatives have blocked an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, giving President Donald Trump’s controversial Pentagon chief a political reprieve despite mounting criticism over the administration’s military actions in Iran and elsewhere.
The 211-204 procedural vote on Tuesday prevented eight articles of impeachment from advancing to a full House vote. However, the decision may offer only temporary relief for Hegseth, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January and consider renewing efforts to hold him accountable.
The failed impeachment attempt also highlights growing divisions over the eight-month-old Iran war, the limits of presidential authority in military operations and the political future of the Trump administration’s defence policy.
How Did Republicans Stop the Impeachment Effort?
The impeachment effort was sponsored by Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who sought to build bipartisan support for removing Hegseth from office.
Stay ahead of the geopolitical week.
MD Briefing delivers expert analysis across five global fronts — the Indo-Pacific, energy, geoeconomics, European security, and the Middle East — every Monday morning. Free.
The House voted 211 to 204 in favour of referring the eight articles of impeachment to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee. Massie had warned that sending the articles to the committee would effectively kill the initiative.
No other Republicans joined him, despite his efforts to attract lawmakers concerned about Hegseth’s leadership and the political consequences of the Iran conflict.
Democrats had broadly supported the impeachment articles, which accused Hegseth of committing high crimes and misdemeanors through allegedly unlawful military orders. The accusations included directing military operations in Iran and Yemen, authorising attacks on boats in the Caribbean Sea and participating in the January capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
However, 11 Democrats did not participate in the vote, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. Her spokesperson said she had travelled to San Francisco for an annual veterans’ event and would have opposed the procedural motion had she been present.
Had eight additional Democrats voted against referring the articles to committee, the measure would have failed, potentially allowing the impeachment process to advance.
The result therefore reflected both Republican unity behind Hegseth and the difficulty of securing the votes required to move forward with impeachment.
Why Is the Iran War Central to the Impeachment Push?
The Iran conflict has become one of the most politically damaging issues facing the Trump administration.
The war, which has settled into an effective stalemate centred on securing the Strait of Hormuz, has generated public frustration over its costs, strategic objectives and legal basis. The conflict was never formally authorised by Congress, the constitutional branch responsible for declaring war.
Massie’s impeachment initiative sought to turn those concerns into a direct challenge to Hegseth’s authority as defence secretary.
Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries accused the Pentagon chief of abusing his power, undermining national security and helping lead what he described as a reckless and costly war of choice.
Hegseth has rejected the accusations and defended the administration’s military campaign. At his first Pentagon briefing in six months, he argued that the conflict would eventually be judged differently by history and maintained that his orders to American forces were lawful.
He also praised Trump for his leadership, arguing that Iran’s military capabilities had been severely damaged.
The political consequences of the war, however, are becoming increasingly difficult for the administration to contain. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday found that a majority of Americans want the incoming Democratic-majority Congress to take action to bring the conflict to an end.
The issue has also exposed differences within the Republican leadership. Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned the war and linked it to the party’s poor performance in the midterm elections, although he defended Hegseth ahead of Tuesday’s vote.
Vance argued that the impeachment effort was not really about Iran but about Hegseth challenging the Pentagon bureaucracy.
Trump and Republicans Rally Behind Hegseth
Trump welcomed the House vote, declaring on social media that the impeachment effort had failed and describing Hegseth as a great American patriot.
The president’s response reinforced the political importance of protecting his defence secretary at a time when the administration is facing criticism over its military decisions.
Hegseth has also developed a controversial reputation within the Pentagon. Since taking office, he has criticised diversity initiatives and promoted a military culture he says should be stronger and less politically influenced.
His decisions have included removing the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Navy’s top admiral, among other senior military officials. The dismissals have attracted scrutiny, particularly given the absence of public explanations from some of the officers involved.
Republican support for Hegseth also reflects the administration’s broader effort to maintain control over military leadership and defence policy. Nevertheless, some Republicans have warned that his strained relationship with Congress could become a political liability.
The administration is seeking to increase the US military budget to $1.5 trillion from approximately $950 billion, making congressional support particularly important.
For lawmakers concerned about government spending and military accountability, Hegseth’s leadership could become a more difficult issue as budget negotiations approach.
Could Democrats Try to Impeach Hegseth Again?
The failed vote does not necessarily end the political threat to Hegseth.
Democrats are expected to assume control of the House in January, giving them greater influence over congressional investigations and oversight of the Pentagon. Jeffries has said he will discuss the possibility of another impeachment effort with party members at the appropriate time.
A Democratic-led investigation could go beyond the original eight articles. Lawmakers may seek testimony from senior military officials, including generals and admirals dismissed by Hegseth who have so far remained publicly silent.
Such hearings could examine the legality of military operations, the administration’s decision-making process and the relationship between civilian political leadership and the military command structure.
Democrats could also broaden their scrutiny to include Pentagon policy toward Ukraine and US military strikes against suspected drug-trafficking boats in Caribbean and Pacific waters.
The political significance of these investigations would extend beyond Hegseth’s position. They could provide lawmakers with an opportunity to challenge the administration’s wider approach to military intervention and executive authority.
What Happens Next?
Hegseth has survived the immediate impeachment challenge, but his political position remains exposed to developments in the Iran war and the incoming Congress.
The Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections has strengthened the prospects for more aggressive oversight of the administration’s defence decisions. Public dissatisfaction with the conflict could also increase pressure on lawmakers to demand greater accountability from the Pentagon.
For Trump, retaining Hegseth may be important to maintaining continuity in defence policy and demonstrating loyalty to senior officials. Yet the administration will have to manage growing congressional resistance while seeking approval for a substantial increase in military spending.
The latest vote has prevented an immediate impeachment confrontation, but it has not resolved the underlying disputes over military authority, civilian oversight and the strategic consequences of the Iran war.
As Democrats prepare to take control of the House, Hegseth may face a more sustained political challenge in the months ahead.
With information from Reuters.

sources.news_title: The bizarre excuses of Democrats who undermined a push to impeach Hegseth
sources.text:
Lame-duck Republicans have successfully blocked an attempt to impeach the US Defence Secretary Peter Hegseth for “high crimes and misdemeanours” in relation to the Iran war and extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean.
But the vote in the House could have gone the other way with the backing of eight of the 11 Democrats who were absent for the vote.
Kentucky Republican congressman Thomas Massie, who lost his party’s nomination for re-election to a Trump pick, had brought the articles of impeachment to the House and sought to push them to a vote, two months before a Democrat wave of midterms winners take their seats.
However, the attempt has failed, with a motion passed 211 to 204 on Tuesday to shunt it off to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, effectively killing it.
Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans did not register a vote on the motion.
‘Stuck behind a motorcade’
Democrat absentees included former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi – who reportedly flew back to California before the vote to attend a Veterans Day event and receive a “lifetime advocate” award.
Another Democrat absentee, Lou Correa, said he “vehemently” supported the impeachment but had been forced to stay in California for a medical procedure and his doctor had advised him not to travel.
Several Democrats who were present in Washington blamed traffic delays for not making it to the Capitol in time.
“While en route to the floor to [vote to support the impeachment], a traffic incident and a police-escorted bus caused a delay that resulted in the vote closing before I, along with other Members, could reach the chamber,” Nevadan Democrat Steven Horsford told The Washington Sun.
Illinois Democrat Jonathan Jackson gave the same excuse in a statement on X, and Washington Democrat Marilyn Strickland’s office told a newspaper she was “stuck behind a motorcade and missed the vote by one minute”.
Colorado Democrat Brittany Petterson reportedly said she was “denied the ability to vote” but did not give details.
California Democrat Sydney Kamlager-Dove did not hide her frustration with her colleagues afterwards.
“We knew that this vote was coming, so people should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote,” she told reporters. “There is no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues.
“[Hegseth was] doing stuff that’s unconstitutional and illegal. So you need to go. So, shame on folks who were not here.”
New York Democrat Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez told CNN the representatives who missed the job had been sent to DC “to do a job”.
“The same way I had to clock in when I worked at a restaurant, we got to clock in and do our work here,” she said.
‘Make the argument’
Massie had brought on the vote because, he said, he wanted to force Hegseth to answer to his conduct in office, or to resign.
The articles of impeachment alleged that the Secretary had unlawfully made war with Iran, ordered the murder of Iranian civilians, and ordered the extrajudicial killings of at least 221 people alleged to be smuggling narcotics in the Carribbean, including illegal secondary strikes against shipwrecked survivors.
Anticipating a response from Hegseth he said: “I hope he addresses the articles, and doesn’t just get up and misquote the Bible in Quentin Tarantino fashion and do some pull-ups and, you know, call everybody fat and gay for being [in favour of] this impeachment,” Massie told reporters on Monday.
“I would like to see him go through the eight articles of impeachment and just make the argument from a podium… tell us why you are not guilty.”
‘You hate the president’
Behind a podium at the Pentagon on Tuesday, hours before the vote, Hegseth told reporters the impeachment attempt was “a political spectacle driven by ego and resentment… a farce and a stunt”.
“In the 250 years of our American Republic no Secretary of War, or Secretary of Defence, has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations. And in our case, successful ones at that.”
He said his actions had been lawful and the Massie’s accusations amounted to a “policy disagreement” rather than high crimes and misdemeanours, the level of misconduct required for impeachment.
“Every one” of the military operations “was a lawful operation ordered by the commander in chief, then ordered by myself, notified to Congress and executed by American warriors who did their jobs”.
Hegseth also accused the media of “never admitting the military success” of US attacks on Iran “because you hate the president more than you love our country or our troops”.
He said US attacks on boats in the Caribbean meant that 218 “narco terrorists” were “dead, where they should be”.
Hegseth then took questions from right-wing media, ignoring questions from NBC and other established news outlets.
Trump scored the press conference in comments afterwards on social media, an “A plus plus plus” and “a must see!”.
‘Just the beginning’
Before the vote, there had been speculation that some Republicans would sit out of the impeachment over a war whose unpopularity had lost many their seats.
However, in the end, there were more Democrat absentees than Republicans.
“What I found out tonight is [Republicans] still haven’t broken from the spell of Donald Trump,” Massie said afterwards. “He still controls this conference.”
Republicans had grown more reluctant to back the impeachment after Trump reasserted his support for Hegseth, with some reportedly worried that a successful impeachment would also implicate the president in illegal actions.
House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries told a Politico reporter he hadn’t “had a conversation with anyone on the floor team about what may or may not have happened”.
However, he added “this is not the end of it, it’s just the beginning”.
Jeffries said he would talk to members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next Congress. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.
A Democratic-led push to impeach Hegseth could involve lawmakers calling in generals and admirals fired by Hegseth to testify.
Trump afterwards said the “Democrats” attempt to impeach Hegseth had “miserably failed”.

sources.text:
US House blocks bid to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
- By Reuters -
- Nov 11, 2026
Republicans in the US House of Representatives blocked an effort on Tuesday to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, winning a reprieve for the polarizing Pentagon chief before Democrats take control of Congress next year and possibly try again.
The vote on a procedural motion came just hours after Hegseth blasted efforts to impeach him as a farce and delivered a defiant defense of his record at the helm of the US military, winning praise from President Donald Trump.
The chamber voted 211 to 204 in favor of a motion to refer eight articles of impeachment, opens new tab to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, a move that the sponsor of the impeachment push, US Representative Thomas Massie, warned would kill it.
Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, had hoped to draw votes from Republicans upset with Hegseth’s policies and wary of the unpopularity of the eight-month-old Iran war but no other Republicans joined him. The US-Israeli led conflict has never been approved by Congress, which is the only branch of government constitutionally permitted to declare war.
Democrats had voiced strong support for the impeachment articles, which accuse Hegseth of the “high crimes and misdemeanors” of illegally ordering the military to wage war in Iran and Yemen, attack boats in the Caribbean Sea and capture Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. But 11 Democrats, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, did not vote.
If eight of them had, the procedural measure would have been defeated, paving the way for a full House impeachment vote.
Ian Krager, a spokesperson for Pelosi, said she had missed the vote because she had returned to San Francisco for an annual event to honor veterans, but would have voted against the procedural measure.
Trump cheered the results in a social media post, saying the effort to impeach Hegseth “has miserably FAILED!” He wrote that Hegseth’s performance on Iran, Venezuela and other issues “led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.”
Pete Hegseth would have been the first US defense secretary to be impeached. The last time any civilian leader of the US military was impeached was in 1876, when William Belknap held the title “secretary of war.”
Hegseth calls himself secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and “woke” when he took office last year. Trump cannot change the name of the Defense Department without approval from Congress.
IRAN WAR ANGER
Voter anger over the Iran war, which has settled into an effective stalemate focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday found a majority of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress, which takes office in January, to act to end the war with Iran once and for all.
Although Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned the war and blamed it for the Republicans’ midterm rout, he voiced support for Pete Hegseth on Tuesday.
“This isn’t about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon,” Vance wrote on social media.
Before the vote, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday: “Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America’s national security, and he’s the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran.”
Pete Hegseth has repeatedly defended the conflict, calling Trump courageous and saying Iran’s military has been left in ruins. He also said his orders to US forces were lawful, despite Massie’s accusations of “high crimes and misdemeanors”.
“History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now,” Hegseth said on Tuesday at his first Pentagon briefing in six months.
Jeffries said he would talk to members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next Congress. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.
A Democratic-led push to impeach Hegseth could be far more intense, with lawmakers calling in top brass to testify, including generals and admirals fired by Hegseth who have remained silent so far. Pete Hegseth, who has railed against diversity efforts at the Pentagon, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who is Black, and the Navy’s top admiral, a woman, among others.
In such an effort, Democrats could also raise other issues of concern to voters including Pentagon policy toward Ukraine and the US military’s strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Caribbean and Pacific waters.
Some Republicans say Pete Hegseth’s strained relations with Congress are becoming a political liability as the Trump administration seeks a huge increase in the military’s budget to $1.5 trillion from $950 billion.
Massie said he was disappointed by the vote, comparing Republicans to passengers content to go down with the Titanic.
“They know it’s a sinking ship but committed to stay on board,” he said.

sources.news_title: A Failed Impeachment, for Now
House votes to set aside Hegseth impeachment
sources.text:
The House of Representatives voted 211-204 Tuesday evening to refer to the Judiciary Committee a resolution to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, effectively killing the measure for the duration of the lame duck session of Congress, which began this week.
Republicans hold 218 seats in the lame duck House and Democrats 214, with two vacancies and one independent, Kevin Kiley of California, who voted with the Republicans. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, the Republican who drafted the resolution, was the only Republican to vote against referral.
All 203 Democrats who voted opposed the motion, but 11 did not vote, more than enough to change the outcome. Had eight of them voted, the motion would have failed and the House would have been compelled to take up the articles of impeachment. The Democrats, in other words, saved Hegseth from impeachment.
The absentees included former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is leaving Congress. Pelosi was on Capitol Hill Tuesday morning, but she flew back to San Francisco to receive a “Lifetime Advocate for Veterans Award” at a Veterans Day event, according to her office. Four others blamed traffic.
The Democratic leadership, which had declared its support for impeachment, did not whip the vote, the minimum a party does on a vote it intends to win. It thereby ensured that the referral would pass and the impeachment would die. Asked about the next step, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said only, “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time.”
In January, when the Democrats will hold large majorities in both houses of Congress, they may reintroduce an impeachment resolution, though it is likely to focus on a narrower set of charges than Massie’s. Massie is leaving Congress after losing the May Republican primary to a Trump-backed candidate.
The Massie resolution listed eight impeachable offenses. Three concerned the war against Iran, which Massie charged was waged in violation of the War Powers Resolution. The law requires the president to withdraw US forces from hostilities within 60 days, with a 30-day extension, unless Congress authorizes them.
The resolution also condemned the killing of fishermen in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific (labeled “narco-terrorists” by Hegseth without evidence), the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, and the Pentagon effort to bring criminal charges against six Democratic members of Congress for issuing a video appeal to US soldiers not to obey illegal or unconstitutional orders.
Several Republicans had indicated support for removing Hegseth but publicly balked at several of the charges. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who is retiring, said he would vote to impeach Hegseth over his firing of numerous military officers and over cuts in US military aid to Ukraine, but not over Iran.
The impeachment effort is a cynical operation. The Democrats backed Massie’s resolution, but the Democrats have ruled out any action against Trump himself. Trump appointed Hegseth, ordered every operation listed in Massie’s articles and has just made the fascist Stephen Miller White House chief of staff. Concentrating on Hegseth alone protects the man responsible and leaves the administration’s drive to dictatorship untouched.
The actual priority of the incoming Democratic majority is to revive the massive US financial and military commitment to Ukraine, and the Hegseth impeachment is likely to be a component part of their negotiations with the White House. Senate Democrats have already floated Hegseth’s ouster as leverage in defense spending talks, according to the Hill.
The behind-the-scenes maneuvering is accompanied by stepped-up fascist pronouncements from Trump, Hegseth and other leading figures in the Republican Party.
The morning of the impeachment vote, Hegseth gave a press briefing which consisted of a nonstop diatribe against Massie. While not addressing the main charge brought by Massie, that the US war in Iran was illegal and in violation of the War Powers Act, the Pentagon boss claimed that the impeachment resolution amounted to a criminal complaint against every US soldier who carried out orders from himself and Trump.
The resolution placed “a target on the backs of American warriors by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time,” Hegseth claiming. “This is not patriotism,” he added. “This is sabotage.”
The last charge is particularly provocative, as sabotage of US military operations in wartime would be the basis for charges of treason, which carries the death penalty.
“Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does,” Hegseth said. “It tells our enemies—Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching—that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership.”
Hegseth also cited military operations ordered by Democratic presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, effectively declaring that the war crimes of Democrats made it hypocritical for them to charge Republican officials like himself with war crimes.
The news conference was the first Hegseth has held at the Pentagon in six months, as he has rejected any public accountability for US military operations in the Middle East, the Caribbean or anywhere else.
Moreover, journalists reported that they were accosted by a Hegseth security aide, who said that anyone who acted “unprofessionally” would be physically removed. In any case, Hegseth took questions only from pro-Trump right-wing media, while he attacked other corporate-controlled media outlets which reported more critically on the war in Iran.
Shortly after the news conference, Trump posted his support on social media, writing that Hegseth “gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!”
Despite these fulminations, there have been numerous media reports that Trump is preparing to dump Hegseth if it suits his purposes in the deal-making with the Democrats. Hegseth has been said to be inquiring about an appointment to the US Senate seat from Tennessee. Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn was elected governor on November 3 and will thus have the power to select her own replacement.

He has fired experienced generals who disagree with him and the president. And under his leadership, the military has blatantly discriminated against women, LGBTQ+ service members, and others. Our troops deserve a Secretary of Defense who puts their safety first and honors our Constitution."
No public explanations had been given for the absences of Representatives Julia Brownley, Haley Stevens, Brittany Pettersen and Frederica Wilson as of Wednesday morning.
Newsweek contacted each of them for comment via email and telephone on Wednesday morning.
The Seven Republicans Who Didn't Vote:
Monica De La Cruz (Texas)
Neal Dunn (Florida)
Russell Fry (South Carolina)
Julia Letlow (Louisiana)
Tom Tiffany (Wisconsin)
Derrick Van Orden (Wisconsin)
Rudy Yakym III (Indiana)
What Massie's Articles Allege
Massie brought eight impeachment articles against Hegseth, three of which allege Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution, an act that limits the White House's power to use the U.S. military in foreign wars without congressional approval.
Massie also alleges Hegseth disregarded laws that keep civilian casualties to a minimum, suppressing free speech and of ordering "extrajudicial killings" through U.S. attacks on alleged drug boats in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea. At least 240 people have been killed in these strikes since September 2025.
A further two articles accuse Hegseth of "kidnapping" a sovereign foreign leader, referring to the capture of Venezuela's former President Nicolás Maduro, and directing an "unlawful war" in Yemen.
Massie had brought impeachment articles against Hegseth in September, but House Speaker Mike Johnson quickly recessed the chamber without a vote taking place, meaning Republicans did not have to pass public judgment on Hegseth's leadership of the Pentagon ahead of this week's elections.
What Happens Next?
Tuesday's failed vote effectively ends this impeachment effort.
Members who miss a vote are recorded as "Not Voting." They can submit statements indicating how they would have voted, but those statements do not alter the official tally or outcome.
In addition to the Kentucky Republicans' push, Democratic Representative Maxwell Frost of Florida has said he has drafted separate articles of impeachment against Hegseth and could pursue them when Democrats assume control of the House in January. Democratic leaders have also signaled continued scrutiny of the defense secretary.
Expected by many to become the new House speaker, Hakeem Jeffries recently said Democrats would "run Pete Hegseth out of town," underscoring the likelihood that Hegseth will remain a target of congressional investigations and potential future impeachment efforts despite Tuesday's vote.

sources.text:
Normally, the prospect of a cabinet secretary’s impeachment would be a reason for a president to cut him loose. In the case of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the threat of impeachment is one very big reason why he will stay in his post at the Pentagon, at least for now.

sources.news_title: House Democrats Blame Traffic for Missing Key Hegseth Impeachment Vote
sources.text:
Eleven House Democrats missed a crucial vote Tuesday that could have kept an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth alive, drawing criticism from colleagues as several lawmakers blamed traffic delays for their absence.
The House voted 211-204 to send eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, effectively blocking an immediate vote on impeachment.
The 11 missing Democrats had enough votes to defeat the motion, which would have failed 215-211 had they all voted against it, keeping the impeachment effort alive.
“We knew that this vote was coming, so people should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote,” Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-California) told reporters. “There is no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues.”
Trending
“Shame on folks who are not here,” she said. “Because these people lost. They lost, and they still found a way to show up to table this bill. Shameful.”
A senior Democratic aide disputed that the votes of members blocked by traffic from returning to the Capitol would have changed the outcome, arguing that Republicans had only two members unavailable and closed the vote even though they knew more members were en route.
The Washington Sun contacted the offices of the absent Democrats seeking explanations for their missed votes.
Three of the absent lawmakers, Reps. Laura Gillen (D-New York), Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois) and Melanie Stansbury (D-New Mexico), blamed a traffic incident and a police-escorted bus that stalled intersections for preventing them from reaching the House floor in time.
“While en route to the floor to oppose that motion, a traffic incident and a police-escorted bus caused a delay that resulted in the vote closing before I, along with other Members, could reach the chamber,” Jackson said in a statement to The Sun.
Stansbury and Gillen offered a similar explanation, adding that they reached the chamber just as the vote ended.
Both Jackson and Stanbury said they subsequently entered their opposition to the motion in the Congressional Record. Those statements did not change the official vote tally.
The office of Rep. Marilyn Strickland (D-Washington) also blamed a motorcade for her absence.
“The Congresswoman was stuck behind a motorcade and missed the vote by 1 minute. She would have voted against the motion to refer,” her chief of staff, Andrew Noh, told The Sun.
Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nevada) missed the vote because of a personal emergency, according to his office, adding that he would have voted against the motion to refer. He plans to enter his opposition in the Congressional Record.
Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-California) was in San Francisco attending a Veterans Day celebration, where she was being honored for her advocacy on behalf of veterans.
“Speaker Emerita Pelosi returned to San Francisco to join and honor local veterans at Swords to Plowshares’ 30th Annual Veterans Day Celebration tonight, an important and longstanding district tradition she regularly attends and will mark for the last time as a Member of Congress by receiving the Lifetime Advocate for Veterans Award,” Pelosi spokesperson Ian Krager told The Sun.
“She supports impeaching Secretary Hegseth and would have voted ‘No’ on the motion to refer,” Krager added.
Rep. Lou Correa (D-California) was also in his home state, where he said he was preparing to undergo a medical procedure and had been advised by his doctor to avoid traveling until he was medically cleared.
He did not say how he would have voted on the impeachment motion.
Rep. Eugene Vindman (D-Virginia) said the absent Democrats had been attending an event and failed to return in time.
“Should have never happened, but that’s the way it played out,” Vindman said.
The other absent Democrats were Reps. Haley Stevens (D-Michigan), Julia Brownley (D-California), Brittany Pettersen (D-Colorado) and Frederica Wilson (D-Florida).
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters Tuesday that he would discuss another impeachment effort against Hegseth with his members in the next Congress, when Democrats are set to take control of both the House and Senate.
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) introduced the articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of violating congressional war powers, conducting unlawful military operations and abusing his authority at the Pentagon. Massie lost his reelection effort in a Republican primary to Trump-backed candidate Ed Gallrein.
Correction: A previous version of this story misattributed a statement to Rep. Steven Horsford that was also included in a photo caption. The statement was from Rep. Jonathan Jackson, who said traffic delayed his return to vote on the impeachment motion.
