sources.news_title: How the Hegseth Impeachment Almost Came Together—and Then Fell Completely Apart
sources.text:
Sign up for the Slatest to get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.
On Monday afternoon, Kentucky GOP Rep. Thomas Massie seemed as if he could almost taste it. He had just filed his impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for a second time. The first time, in September, had prompted Republican leaders to send members home until after the election. This time, he would be able to force a vote on it within the next two days. He argued to reporters that the timing for success felt right: All Democrats were on board, and dozens of House Republicans who’d just lost their races had nothing to lose. Massie mocked news that Hegseth was planning to address the press to stave off the impeachment, telling reporters that he hoped Hegseth would address “the eight articles, and doesn’t get up and misquote the Bible in Quentin Tarantino fashion and do some pullups and call everybody fat and gay for being for this impeachment.”
When a reporter asked if any other Republicans had committed to him that they would vote for this, though, his answer was simple: “No.”
“A lot of them tell me they don’t like Hegseth,” he added after a pause, before moving on to the next question.
That dislike was worth exactly zero Republican votes late Tuesday afternoon. By a 211-to-204 vote, the House will refer the impeachment to committee—i.e., to kill it—with Massie remaining the lone Republican opponent. He joined all voting Democrats in that position, though 11 Democrats did not cast a vote. (Those 11 Democrats are likely to get an earful in the coming days.)
These were not the vibes heading into the week as this vote loomed. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz described Hegseth’s impeachment this week as “extremely likely” unless the secretary resigned first. House Republican leaders were acknowledging that they might lose, relying on the Senate to dismiss the charges either before a trial or at the conclusion of it. Senate Republicans were prepared to receive the articles, with several retiring senators—Thom Tillis, Joni Ernst, Bill Cassidy—even speculating that they were eager to entertain them. House Republicans were nervous about their attendance given the high levels of senioritis on their side and the many members who blamed their loss on the Iran war, which Hegseth has managed. In the end, though, only seven Republicans missed the impeachment vote—fewer absences than the Democrats had, even though angry, despondent Republicans had good reason to let it all burn down.
Why couldn’t Massie lure any of his own to the dark side? The problem may have been Massie himself, along with the articles that he wrote.
Massie is a longtime irritant of his fellow House Republican members, as well as the president. A quirky libertarian, Massie was defeated by a Trump-backed primary challenger earlier this year after repeatedly casting votes against his party on issues ranging from spending to foreign policy to the release of the Epstein files. He’s not indicative of where other House Republicans are.
That showed in his impeachment resolution. What were his eight articles? Several were about how Hegseth has violated the War Powers Resolution. Others charged Hegseth with ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties, authorizing extrajudicial killings against alleged drug smugglers, using the Department of Defense to retaliate against a sitting senator (Sen. Mark Kelly) for free speech, illegally capturing Venezuelan foreign leader Nicolás Maduro, and waging unauthorized war in Yemen.
Why, you might be asking, isn’t Massie directing these charges toward the guy who signs off on them—President Donald Trump?
“I think the president needs to see—this is a metaphor—one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he will see things differently,” Massie told reporters Monday. “I think politically, it’s an impossible hurdle, but also I think this is the better target. Sometimes you apply the ordnance where the best target is, and the best target is Pete Hegseth.”
Hegseth may have been the ripest political target for impeachment. But these articles weren’t written to maximize votes. Most Republicans have issues with Hegseth—his management of the Pentagon, his demotion of generals, whether he’s been accurately relaying information about the war to the president, his apparent discovery of the importance of the Strait of Hormuz only after hostilities began. They don’t have a problem with what Hegseth has done in Venezuela, or Yemen, or to people in the Caribbean, or his creative interpretations of the War Powers Resolution of 1973. Most of them support most of that. And even though many don’t like that they lost their elections over high gas and other input prices sparked by the Iran war, they’re not outright opposed to confronting Iran. Massie was asking them not merely to impeach Hegseth; he was asking them to reject the foreign policy of Trump’s first two years. They weren’t about to take that leap on either the policy or the politics.
Even retiring members.
“I’m not a fan of the secretary,” retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon, a moderate, internationalist Republican, told reporters Tuesday. “But if you read the impeachment—and it’s written by Mr. Massie, who’s anti-Iran, anti-Ukraine, anti-Israel—I just don’t really align with the impeachment itself. But, surely, if you had put in about firing 80 generals and not spending appropriated money, I’d feel a little differently about it.”
Hegseth had put his own work into saving his hide. At a Pentagon press conference Tuesday morning, the first such occasion in six months, Hegseth gave a speech defending his record and castigating Massie. That defense was directed less toward House Republicans themselves than the audience of one in the White House.
The most telling moment in Hegseth’s prepared remarks, as he described how “we’ve seen this show before,” was when he noted that “they” had “impeached President Trump over a perfect phone call.” That’s Trump’s specific phrasing for the 2019 call in which he pressured newly elected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to dig up dirt on the Bidens in exchange for military assistance, which led to Trump’s first impeachment. Hegseth then observed that “they impeached him again in his final week in office” (reason omitted.)
“Now they’re trying a third time, this time against a member of his Cabinet,” he continued. “They will fail again, and if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.”
The speech went on much like this—Trump’s great, the military is doing great because of Trump, and Trump’s great—and earned its desired review in a Trump post: “Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!”
In other words, Trump gave the signal: He would stick by his man, for now, and Republicans had better too. If this was a test of Trump’s strength with House Republicans, even after his presidency had just brought them to their lowest point in decades, this impeachment effort didn’t put up much of a fight.

sources.news_title: Pete Hegseth impeachment blocked in 211–204 House vote; Trump attacks Massie
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump declared Secretary of War Pete Hegseth exonerated and branded Republican Congressman Thomas Massie a “major LOSER” after the House of Representatives voted 211–204 on Tuesday to block an immediate impeachment showdown over US military operations in Iran and other countries.
The Republican-controlled House voted to refer eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee rather than consider the charges directly. Massie, who introduced the resolution, was the only Republican to oppose the procedural move, joining 203 Democrats. One independent supported the referral.
Advertisement
The vote handed Hegseth a reprieve in the outgoing Congress, but Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries signalled that the matter could return when his party takes control of the House in January.
Trump attacks Massie as Pentagon claims victory
Celebrating the result on Truth Social, Trump described the impeachment attempt as a failure and singled out Massie for defying his Republican colleagues.
“The Democrats’ attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!” Trump wrote.
He said every Republican except Massie had voted in Hegseth’s favour, although seven Republican lawmakers did not participate in the vote.
Trump also credited what he described as military victories in Venezuela and Iran, recruitment gains and improved morale for what he called the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot”.
His declaration went beyond what the House had decided. The resolution was referred to the committee without lawmakers voting on whether the impeachment allegations were justified.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell also celebrated the result, describing the referral as a “TOTAL VICTORY” for Hegseth and the Department of War.
In a statement posted on X, Parnell called the impeachment effort a political exercise lacking merit or evidence and said the department expected the matter to be brought to an end in committee.
Earlier, Hegseth had dismissed the impeachment attempt as a political spectacle and defended the military operations carried out under Trump’s administration.
“I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow,” he said during a Pentagon news conference.
Trump had separately praised his war secretary’s response, awarding him an “A” PLUS PLUS PLUS on Truth Social while attacking Massie as a defeated political opponent.
Why Massie sought Hegseth’s impeachment
Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, introduced eight articles accusing Hegseth of constitutional and legal violations arising from military operations in Iran, Yemen and Venezuela, as well as other alleged abuses of authority.
The central dispute concerns Congress’s constitutional powers over war and the limits imposed on military operations by the War Powers Resolution of 1973.
In his third article of impeachment, Massie accused Hegseth of continuing military operations against Iran beyond the statutory period permitted without congressional authorisation.
He argued that Operation Epic Fury had continued for 256 days despite Congress not authorising the operation.
Under the War Powers Resolution, the president is generally required to end unauthorised military involvement after 60 days, subject to provisions including a possible 30-day withdrawal period.
Massie’s additional allegations included ignoring congressional directions to end hostilities, unlawful military action in Yemen, extrajudicial killings, retaliation against Senator Mark Kelly over protected speech and the operation that captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
Hegseth rejected the impeachment bid and maintained that his actions followed the president’s lawful military directives.
At his Pentagon briefing, he compared the attempt against him to the impeachment proceedings Trump faced during his first presidential term.
Democrats warn the fight is not over
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries indicated that Tuesday’s defeat would not prevent Democrats from pursuing the matter in the next Congress.
Asked about the outcome, including lawmakers who were absent during the vote, Jeffries told reporters he had not discussed the floor proceedings with his team.
“This is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning,” he said, according to CBS News.
Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the November 3 midterm elections. Their majorities will take effect when the new Congress convenes in January.
The change gives Democrats the ability to determine whether Hegseth’s conduct becomes the subject of renewed impeachment proceedings or congressional investigations.
What the 211–204 vote actually decided
The official House roll-call record shows that 211 lawmakers supported referring the impeachment resolution to committee, while 204 opposed the move. Eighteen did not vote.

Voting was overwhelmingly along party lines. Massie was the lone Republican opposing the referral.
The referral means the current House did not adopt articles of impeachment against Hegseth. It also means lawmakers did not reach a final judgment on the substance of the allegations.
The incoming Democratic majority could initiate fresh proceedings, but Tuesday’s vote does not establish that another impeachment resolution will be introduced or approved.
For now, Hegseth remains in office, backed by Trump and most House Republicans who participated in the vote, while the dispute over the administration’s military operations remains unresolved.

sources.text:
House effort to impeach Hegseth fails, largely along party lines
The rare effort to impeach a Cabinet secretary comes in the wake of a withering midterm election defeat for Republicans. Yet GOP ranks stuck with the Trump administration.
Americans’ frustration with the Iran war helped drive a historic Democratic victory in last week’s midterms. And as lawmakers began a lame-duck session, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has overseen a conflict that Congress did not authorize, was fighting to hold on to his job amid impeachment charges tied to that war and other military decisions.
He has succeeded, at least for now.
After a House vote Tuesday derailed the impeachment effort, President Donald Trump called Mr. Hegseth a “great American patriot” in a social media post and said Democrats “must be stopped.”
Congressional lawmakers from both parties have criticized Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for executing unlawful orders related to the Iran war, the capture of Venezuela’s president and more. He defends the actions that sparked scrutiny in Congress.
An outgoing Republican House member, Thomas Massie of Kentucky, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Secretary Hegseth. This week, Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, widely expected to become House speaker after the new Congress begins in January, told ABC News he was a “hard yes” for impeachment. And on Monday, Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas said on a podcast that Mr. Hegseth faced two outcomes: Either he leaves by resignation or firing, or it is “extremely likely” he will be impeached.
But late on Monday, President Trump defended Mr. Hegseth, using social media to call on lawmakers to “stand up for Pete!!!”
House Republicans did so, thwarting the impeachment effort as a 211-204 vote sent Mr. Massie’s articles to the Judiciary Committee. Eleven Democrats were absent for the procedural vote, and all Republicans except Mr. Massie supported the motion to refer.
“I’d really like to understand why 11 Democrats don’t show up,” said Democratic Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut. “It’s a weird world when attendance is determining affairs of the state.”
Democrats don’t appear to have a clear plan for what to do next. Rep. Mark Takano of California told the Monitor he hopes to see another attempt before this Congress ends Jan. 3. If not, he said he expects a bipartisan impeachment vote next year.
Mr. Himes, who is slated to chair the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, took a more cautious approach, suggesting that Democrats should focus on oversight going forward and calling Mr. Massie’s move “not careful.”
Mr. Jeffries declined to tell reporters whether Democrats would pursue impeachment after assuming the majority in January, saying they would have that conversation “at the appropriate time” with input from relevant committee leaders.
Republicans, for their part, appear to be taking the vote as confirmation that Mr. Hegseth’s position is secure.
“I think it’s time to move on,” said Republican Rep. Burgess Owens of Utah. “He’s got a president who believes in him. ... We’re very proud of what he’s doing.”
Mr. Massie told reporters after the vote that he was “not surprised, but disappointed.” He suggested that if Democrats tried to impeach Mr. Hegseth on different charges, such as for firings or withholding Ukraine aid, they might be able to gain Republican support. But he also said Republicans did not learn from the midterm results.
“They all know they lost the election over this war, and they’re still voting for it,” he said.
Republican Rep. Dan Crenshaw of Texas criticized Mr. Massie for inflating what he called a policy dispute.
“It’s for show,” he said.
Mr. Massie’s articles accused Mr. Hegseth of violating both federal law and the Constitution. The charges include directing U.S. troops into war with Iran without congressional authorization; overseeing deadly strikes against suspected drug-smuggling boats; and leading an “act of war against a sovereign country” in the operation to remove Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from the country.
Mr. Hegseth defended himself Tuesday morning in a rare news conference, calling the impeachment charges a “farce” put forward by a “disgruntled and defeated congressman.” He defended his and the president’s decisions in Iran and other areas, and said Mr. Massie’s accusations should be dealt with through legislation, not impeachment.
“This is not patriotism,” said Mr. Hegseth. “This is sabotage.”
Had the House measure passed on Tuesday, it would have set up a trial in the Senate, where a two-thirds majority would have been required to remove Mr. Hegseth.
Mr. Hegseth’s support in the Senate, where Republicans hold a six-seat majority until Democrats take control, did not appear to be rock solid. A handful of Republican senators, including North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy, had indicated they might be open to voting to convict Mr. Hegseth.
Lawmakers on the right have criticized Mr. Hegseth for keeping Congress in the dark on military decisions and for what some see as unprofessional conduct and messaging.
Since the Iran war started, members of Congress have grilled Mr. Hegseth about the cost of the war (most recently estimated at $47.1 billion), whether the Pentagon’s estimates fall short of the war’s true cost, and the White House’s request for $67.1 billion more in funding, mostly for the war.

Pingree, Golden vote with fellow Democrats as House Republicans stifle Hegseth impeachment
sources.text:
House Republicans effectively halted the effort by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky, and Democrats to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday.
Massie filed the resolution in the House on Monday as lawmakers returned to Washington. Tuesday’s vote was a procedural attempt by Republicans to stop the impeachment push by sending the matter back to committee, the Associated Press reported.
The motion passed 211-204, with multiple Democrats and Republicans missing the vote. Massie was the lone Republican to cross party lines.
Maine’s U.S. Reps. Chellie Pingree and Jared Golden joined fellow Democrats in voting against sending it back to committee.
Massie’s resolution included eight counts of impeachment. It largely focused on the war in Iran but also included references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela, AP reported.
However, Tuesday’s vote may only delay the matter, with Democrats set to take control of both the House and Senate in January.

sources.news_title: Pete Hegseth survives impeachment bid, Trump slams Democrats
House GOP derails Hegseth impeachment over Iran, Kelly and boat strikes
sources.text:
WASHINGTON – House Republicans derailed an attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday over retaliation against Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, among other allegations.
The 211-204 vote sent the eight article resolution to a committee, effectively killing it.
Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who authored the resolution and forced it to the House floor with a procedural maneuver, was the only Republican who opposed quashing it.
He sharply criticized fellow Republicans for standing by Hegseth and President Donald Trump despite last week’s blue wave in the midterm elections.
“My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do, they just can’t bring themselves to do it,” he told reporters after the vote.
Massie lost his seat to a Trump-backed primary challenger, so he won’t be able to refile the resolution in the new Congress, though Democrats will take control in January. Not one voted to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee, whose chairman, Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, was elected earlier Tuesday as minority leader for the new Congress.
Hegseth called the articles a “farce” at a Pentagon news conference Tuesday morning.
“They mock the Constitution, they attack the chain of command and they criminalize the warfighters who execute lawful orders,” he said.
After the House vote Tuesday evening, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell declared “TOTAL VICTORY!” in a post on X.
“The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House Judiciary Committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter,” he wrote. “From the beginning, this effort has been a political exercise devoid of merit, evidence, or seriousness. It collapses under the weight of Secretary Hegseth’s record of restoring the warrior ethos, delivering results, and putting the mission first. The American people see through it.”
Articles of impeachment included allegations about Hegseth’s role in the war against Iran, which has lasted more than six months without congressional approval; the capture of Venezuela’s president, Nicolas Maduro; and deadly strikes against purported drug boats in the Caribbean, including strikes against shipwrecked survivors.
Massie said the article related to Kelly, a Democrat, was the “most ironic” element of the 34-page resolution, noting that Hegseth accused the retired Navy combat pilot of “seditious statements” and “reckless misconduct” for urging military personnel to resist illegal orders.
As a retired Navy officer receiving a pension, Kelly technically remains subject to the Uniform Code of Military Justice. He retired as a captain in 2011 after 25 years in the Navy, flying dozens of combat missions and four space shuttle missions for NASA.
His comments came in a video that he and five other Democratic lawmakers – one former CIA officer and the rest military veterans – posted Nov. 18, 2025.
The impeachment resolution called Hegseth’s efforts to punish Kelly a “politically motivated reprisal.”
Trump called the six Democrats’ comments seditious. In February, a federal grand jury declined to indict them.
A federal judge blocked Hegseth’s effort to punish Kelly, finding that he had “trampled on” the senator’s First Amendment rights.

The resolution seeks to impeach Hegseth for his role in waging President Donald Trump's war on Iran in contravention of the War Powers Act and apparent war crimes committed by US forces in the conflict, including the February massacre of 156 people, at least 120 of them children, in a missile strike on an elementary school in the southern city of Minab.
Massie's resolution also accuses Hegseth of "extrajudicial killings of at least 221 persons aboard seagoing vessels alleged to be smuggling narcotics in the Caribbean Sea and the Eastern Pacific Ocean, principally in international waters" as part of Trump's boat-bombing spree; the invasion of Venezuela and kidnapping of President Nicolás Maduro and his wife; waging an illegal war on Yemen that has killed hundreds of civilians; and suppressing free speech at the Pentagon.
The 11 Democrats who were not present for the vote are: Julia Brownley (Calif.), Lou Correa (Calif.), Laura Gillen (NY), Steven Horsford (Nev.), Jonathan Jackson (Ill.), Nancy Pelosi (Calif.), Brittany Pettersen (Colo.), Melanie Stansbury (NM), Haley Stevens (Mich.), Marilyn Strickland (Wash.), and Frederica Wilson (Fla.). Correa is recovering from an undisclosed medical procedure and cannot travel.
Seven Republicans also did not vote. Observers noted there was a chance for Democrats to keep Massie's impeachment bid alive if more of them attended the session and voted.
Jeffries (D-NY)—who backs impeaching Hegseth—"didn’t think it was important to make sure 11 Democrats didn’t skip the Hegseth impeachment vote," author Jared Yates Sexton wrote on Bluesky.
Migrant Insider editor Pablo Manríquez accused Democrats of having "a serious leadership problem."

Hegseth also said he "stand[s] behind every one of" the massacres and killings listed in the resolution, and that he "was proud to execute them, and... would do it again tomorrow.”
Asked by Politico's Riley Rogerson about the 11 Democrats' absence, Jeffries said: "I haven't had a conversation with anyone on the floor team about what may or may not have happened in terms of the Hegseth resolution, but this is not the end of it. It's just the beginning."
While numerous Democrats said they would renew efforts to impeach Hegseth once they're in control of Congress, many observers pointed to Tuesday's vote as further evidence that new party leadership is needed.

sources.news_title: House votes to effectively end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
sources.text:
The House has voted 211 to 204 to refer the articles of impeachment filed against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, effectively killing the impeachment effort spearheaded by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.
Tuesday’s vote short-circuits any potential floor vote on the articles of impeachment, and virtually guarantees the measure will not be taken up before the current session of Congress expires.
The vote provided a surprise reprieve for President Trump’s embattled Defense Secretary, who was facing an impeachment vote by the full House as early as Wednesday.
Massie reintroduced the articles of impeachment on Monday, accusing Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors in connection to the war with Iran and U.S. strikes against Iran and on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean.
Massie’s impeachment resolution sought to oust Hegseth over the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization, and the effort to punish Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for a video telling service members they can refuse illegal orders.
Hegseth defended himself against the impeachment effort during a rare press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday, criticizing Massie as a “disgruntled and defeated congressman.”
“I stand behind every one of these operations,” Hegseth said. “I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow.”
On Monday, Trump expressed support for Hegseth during a wide-ranging, impromptu press briefing at the White House.
“I’ll stand by him,” Trump said. “He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won.”
The impeachment measure was Massie’s second attempt against Hegseth. He first sought to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterm elections, prompting Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to call an early recess to avoid the vote. That caused the resolution to expire, which is why Massie reintroduced the resolution again this week.
While the impeachment push may be quelled for now, Hegseth’s troubles on Capitol Hill are not over. Democrats have promised vigorous investigations into Hegseth’s Pentagon once they assume the majority in January.
Whether they will mount another impeachment effort remains unclear, but in an interview with NPR last week, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next Speaker of the House, said simply of Hegseth, “He’s got to go.”

sources.news_title: House Republicans block bid to impeach Pete Hegseth, Donald Trump calls it ‘exoneration of a great American patriot’
sources.text:
The House Republicans stalled the motion to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday after the majority voted to refer the eight articles to the House Judiciary Committee. The Republican-controlled House of Representatives voted 211 to 204 in favour of referring the articles of impeachment to the GOP-led House Judiciary Committee.
Thomas Massie, the outgoing Kentucky Republican Representative, had earlier warned that vote would kill the impeachment motion.
Allegations against Pete Hegseth
Massie's eight articles of impeachment accused Hegseth of waging war illegally without congressional authorisation and of abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.
Several related to the eight-month Iran war, accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution, which places limits on US military interventions without congressional authorisation.
Other allegations involved the 2025 conflict with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which Massie branded “extrajudicial killings.”
Also Read | ‘Pete Hegseth won two wars’: Trump says as Republican moves impeachment motion
He also accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech by trying to punish Democratic Senator Mark Kelly over a video urging military and intelligence personnel to refuse illegal orders.
What is next for Pete Hegseth?
Massie had hoped to draw votes from Republicans upset with Hegseth's policies and wary of the unpopularity of the Iran war, but no other Republicans joined him. Democrats who had supported the impeachment effort will now have to wait until at least January, when they take control of Congress.
This is not the first time House Republicans, despite some calling for Hegseth's impeachment, have stalled the vote. In September, when Massie initially moved to impeach Hegseth, House Speaker Mike Johnson abruptly cancelled the final scheduled day of legislative business and sent lawmakers home early, delaying the vote until the midterm elections are over.
On Tuesday, Johnson called the impeachment motion a “political gambit for attention” and predicted Republicans would defeat it “one way or the other.”
Donald Trump calls it exoneration
US President Donald Trump, who continues to publicly support Hegseth, a former Fox News host, celebrated the development, saying the effort to impeach "has miserably FAILED!"
“Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
Trump added that Hegseth's performance on Iran, Venezuela and other issues “led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.”
Also Read | ‘Only kidding’: Donald Trump says on offering Dana White press secretary job
Vice President JD Vance also backed the defence secretary, saying he had "obviously not" committed impeachable offences.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, in a post on X, called the vote a “TOTAL VICTORY! We look forward to ending this sham impeachment in the committee room, where facts will continue to prevail and this distraction can be put to rest."
Hegseth earlier Tuesday dismissed the impeachment effort as a "farce" and defended his record leading the Iran war and other military operations under Trump.
"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," he said at a Pentagon press conference, branding the accusations "slander" and "sabotage."

sources.news_title: House Republicans Reject Impeachment Effort Against Hegseth
sources.text:
House Republicans voted to reject efforts by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) and the Democrats to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.
In a 211-204 vote, House Republicans voted to have Massie’s impeachment resolution referred to the House Judiciary Committee, Fox News’s Bill Melugin reported in a post on X.
The move to refer the impeachment resolution to the committee “ends efforts to impeach Hegseth over the Iran war and other issues until the next Congress,” the Hill reported.
While Massie voted with the Democrats, Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-CA) voted with the Republicans, according to the outlet.
Earlier in the day, Vice President JD Vance issued a statement defending Hegseth, expressing that “impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking.”
“Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not,” Vance wrote in a post on X. “Like so much of Congress, impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking. Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements. Rather than use them, they’re going to try to impeach Pete Hegseth. They did the same to Donald Trump.”
Prior to Vance’s statement, Hegseth defended actions that he has taken regarding “the conflict with Iran,” along with “the extraction of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro.”
“It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” Hegseth during a press conference.

sources.news_title: Pete Hegseth survives impeachment push in narrow 211-204 vote, Trump says Democrats' move 'miserably failed'
Fox News’ Jesse Watters Praises Pete Hegseth’s ‘Lethal and Brilliant’ Military Action as House Quashes Impeachment Effort
sources.text:
Fox News host Jesse Watters championed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s military efforts, saying he should not be impeached because his actions were not unlawful.
The anchor’s remarks came after House Republicans quashed a resolution that would have impeached the defense secretary. The effort, brought forward by Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats, would have the Pentagon chief removed for his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran.
“Bill Clinton hit the Chinese embassy. The only thing he got impeached for was oral sex,” Watters told his co-hosts on “The Five.” “So this is crazy town. Everything was lawful.”
Watters compared Hegseth’s actions to strikes made by former presidents, including Obama’s Libya strikes and Biden hitting Yemen.
“Pete is taking this on the chin for what? The most surgical, lethal, and, I don’t know, brilliant military excursions we’ve seen in a very long time,” Watters said.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican who will leave Congress in January after losing his seat to a Trump-backed opponent, said Hegseth has “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders.” He claimed that the defense secretary waged war against Yemen and Venezuela without congressional authorization.
In his first press conference since May on Tuesday, Hegseth said that his impeachment attempt felt like a “political spectacle.”
“I actually think what Pete did today proves he should be out there more,” Dana Perino said of his rare press conference. “He’s a very effective communicator.”
The defense secretary undercut the death toll tied to American military men in the Iran war. He said that 18 Americans died in Operation Epic Fury when the Pentagon count puts the number of U.S. troops who died in operations related to the Iran war at 23.
Hegseth also only called on conservative outlets at the press conference, fielding questions from reporters at One America News Network, Real America’s Voice, The Daily Wire, The Daily Signal, Fox News and The Washington Times.
When Fox News correspondent Lucas Tomlinson asked whether Hegseth agreed with Vice President JD Vance that the Iran war was a major reason Republicans lost the midterm elections. Hegseth dodged the question, saying that “politics is not really my thing” and continued to defend the war.
President Donald Trump said that Hegseth’s news conference was a “A PLUS, PLUS, PLUS” in a Truth Social post before calling Massie “a total loser.”

sources.news_title: House votes down bid to impeach Hegseth, but it’s clear Democrats will be gunning for him
sources.text:
Pete Hegseth has dodged the impeachment bullet, at least for a few months, but Congress has signalled that it is preparing an arsenal of politically lethal weapons against the U.S. Defence Secretary and the White House.
The two-day Capitol Hill rebellion against Mr. Hegseth was postponed Tuesday but not cancelled − both a beginning and an ending.
The beginning was the power, even the audacity, of the surging new Democratic Party’s energy and determination, displaying its force two months before its new members are even sworn in on Capitol Hill. The ending was the compliance that Congress has displayed for the past 22 months, relinquishing its prerogatives and constitutional remit by permitting President Donald Trump to unilaterally conduct war and trade policies, areas the country’s Founding Fathers expressly assigned to the legislative branch.
The Republican-controlled House of Representatives killed the impeachment effort on a procedural vote by a 211-to-204 margin. But the issue will almost certainly resurface in January, when the Democrats will control the chamber and have sufficient support to impeach Mr. Hegseth and set up a trial in the Senate.
Reuters
The actual eventual punishment of impeachment − perhaps merely symbolic, but a threat to his tenure if the Senate in turn musters the 67 votes required to propel the Pentagon chief out of office − would be the least of what was set in motion Tuesday in an extraordinary post-election episode in the House.
The change in the aggressiveness of a branch of the U.S. government that, until recent hours, was somnolent − at best a passive participant in the dance of American politics − is perhaps the more significant development. It is an unmistakable foreshadowing of months of wrangling with the Trump administration and a constant source of rebuffs to the President and, with the Democrats’ new investigatory powers, subpoenas to White House officials.
Unless the Senate convicts him next year, the vote to submit him to the sanction set out in Article II, Section 4, of the Constitution, which speaks of “treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors,” may be destined to become a footnote in history, much like the 1868 impeachment of William Belknap for corruption, remembered only by high school students marinating themselves in historical arcana in preparation for university entrance exams. The impeachment of secretary of homeland security Alejandro Mayorkas over immigration issues has already been largely forgotten, even though it occurred only 21 months ago.
Both were acquitted in the Senate.
U.S. House derails attempt to impeach Hegseth
By sending the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, the House essentially buried the measure for the time being; it almost certainly will not emerge from the committee before the year, and thus this Congress, expires.
But the case will likely re-emerge next year, when the Democrats control both chambers of Congress. Though the current Senate would almost certainly have acquitted him, the new Senate may not. The Democrats could have as many as 56 seats, 11 short of the number required for conviction.
If impeached, the combative Mr. Hegseth, who has spent nearly two years speaking an argot of “warriors” without compunction, likely will do as Mr. Trump has done, which is to transform historical ignominy into political opportunity and a symbol of indomitable courage in the face of relentless attack.
The significance of the drive to impeach Mr. Hegseth, and the advent of a Democratic-controlled Congress in January, rests in the willingness of the legislative branch to return to being an active participant in policy-making in Washington. It likely foreshadows a more activist role in trade policy, where the powerful House Ways and Means Committee has customarily been a force in tariffs − a sea change that could affect trade duties imposed by Mr. Trump on Canada. It also signals more congressional intrusion in foreign policy, where for centuries there has been a collision between presidential prerogatives and congressional authority.
U.S. Republican Rep. Massie files resolution to impeach Hegseth
The irony of this episode is that the drive to impeach Mr. Hegseth was spearheaded by a Republican, though one spurned by Mr. Trump and then defeated in a primary by a candidate endorsed by the President. Representative Thomas Massie submitted eight articles of impeachment ranging from the conduct of the Iran and Yemen wars to military strikes against suspected drug traffickers and the capture of Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro. In his defence at an extraordinary early-morning Pentagon briefing, Mr. Hegseth dismissed Mr. Massie, who was elected to the House in 2010, as a “disgruntled and defeated” lawmaker.
Mr. Massie has been a Republican outlier, an early opponent of the Iran war, a leader in the congressional effort to mount an aggressive investigation into the conduct and contacts of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and enough of a Trump irritant to prompt the President to attack him Tuesday morning as “a TOTAL LOSER.”
But Mr. Massie is not the lone Republican to express skepticism and impatience with Mr. Hegseth, who has tepid relations on Capitol Hill and hasn’t been able to win the support of Republican lawmakers who have balked at approving, without adjustments, the US$1.5-trillion military budget he has submitted for congressional approval. Even with Tuesday’s failure to advance the impeachment resolution to a floor vote, the Democrats delivered a message to Mr. Hegseth. It ended up being a message to Mr. Trump as well.

sources.news_title: House Republicans block Hegseth impeachment bid
sources.text:
House Republicans on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, voting 211-204 to send a resolution introduced by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) to committee, effectively halting the proceedings for the remainder of the current Congress.
The narrow procedural vote spared Hegseth an immediate confrontation over eight articles of impeachment related to American military operations in Iran and other countries. The effort could be revived in the next Congress, when Democrats are expected to control both the House and Senate with substantial majorities.
Every Democrat voted against referring the resolution to committee, while Massie was the only Republican to join them. Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-CA), who left the Republican Party earlier this year and lost his reelection bid last week, sided with Republicans.
President Donald Trump welcomed the outcome in a lengthy post on Truth Social, portraying the vote as a vindication of Hegseth's leadership.
"The Democrats’ attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED! Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete. Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot. The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped! MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN."
Massie, an outspoken opponent of the American military campaign against Iran, had reintroduced the impeachment articles on Monday despite losing his Republican primary earlier this year.
The Kentucky lawmaker was defeated by former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein, who received the backing of Trump and Hegseth. The Pentagon chief personally traveled to Kentucky to campaign for Gallrein, who subsequently won election to Congress last week.
Massie's impeachment resolution accused Hegseth of violating constitutional and federal legal restrictions during military operations in Iran, Yemen, the Caribbean and the Eastern Pacific, as well as the American operation that captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year.
Three of the eight articles specifically concerned the Iran war. Massie argued that the administration had conducted the campaign without congressional authorization and that Hegseth had disregarded a congressional vote calling for an end to the conflict.
Another article alleged that Hegseth ordered the removal of Pentagon safeguards designed to distinguish civilian targets from legitimate military objectives, contributing to civilian deaths.
A fifth article accused the defense secretary of acting as an “executioner" by directing military strikes against suspected drug-trafficking vessels in waters near South America. According to the figures cited, at least 244 individuals described as “narco-terrorists" have been killed in the operations.
Massie also accused Hegseth of retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) for telling American service members that they could refuse unlawful orders.
The allegations concerned disciplinary proceedings initiated against Kelly that could potentially result in a reduction of his military rank. Massie argued that the measures violated protections for free speech.
Before Tuesday's vote, Massie had indicated that he would seek separate votes on each impeachment article if the House rejected the motion to refer the resolution to committee.
Hegseth forcefully rejected the accusations during a Pentagon press conference Tuesday morning, his first in more than six months.
He characterized Massie as “one disgruntled and defeated congressman" pursuing “a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment."
Hegseth further accused the Kentucky Republican of attempting to “do damage to this president, this country, and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it" during his final weeks in office.
“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it. In the 250 years of our American republic, no secretary of war or secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations, and in our case, successful ones at that," Hegseth told reporters.
Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other senior administration officials also defended the Pentagon chief, dismissing the impeachment initiative as “absurd."
Speaking at the White House on Monday, Trump had already pledged to stand behind Hegseth if the House proceeded with impeachment.
“Yeah, I’ll stand by him," the President said.
Trump also criticized Massie personally, calling him “a stone cold loser" and accusing him of harboring resentment.
“Massie has a lot of hatred in his heart," Trump said.
“I don’t want to waste my time watching him. We won two wars, and we’ve made the world a lot safer place, and then we’re supposed to be impeached?"

sources.news_title: US Republicans shield Hegseth from impeachment, handing Trump a political victory
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, Nov 11 — Republicans in the US House of Representatives yesterday blocked an effort to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war, handing President Donald Trump a victory days after his party’s crushing midterm election defeat.
The House voted 211 to 204 to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively derailing a planned vote today on whether to bring formal charges against the embattled Pentagon chief.
The resolution was introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, a Trump critic who was the only member of his party to oppose the procedural maneuver, according to US media.
The impeachment drive had threatened to deepen Trump’s troubles after Democrats swept last week’s midterms, with anger at the sputtering Iran war and soaring fuel prices helping drive voters to a historic rejection of Republicans.
Republicans still hold a narrow House majority until January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. And 11 Democrats missed the vote.
Trump hailed the procedural defeat as an “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot,” in a post on Truth Social, while Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, in a post on X, called the vote as a “TOTAL VICTORY!”
“We look forward to ending this sham impeachment in the committee room, where facts will continue to prevail and this distraction can be put to rest,” Parnell added.
Hegseth earlier yesterday dismissed the impeachment effort as a “farce” and defended his record leading the Iran war and other military operations under Trump.
“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” he said at a Pentagon press conference, branding the accusations “slander” and “sabotage.”
Moments after Hegseth’s televised appearance, Trump signaled his support.
“Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS,” the 80-year-old president wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Vice President JD Vance also backed the defense secretary, saying he had “obviously not” committed impeachable offenses.
‘Would do it again’
Massie’s eight articles of impeachment accused Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorization and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.
Several related to the eight-month Iran war, accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution, which places limits on US military interventions without congressional authorization.
Other allegations involved the 2025 conflict with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which Massie branded “extrajudicial killings.”
He also accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech by trying to punish Democratic Senator Mark Kelly over a video urging military and intelligence personnel to refuse illegal orders.
Hegseth defended the operations in Yemen, Iran, Venezuela and against alleged drug smugglers, while seeking to equate the impeachment effort with an attack on US troops.
“I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow,” he said.
The decision to send the resolution to committee halts the immediate impeachment drive but does not prevent Democrats from reviving the effort after taking control of Congress in January.
Massie, who lost his Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger, will leave Congress at the end of his term. — AFP

sources.news_title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
sources.text:
US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth
- Published
An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill.
A majority of the House of Representatives voted to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky.
During an earlier briefing, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".
The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.
That calculation might change in January, when the opposition Democratic Party assumes control of both chambers of Congress, following its successes in the US midterm elections. For now, Trump's Republican Party remains in control.
After Tuesday's vote, the most senior Democrat in the House, Hakeem Jeffries, said: "This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning."
The question on which lawmakers were voting on Tuesday was whether or not to refer the resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, which is led by Republicans. The alternative would have been to allow the resolution to proceed in the House itself.
All Republicans other than Massie voted to refer the resolution to the committee, meaning that the congressman's effort failed in a 211-204 vote.
The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress.
More than a dozen members missed the ballot. They included 11 Democrats, several of whom blamed traffic issues for their absences.
Several members of the party criticised their fellow lawmakers for missing the vote.
"You should show up and do your job," said Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed during an interview with CNN, making a direct address to those who did not vote. The Michigan lawmaker recently won a US Senate race in Michigan, having criticised US ties to Israel and the war in Iran on the campaign trail.
- Analysis: Hegseth fights for his political life with appeal to Trump 
  - Published1 day ago
Meanwhile Trump celebrated Tuesday's outcome in a post on Truth Social, saying the effort "has miserably FAILED".
"Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," Trump said, referring to Hegseth.
After the vote, Massie said he "wasn't surprised" but "was disappointed", according to BBC's US media partner CBS.
"My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do," he added. "They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically."
Massie had previously acknowledged his impeachment bid may not succeed immediately, but argued it could help push Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.
The Kentucky congressman also said that removing Hegseth now would give the Senate time to approve a replacement while Republicans were still in power.
Impeachment resolutions can be carried past the end of a congressional term, meaning Democrats would be able to take it up next year.
The Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January following a successful midterm election that allowed them control of both chambers.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, had predicted earlier in the day that the impeachment bid would fail.
In the eight articles of impeachment formally introduced in the House on Monday, Massie said Hegseth was "breaking the law and must be held accountable" for fighting a war in Iran for more than 90 days without lawmakers' approval.
The impeachment articles also accused Hegseth of overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the US campaign against boats alleged to be carrying drugs in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth called efforts to impeach him a political stunt by a Trump administration opponent who was "disgruntled and defeated".
Hegseth also argued Massie's resolution endangered national security, because it communicated to US adversaries "that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations".
"This is not patriotism. This is sabotage," he said.
He echoed some statements Trump had made during a surprise appearance at the White House briefing room on Monday, including touting a rise in military recruitment levels.
But Hegseth said Massie was motivated by policy differences and "not high crimes, not misdemeanours, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offences the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause".
Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year to a Trump-backed opponent, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it began in February.
He had already incurred the president's ire for demanding the Trump administration release files on deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
While Hegseth has survived politically for now, many lawmakers - including some Republicans - have questioned how long he can last in the administration.
Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a Republican, said on Tuesday he expected Hegseth to resign or be fired by Trump.
- Top House Democrat 'a hard yes' on impeaching Hegseth 
  - Published3 days ago

sources.news_title: Pete Hegseth escaped impeachment. Black leaders say his removal is inevitable.
sources.text:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth managed to dodge a congressional effort to impeach him from office. But Black leaders tell theGrio that the nation’s top military chief must go one way or the other.
“There’s no question that Pete Hegseth is a present danger to our national security,” U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock told theGrio on Tuesday. “We have to use the powers of oversight to hold him accountable.”
Critics of Hegseth say the eight articles of impeachment against him, which were introduced by Republican U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, are necessary for accountability for the Trump administration’s costly and deadly war in Iran. However, every Republican, except Massie, in the U.S. House of Representatives voted against the impeachment measure–even though there are several GOP lawmakers who have been critical of Hegseth’s handling of the Iran war.
While Massie and Democrats were unsuccessful in advancing the impeachment measure, a Democratic-controlled Congress in January would likely have greater success.
“They are only prolonging the inevitable,” said Victor LaGroon, a U.S. Army veteran and strategist who served as chief diversity officer for the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs in the Biden administration. He told theGrio, “At the end of the day, the American people have spoken; they demand change.”
The articles of impeachment accused Hegseth of violating the U.S. Constitution and formally charged him for several actions, including his directing of U.S. armed forces into hostilities against Iran without a declaration of war or congressional authorization; extrajudicial killings such as the U.S. airstrikes on small boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean; the killing of civilians; and retaliation against a sitting U.S. senator.
The Iran war has lasted eight months and has caused gas and energy prices to skyrocket to record levels.
“He has dragged us into a lawless and reckless war of choice because he is so in over his head. There are no clear objectives for this war…He cannot even articulate clearly what victory looks like,” said Senator Warnock.
The Georgia lawmaker told theGrio, “As a result, Americans are less safe and gas is more expensive, and we need to get out of this war.” He added, “There’s no question that Hegseth needs to be held accountable.”
The rebuke against Hegseth was largely focused on the Iran war and other military actions, however, Black veterans who spoke with theGrio say the Defense Secretary should also be removed from office for how his leadership has harmed Black service members.
“While the articles related to the war and the boat strikes are certainly valid, I think his actions towards DEI are equally not only repugnant but a violation of military code as well as the law,” said Ed Anderson, a lead organizer with Common Defense and U.S. Air Force veteran.
Hegseth has used his office to block the promotions of Black and other minority service members, including women, and has eliminated DEI-related programs designed to be more inclusive for Black and brown military service members.
“These articles of impeachment include Hegseth’s removal of the military’s top lawyers, but do not include the removal of already approved Black and women officers from promotion lists,” said Kyle Bibby, co-founder and co-CEO of the Black Veterans Project.
Bibby told theGrio, “According to new reporting, these officers had promotions withheld over things like supporting command Pride events, sitting on a minority aviation panel at the Naval Academy, or disciplining service members who refused the mandatory COVID vaccine. Impeachment or not, these promotion decisions need to be investigated.”
“His relentless efforts to devalue and undermine the careers of leaders of color and women are in direct violation and serve as contradiction of what our armed forces seek to represent,” said LaGroon. “For many veterans, he is unworthy of appropriately representing America’s fighting forces and its legacy of service and sacrifice.”
Hegseth and the White House were defiant in the face of the impeachment effort. During a Tuesday morning press conference, the controversial secretary of the renamed Department of War said removing him from office would 
put a “target on the backs” of U.S. service members and said it undermines U.S. missions in “real time.”
But Anderson argued it’s Hegseth who has put a target on the backs of U.S. service members. The veterans activist called out the firing of senior officials, including the Pentagon’s top military planner.
“How do you, in the middle of a war, or whatever you want to call it, get rid of your top defense official in charge of planning? It just doesn’t make any sense,” he said.
LaGroon says Hegseth’s conduct already undermines U.S. service members, telling theGrio he “violated every moral code we expect our service members to exemplify.”
He continued, “Values like duty, honor, respect, loyalty, discipline, and professionalism.” The Black veteran added, “He has demonstrated through his lack of respect and integrity that he is unable to represent our country and its fighting forces.”

sources.news_title: Hegseth Survives Impeachment Attempt
sources.text:
Self-styled Secretary of War Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment Tuesday night, as solidarity from House Republicans blocked a bill introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., charging Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors.”
Though Democrats overwhelmingly joined Massie’s effort following their midterm election landslide, the House voted 211 to 204 to refer the charges to a committee, allowing Republicans to slow the process. With 11 Democrats absent, they lacked the numbers. Massie, however, dismissed the impact of Democratic absences to The Intercept. “No, there were enough Republicans to rally to get here,” he said.
The procedural vote spared Republicans a more difficult vote on whether to impeach Hegseth on Massie’s eight charges, including waging wars without congressional authorization and undercutting measures to prevent civilian casualties. It followed a week of increasingly desperate efforts by the Pentagon chief to shore up congressional and White House support, including a campaign-style video intended to influence Trump, a social media campaign by underlings, and a rare appearance by Hegseth himself before the Pentagon press corps.
For half an hour on Tuesday morning’s news conference, Hegseth wove a web of lies designed to refute or obfuscate Massie’s eight charges. He claimed that the effort to impeach him was a stunt by just “one disgruntled congressman.” That, too, turned out to be false as 203 members of Congress voted with Massie.
On Tuesday, a coalition of more than 40 civil society organizations — including Oxfam America, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), Common Defense, Demand Progress, MoveOn, and the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft — sent a letter calling on all House members to vote for every article of impeachment filed against Hegseth.
“Pete Hegseth’s time at the Pentagon has done grievous harm to the nation and to the Constitution,” said Demand Progress senior policy adviser Cavan Kharrazian. “This is a man who ignored the will of Congress to execute an illegal war in Iran, kidnapped a foreign leader for oil, restarted war on Yemen, sent missiles to kill suspected drug traffickers and weaponized the Pentagon against a political enemy.”
The House has only impeached two Cabinet secretaries: William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024. In neither case did the Senate vote to convict.
After the vote, Massie called out the display of inaction from his Republican colleagues.
“They diagnosed why they lost the election,” Massie said of fellow Republicans, following the vote on Tuesday night. “But tonight they were paralyzed to do anything about it. And that’s the story of Congress.”
Absent from the vote were Democratic Reps. Julia Brownley, Lou Correa and Nancy Pelosi, of California; Laura Gillen of New York; Steven Horsford of Nevada; Jonathan Jackson of Illinois; Brittany Pettersen of Colorado; Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico; Haley Stevens of Michigan; Marilyn Strickland of Washington; and Frederica Wilson of Florida. The absent Republicans were Reps. Monica De La Cruz of Texas; Neal Dunn of Florida; Russell Fry of South Carolina; Julia Letlow of Louisiana; Tom Tiffany and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin; and Rudy Yakym of Indiana.
A senior congressional staffer predicted that Hegseth would face a very rough road if he survived impeachment. “Oversight is going to come crashing down on his head,” that staffer said. “Will Hegseth continue to obstruct? Yes. But wait until the subpoenas start.”
Congressional committees have broad investigative powers, including the authority to subpoena administration officials to testify under oath and compel them to turn over documents. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., who will head the House Armed Services Committee in the next Congress, said Hegseth and Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg would be first on the list to testify.
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., one of the leading voices for Hegseth’s impeachment, told The Intercept there were “many ways” for Democrats to hold him accountable in the next session, specifically compelling him to testify before the American people. “I would be surprised to see him last the next two years in this administration,” she told The Intercept. “I think that he is not only one of the most incompetent members of the administration, but also the most unpopular — and it’s on a bipartisan basis. So the pressure will continue to grow for there to be some change at the Pentagon.”
Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., told The Intercept that the incoming Democrats have Hegseth in their sights. “I want Pete Hegseth not just impeached, I want him prosecuted. They murdered people in the Caribbean. And we killed 163 little girls in Iran,” he said. “Everybody in my class is ready for him to go. We tried it. It didn’t work. We’ll do it again.”
In a Truth Social post, President Donald Trump celebrated the outcome while expressing confusion over the vote. Trump called it the “Democrats’ attempt to impeach” Hegseth, despite the fact the effort was introduced by Massie, a Republican, who he called “a major LOSER.” He claimed it was an “EXONERATION” of Hegseth and added: “The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

Massie tried to turn a bitter policy fight into an impeachment spectacle. The House refused to give him the floor victory he wanted.
The immediate reaction captured the political reality: Massie’s resolution was going nowhere.

PETE HEGSETH WINS! And by extension, THE TROOPS 🇺🇸

Massie wanted a showdown. What he got was a trip to committee and a brutal vote tally showing that he stood alone among Republicans against ending the floor fight.
Hegseth remains in place, President Trump’s party closed ranks, and this impeachment push is dead on arrival.
This is a Guest Post from our friends over at WLTReport. View the original article here.

We would be, but would we have been right to be? It was a bad mistake, but it wasn’t the end of the world. He deserved a rap on the knuckles for that, not impeachment. And it doesn’t justify calling him unqualified, let alone the imputation of drunkenness, which is pure Dem propaganda.
Come January we will begin to see what living under Eastern European Soviet control felt like. That “magnanimous in victory” garbage is long gone. Rush always said the Dems didn’t want a level playing field… today he might say the Dems want us buried under the playing field.

Well, not exactly. There are how many more petty little asshat bureaucrats waiting in the wings?
I’ve seen Brian Cox’s analysis of the impeachment motion, which he shreds mostly on the basis that the War Powers Act is unconstitutional, and therefore Hegseth was entitled to do all the things he’s accused of.
The thing is, that has always been the opinion of the executive branch, ever since Congress passed the thing over Nixon’s veto. Every president has taken the position that it’s invalid, and that while they would voluntarily obey it just to keep the peace with Congress, this should not be taken as a concession that it’s valid.
So if the allegations are true, all it means, from the executive branch’s point of view, is that this president decided to abandon that practice of voluntary compliance, because the circumstances called for action. No violation of any law, thus no high crime or misdemeanor, and no grounds for impeachment.
But the thing is, for all that time Congress has consistently taken the position that the WPA is valid law that binds the executive branch. As far as I know no court has ever ruled on the question, so Congress is entitled to its view just as the presidents have been entitled to theirs. Which means that from Congress’s point of view Hegseth’s alleged offenses, if confirmed, are criminal, and grounds for impeachment.
So I think Cox’s argument for why the House should not impeach Hegseth fails. All you can say is that he acted in good faith, but that’s not a defense. It might come down to the courts having to intervene and answer the question of whether the WPA is law; but the courts would probably say it’s a political question and not one they should answer.
The ultimate answer, of course, is that even next year there will not be the numbers in the senate to convict him, so as long as the President retains his confidence in him he will remain in office for the next two years. Basically, in practice the WPA is invalid because the executive branch says so and the legislative branch hasn’t got what it takes to enforce its view.

The problem is that the Democrats won’t vote to convict a fellow Democrat, even in the face of convincing evidence of an actual crime, for which ordinary people actually serve time in prison.
During the Clinton impeachment, when the Democrats were trying to argue that perjury in a civil case, or at least perjury about ones sex life in a civil case, is not really a big deal and should be treated differently than ordinary perjury, the NYT found eight people who were at that very time sitting in federal prisons for exactly that. If Clinton had any sense of shame at all, he would have pardoned those eight people. He didn’t.
So impeachment of a Democrat is impossible. Impeachment of a Republican is possible, if the case against him is strong enough.

sources.news_title: Pete Hegseth has escaped Impeachment for Now, but the New Congress will be less Forgiving
‘EXONERATION!; Trump Celebrates Defeat of Pete Hegseth Impeachment Push
House Republicans quash effort to impeach Hegseth - American Press
sources.text:
House Republicans quash effort to impeach Hegseth
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
The House on Tuesday turned aside a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, halting an effort to remove the Pentagon chief for his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran.
The vote came as Republicans grapple with the fallout from sweeping midterm losses that some in the party have blamed on the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gas prices. But after President Donald Trump signaled strong support for Hegseth, GOP lawmakers largely stood by the secretary Tuesday, blocking the effort in a near party-line vote.
The effort was led by Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats. The vote Tuesday may only delay an impeachment push against Hegseth, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take charge in January, stood firmly behind the push, saying Hegseth has “abused his power” and “undermined America’s national security.”
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer endorsed Hegseth’s impeachment as well.
Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, portraying Massie as a rogue lawmaker and arguing he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal. He framed the effort as an indictment against the nation’s service members and their successes and said it was undermining American forces “in real time.”
“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth said. “This is sabotage.”
Massie’s resolution included eight counts of impeachment. It largely focused on the war in Iran but also included references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican leaving Congress in January after losing his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, says Hegseth has “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders.”

sources.text:
Thomas Massie's Attempt To Impeach Pete Hegseth Is Derailed
The House voted 211-204, largely along party lines, to refer the impeachment effort to a committee, effectively killing the proposal.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth will keep his job—at least for now.
A congressional motion to impeach Hegseth over his handling of the Iran War and other conduct, like the Pentagon's extrajudicial killings of suspected drug traffickers, failed to clear a key procedural vote on Tuesday evening in the House of Representatives.
The House voted 211-204, largely along party lines, to refer the impeachment effort to a committee, effectively killing the proposal.
Rep. Thomas Massie (R–Ky.), who led the impeachment effort, was the only Republican to vote against sending it to committee.
Massie said on the House floor on Monday that Hegseth had "demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution, if allowed to remain in office."
Massie filed eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth. Four of them focus on the war in Iran. Massie claims Hegseth violated the War Powers Resolution by launching the war without evidence of an imminent threat against the United States, continuing the war after Congress passed a resolution ordering the conflict to end, and ignoring the withdrawal deadlines Congress set in that order. Hegseth has "treated mandatory statutory deadlines as discretionary," the articles claim.
The final article on Iran has to do with the February 28 strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School, which killed more than 100 civilians, many of them children. Pentagon officials ignored warnings about outdated intelligence in the lead-up to that attack.
Massie's fifth article charges Hegseth with ordering "extrajudicial killings" in counternarcotics operations off the coast of Venezuela. On the House floor, Massie said that Hegseth "asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die" without authorization from Congress or evidence of a clear threat to American forces or interests.
Other articles of impeachment focus on American military conduct in Venezuela and Yemen, and on Hegseth's attempt to illegally retaliate against Sen. Mark Kelly (D–Ariz.) after Kelly criticized him.
During a fiery press conference on Tuesday morning, Hegseth said the orders he'd given during the Iran War were legal and ordered by Trump—and, in fairness, the commander in chief probably should be the person held accountable for the war.
Despite the failed impeachment, Hegseth's future as the head of the Pentagon is uncertain. Trump said this week that he would "stand by" Hegseth despite the impeachment effort, but the president has also said that Hegseth was "one of the guys most responsible" for the war with Iran, which played a major role in Republicans' midterm election losses a week ago. Democrats could also try to oust Hegseth after they assume control of Congress in January.
"After Tuesday's electoral shellacking, GOP members should be looking for clear opportunities to distance themselves from Trump's disastrous and unnecessary war," wrote Reason's Gene Healy last week as he urged lawmakers to impeach Hegseth. Doing that would serve an important secondary purpose too: reinvigorating "a valuable constitutional weapon."
It's a shame that Republicans in the House missed their best opportunity to do that. Voters sent a clear, decisive signal about the Iran War last week. Congress should listen to that, rather than protecting a rogue defense secretary who remains a threat to the constitutional order.
