sources.news_title: US Lawmakers Reject Move to Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth
sources.text:
The US House of Representatives rejected an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his conduct in office and handling of the war in Iran, with Republicans largely backing the Pentagon chief despite growing political pressure on the administration.
The vote on Tuesday followed significant Republican losses in the midterm elections, which some party members have linked to the Iran conflict and the resulting rise in fuel prices. However, President Donald Trump had signalled strong support for Hegseth, prompting most Republican lawmakers to oppose the impeachment initiative in a largely party-line vote.
The resolution was introduced by Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky and supported by Democrats. The vote may delay, rather than end, efforts to remove Hegseth, as Democrats are expected to take control of both the House and Senate in January.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next House speaker, backed the impeachment effort, accusing Hegseth of abusing his authority and undermining US national security. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer also endorsed the move.
Hegseth calls impeachment effort 'sabotage'
Hegseth criticised the impeachment initiative during his first news conference in months, describing Massie as a rogue lawmaker and arguing that he had committed none of the constitutional high crimes required for removal from office.
He also portrayed the resolution as an attack on US service members and their military achievements, warning that the effort was undermining American forces while operations were underway.
“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth said. “This is sabotage.”
Resolution cites military operations in Iran and beyond
Massie's resolution outlined eight articles of impeachment, focusing primarily on the war in Iran while also referring to Hegseth's role in military operations in Yemen and Venezuela.
The Kentucky Republican accused the defense secretary of knowingly carrying out and implementing unlawful orders. Massie is set to leave Congress in January after losing his primary election to a candidate backed by Trump.
Although the House vote has blocked the immediate impeachment push, the expected change in congressional leadership in January could give Democrats another opportunity to pursue the issue.

sources.news_title: Hegseth survived impeachment but oversight is coming
sources.text:
Hegseth survived impeachment but oversight is coming
Self-styled Secretary of War Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment Tuesday night, as solidarity from House Republicans blocked a bill introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., charging Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors.”
Though Democrats overwhelmingly joined Massie’s effort following their midterm election landslide, the House voted 211 to 204 to refer the charges to a committee, allowing Republicans to slow the process. With 11 Democrats absent, they lacked the numbers. Massie, however, dismissed the impact of Democratic absences to The Intercept. “No, there were enough Republicans to rally to get here,” he said.
The procedural vote spared Republicans a more difficult vote on whether to impeach Hegseth on Massie’s eight charges, including waging wars without Congressional authorization and undercutting measures to prevent civilian casualties. It followed a week of increasingly desperate efforts by the Pentagon chief to shore up Congressional and White House support, including a campaign-style video intended to influence Trump, a social media campaign by underlings, and a rare appearance by Hegseth himself before the Pentagon press corps.
Over half an hour on Tuesday morning, Hegseth wove a web of lies designed to refute or obfuscate Massie’s eight charges. He claimed that the effort to impeach him was a stunt by just “one disgruntled congressman.” That, too, turned out to be false as 203 members of Congress voted with Massie.
On Tuesday, a coalition of more than 40 civil society organizations – including Oxfam America, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), Common Defense, Demand Progress, MoveOn, and the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft – sent a letter calling on all House members to vote for every article of impeachment filed against Hegseth.
